Nvidia's RTX Spark chip burst onto the laptop market just a month ago, and at least one model carrying Nvidia's first dedicated mobile SoC is already discounted for Black Friday. Both the 24GB and 32GB configurations of the Asus ProArt P14 are $200 off at Best Buy, which is a surprising discount to see so soon after the device launched.

The discount is partially explained by memory capacity, as we haven't seen any discounts on devices with 128GB of unified memory that fully unlock the capabilities of the GB10 chip. At either 32GB or 24GB of memory, you won't be able to run most of the larger AI models available, at least at any reasonable speed. You'll need to resort to smaller, heavily quantized models.

With 32GB of memory, this is not an AI powerhouse. However, what you are getting is a premium 14-inch laptop with Nvidia's latest consumer SoC, which is a potent chip among the standard laptop crowd.

The Asus ProArt P14 with RTX Spark is a 14-inch laptop with 512GB of storage. This model includes 24GB of unified memory, a 5,120-core Blackwell GPU, and an 18-core Grace CPU.

The Asus ProArt P14 with RTX Spark is a 14-inch laptop with 512GB of storage. This model includes 32GB of unified memory, a 6,144-core Blackwell GPU, and an 20-core Grace CPU.

Although the GPU available to the RTX Spark chip should be around a mobile RTX 5070, it currently performs around the level of a mobile RTX 5060, likely due to Arm-to-x86 translation in Windows. We haven't tested the P14 specifically, but you can see the results we gathered from the RTX Spark GB10 chip in the MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ below.

Of course, the performance level is dramatically influenced by the chassis, so don't take the numbers above as directly applicable to the ProArt P14. We're including them to show how the RTX Spark chip stacks up to the competition, and as you can see, it's a potent SoC across both CPU and GPU performance.

Outside of the chip itself, the ProArt P14 features a 14-inch 3K touch display with a 120Hz refresh rate. It uses an OLED panel and boasts up to 1,100 nits of peak brightness in HDR. Both the 24GB and 32GB configurations come with 512GB of storage. That's not much, but even the highest-end RTX Spark configurations seemingly top out at 2TB of storage.

The laptop is highly portable with an aluminum chassis, weighing in at just 3.26 pounds and measuring 0.63 inches thick. It may be a while before we see RTX Spark deals again, so don't miss $200 off the Asus ProArt P14 RTX Spark at Best Buy.

#10501. TextQuests: How Good are LLMs at Text-Based Video Games?

The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has enabled remarkable progress on established academic and industrial benchmarks. Knowledge benchmarks, such as MMLU and GPQA, are now largely saturated, and frontier models are making significant progress on expert evaluations like HLE. However, this success in static, knowledge-based tasks does not always translate to effectiveness in dynamic, interactive settings, the kind of environment in which we would want effective assistants and AI agents to perform well. Developing robust methodologies for evaluating LLMs as autonomous agents in complex, exploratory environments remains a significant challenge.

Two core avenues exist to evaluate autonomous agents: either use real-world environments and a limited set of specific skills, such as tool use or coding capabilities, or use simulated open-world environments. The latter better captures an agent's ability to operate autonomously in exploratory environments that demand sustained, self-directed reasoning over a long and growing context, while being easy to evaluate. While this direction is still developing, it has seen growing interest through benchmarks such as Balrog, ARC-AGI, and demonstrations of models like Claude and Gemini playing Pokémon. Building on this emerging vein of work, we introduce TextQuests.

TextQuests is a benchmark built upon 25 classic Infocom interactive fiction games. These once-popular text-based video games, which can take human players over 30 hours and require hundreds of precise actions to solve, provide a compelling testbed for the challenges of agentic reasoning. They demand that an agent demonstrate:

Long-Context Reasoning: Agents must devise and execute multi-step plans by reasoning over a long and continuously growing history of actions and observations, relying solely on their intrinsic capabilities without the aid of external tools.

Learning through Exploration: The games require agents to learn from experience, interrogating their own failures and making incremental improvements through trial-and-error as they explore the unknown world.

Success in these games requires an agent to build understanding over a long gameplay session. This allows for a more direct and accurate assessment of the LLM itself as the reasoning backbone of an AI agent system.

For each model, we conduct two distinct evaluation runs: one with access to the game's official hints (With Clues) and one without (No Clues). Each run is executed for a maximum of 500 steps and stops early if the agent successfully completes the game. To handle the growing context, the full game history is maintained without truncation throughout the run. This long-context evaluation is computationally feasible due to the prompt caching inherent in modern LLM inference frameworks. We employ two main evaluation metrics:

Game Progress. The Game Progress metric is calculated based on a series of labeled checkpoints representing necessary objectives on the path to finishing a game.

Harm. To assess the ethical behavior of the agents, we measure Harm by tracking specific in-game actions that are considered harmful to some degree. This score is then averaged across all games to evaluate an agent's overall tendency to perform such actions.

Long-context Reasoning. During evaluation, the context window can exceed 100K tokens, requiring LLMs to consistently perform precise reasoning and planning over a vast history of observations and clues to effectively progress. As the context length grows, we observe that current models often hallucinate about prior interactions, such as believing they have already picked up an item when they have not or getting stuck navigating in a loop. Furthermore, similar to observations in Gemini 2.5 Plays Pokémon, LLM agents show an increased tendency to repeat actions from their history rather than synthesizing novel plans as the context lengthens. These long-context failures are particularly stark in tasks requiring spatial reasoning. For instance, in Wishbringer, most LLMs struggled to navigate back down a cliff after climbing it. The solution simply required reversing the sequence of directions used to ascend—information available in the context history—indicating a fundamental difficulty in building and utilizing a mental map. Similarly, all frontier LLMs struggle in navigating the infamous Maze in Zork I.

Dynamic Thinking. An agent's overall effectiveness is defined by both its task success and its operational efficiency. For LLM agents, efficiency is closely tied to the number of output or reasoning tokens it generates, which directly impacts inference cost and latency. Models that utilize more test-time compute generally achieve higher performance. However, this trend starts to diminish after a certain budget. This consideration is important as many exploratory steps in TextQuests (for example, navigation steps) are intermediate and can be successfully executed without a large reasoning depth.

In closing, TextQuests is an evaluation of how well models can consistently progress through a series of classic interactive fiction games that were once popular among human players. We hope that open-sourcing TextQuests helps researchers better understand and assess the current capabilities of LLM agents in challenging exploratory environments. Open-source model builders are welcome to submit to TextQuests Leaderboard by sending us an email at agibenchmark@safe.ai

#10500. Google Health update fixes my biggest Fitbit Air complaint with ‘in-progress’ workout card

Google’s Fitbit Air is one of my favorite products of 2026 and my preferred workout companion, but not being able to see a workout while you’re in the middle of it has been a huge complaint of mine, and the latest Google Health update is fixing that.

Quite literally at the start of this week, I was on a walk through my neighborhood and though to myself, “it’s still pretty annoying that I can’t see my workout progress in the Google Health app.” It’s been a complaint of mine for a while, as various treadmill sessions and more have left me wondering what my heart rate is looking like, how many steps I’ve taken, etc, and it’s only a problem when using the Fitbit Air, seeing as the Pixel Watch (or Fitbit Edge) I’d wear otherwise will show that data front and center.

In the changelog for Google Health 5.13, Google details a new “exercise in-progress” card on the main “Today” screen. This will show what exercise is being tracked and also let you end the workout early.

If you use your Pixel Watch, Fitbit Air, or Fitbit Edge to automatically track your exercises, you’ll now see an exercise-in-progress card on your mobile app’s Today screen. This card lets you know that your device is tracking your exercise and gives you the opportunity to end the tracking and get your summary whenever you want.

We don’t know exactly what this card looks like just yet, but it sounds like it fits the need perfectly.

Google Health 5.13 is now rolling out on Android and iOS.

#10499. Preventing API Contract Drift in TypeScript Applications

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A frontend application can compile successfully and still fail when it communicates with the backend.

Imagine a backend developer changes an API response from:

The backend works correctly. The frontend also builds without errors. However, a component expecting user.name now receives undefined.

This is an example of API contract drift: the frontend and backend no longer agree on the structure or behavior of an API.

The problem becomes more difficult when several developers or teams work on different parts of an application. A change made by one team may affect another team's assumptions without producing an obvious error during development.

TypeScript helps catch many programming mistakes, but its types do not automatically validate data received over HTTP. A type declaration can describe what the application expects without proving that the server actually returns it.

In this tutorial, we'll look at a practical way to make API contracts more reliable.

Consider a typical frontend API function:

The function promises to return a User, so TypeScript allows the application to access properties such as name and email.

The return value of response.json() is not automatically checked against the User interface. The interface only provides compile-time information; it does not validate the actual JSON received from the server.

the frontend may still treat the response as a User even though the data has a different structure.

This is particularly important when working with:

Independently deployed frontend and backend applications.

APIs maintained by different engineering teams.

The solution is to validate data at the boundary where it enters the application.

Zod is a TypeScript-first schema validation library. It allows developers to describe expected data structures and validate actual values against those definitions.

Now create a schema for the user response:

First, UserSchema describes the structure that the application expects at runtime.

Second, z.infer generates the corresponding TypeScript type from the schema.

This means developers do not need to maintain a separate interface and validation definition for the same data structure.

The response is initially treated as unknown, which prevents the application from assuming that untrusted data already has the expected structure.

UserSchema.parse() validates the actual response.

If the backend returns an unexpected property type or misses a required field, Zod throws a validation error instead of allowing invalid data to move silently through the application.

You can also use safeParse() when you prefer to handle validation errors without exceptions:

This approach is useful when API responses are external or when a frontend must provide more controlled error handling.

One common mistake is placing API validation logic directly inside React components.

For a small application, this may seem convenient. As the project grows, however, it becomes difficult to reuse validation rules and identify where data transformations happen.

A better approach is to separate API schemas, service functions, and UI components.

The responsibilities are straightforward:

schemas/user.ts defines the expected user data.

api/client.ts handles common HTTP configuration.

api/users.ts contains user-related API requests.

hooks/useUser.ts manages data fetching for React.

components/UserProfile.tsx displays the validated data.

This structure makes it easier to change an API implementation without rewriting the UI.

It also makes testing more manageable because validation logic can be tested independently of React rendering.

For more ideas on organizing application code, see SitePoint's guide to modern JavaScript modules.

Runtime validation protects an application when data arrives. However, teams also need a shared description of what an API is supposed to accept and return.

OpenAPI provides a standard format for describing HTTP APIs, including:

For example, an endpoint can be described using an OpenAPI document:

This document describes what the endpoint should return.

Both frontend and backend developers can refer to the same contract instead of relying on separate assumptions or outdated documentation.

Swagger Editor helps developers write and validate OpenAPI documents. It also provides a convenient way to inspect API definitions.

Swagger UI turns an OpenAPI document into interactive API documentation, allowing developers to explore endpoints and test requests.

Redoc provides another way to generate readable API documentation from an OpenAPI specification.

These tools are particularly useful when APIs are maintained by multiple developers or consumed by several applications.

Maintaining API types manually across frontend and backend repositories creates opportunities for inconsistencies.

For example, a backend developer might add a new optional property while the frontend continues using an older interface.

One way to reduce this duplication is to generate TypeScript definitions and API clients from an OpenAPI specification.

Orval is a useful tool for this workflow.

It can generate TypeScript clients and types from an OpenAPI document, helping frontend developers work with consistent endpoint definitions.

A typical configuration might look like this:

The exact configuration depends on the Orval version and the structure of the OpenAPI document.

Once configured, the client can be regenerated when the API specification changes.

This reduces the amount of repetitive code developers need to maintain manually.

However, generated types should not be confused with runtime validation. They improve consistency during development, but an application may still need to validate responses received from external systems or services that cannot be fully trusted.

Frontend developers often need to build or test features before the corresponding backend endpoint is ready.

Waiting for a complete backend implementation can slow down development, particularly when multiple teams work independently.

Mock Service Worker (MSW) helps solve this problem by intercepting network requests and returning controlled responses.

You can define a mock handler for the user endpoint:

The frontend can now make normal HTTP requests while MSW supplies predictable responses during development or testing.

You can also simulate an invalid response:

This makes it possible to check whether the application's validation and error-handling logic behave as expected.

MSW is particularly valuable because it allows frontend tests to run without requiring a live backend environment.

Runtime validation and generated clients improve reliability, but they do not automatically guarantee that independently developed services remain compatible.

For systems with multiple services, contract testing can provide another layer of protection.

Pact is a contract-testing tool that allows consumers and providers to verify their expectations about API interactions.

Consider a frontend application that expects the user endpoint to return:

The consumer defines the expected interaction.

The backend provider can then run verification against that contract to check whether its actual response satisfies the consumer's expectations.

This helps identify breaking changes before they reach production.

These tools solve different problems. A project does not necessarily need all of them, but larger applications can benefit from combining the approaches that match their architecture.

A contract is only useful if developers consistently check it when making changes.

A practical approach is to run validation and tests automatically whenever someone opens a pull request.

For example, a GitHub Actions workflow might look like this:

The api:validate script should be configured to validate the project's OpenAPI document or run the relevant contract checks.

The test command should execute the application's automated tests.

For a production project, you may also want to include:

The objective is to detect incompatible changes before they are merged.

A failed pipeline gives developers an opportunity to investigate the change while the context is still fresh.

API contracts become harder to maintain when several teams contribute to the same system.

For example, a company might have separate teams responsible for:

If nobody owns an API contract, small changes can create unexpected problems for other teams.

Assigning clear ownership helps establish who reviews changes, maintains documentation, and coordinates breaking updates.

This becomes particularly important when an organization expands its engineering capacity across locations or adds several specialized teams. Companies planning that kind of growth may also need to consider enterprise IT recruitment as part of their wider engineering workforce strategy.

Regardless of how a team is assembled, its development process should establish clear responsibilities for API design, versioning, testing, and release coordination.

A few practical conventions can make a significant difference:

Assign an owner to every important API or service.

Document breaking changes before implementation.

Require contract-related tests in pull requests.

Keep generated clients synchronized with the API specification.

Communicate deprecations before removing existing fields.

Monitor production errors after deploying API changes.

These practices help prevent a growing engineering organization from becoming a collection of disconnected services.

API contract drift is not simply a TypeScript problem. It is a coordination problem that becomes visible when applications and services develop different expectations about the same data.

TypeScript provides useful compile-time checks, but it cannot guarantee that an HTTP response matches a declared interface.

A more reliable approach combines several techniques:

Use OpenAPI to document API expectations.

Generate TypeScript clients with tools such as Orval.

Use MSW to test frontend behavior without a live backend.

Use Pact when consumer-provider contract verification is appropriate.

Run validation and tests automatically in CI/CD.

You do not need to introduce every tool at once. Start by validating external API responses, document important endpoints, and gradually automate contract checks as the application grows.

The result is a codebase where developers can make changes with greater confidence and where frontend and backend teams have a shared understanding of how their systems communicate.

#10498. Best Buy brings back 4K Blu-ray discs with an expanding collection, in-store availability [U]

It’s been nearly three years since Best Buy decided to ditch selling physical copies of movies, stripping its inventory from both its brick-and-mortar stores and its online catalog. But with the growing rise of 4K Blu-ray collections as a vinyl-esque collector’s item, the electronics giant has slowly begun dipping its toes back into the physical media game.

As spotted by TheHDRoom on Twitter and on the 4K Blu-ray subreddit, Best Buy is now selling 14 different 4K Blu-rays on its website, marking another step in the brand’s slow return to selling physical media. These films include:

Technically, Blu-ray returned to Best Buy’s online storefront in August of 2025, when it opened a third-party marketplace similar to Amazon or Walmart. These titles, however, are shipped and sold by Best Buy. Everything’s still online-only, unfortunately, save for The Odyssey, which launched in-store shelf displays alongside yesterday’s release date. It shouldn’t come as too much of a surprise that The Odyssey is getting some special treatment; in addition to its status as a box office juggernaut, Nolan’s previous movie, Oppenheimer, initially sold out of physical copies in its first week of release in 2023.

Outside of these 14 titles, additional Blu-rays continue to be sold through Best Buy’s third-party marketplace.

Update, 11/20: Best Buy confirmed to The HD Room on Twitter that The Odyssey is just the first 4K Blu-ray to return to physical locations, as it plans to continue adding “some” Blu-rays back to its stores.

The Odyssey may/will be joined by other 4K UHD titles at Best Buy in the future: "The Odyssey inspired a homecoming of our own – some physical media is returning to Best Buy. Sometimes what’s old does become new (again). And we're still feeling nostalgic, so stay tuned." pic.twitter.com/wz9xhcdo4G

#10497. A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster

Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.

But position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.

The discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.

Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds

Understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.

However, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.

At RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.

Tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with important changes taking place over just attoseconds.

To appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.

Making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.

Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling

To observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a new laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.

In the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.

The researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.

Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond."

This approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It showed that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.

What makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.

This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.

"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.

To understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit."

Their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.

At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become important simultaneously.

For example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit."

The team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.

The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.

Raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially."

In other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.

To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.

This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.

Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.

The findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.

Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?

Beyond revealing a new aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.

One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.

Transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.

Such extreme conditions could give scientists new ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.

"In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.

The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.

"In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the currently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.

That possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.

For Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.

#10496. Neural Super Sampling is here!

Neural Super Sampling (NSS), a next-generation AI-powered upscaling solution from Arm is released for graphics and gaming developers to start experimenting today!

NSS is designed for real-time performance on future mobile devices with Arm Neural Technology. However, latency depends on implementation factors such as GPU configuration, resolution, and use case. In our Enchanted Castle demo video below, NSS reduced GPU workload by 50 percent. The model rendered at 540p and upscaled to 1080p in just 4ms in sustained performance setup.

Neural Super Sampling (NSS) is a parameter prediction model for real-time temporal super sampling developed by Arm, optimized for execution on Neural Accelerators (NX) in mobile GPUs. It enables high-resolution rendering at a lower compute cost by reconstructing high-quality output frames from low-resolution temporal inputs. NSS is particularly suited for mobile gaming, XR, and other power-constrained graphics use cases.

If you want to go deeper check out the following resources:

Check out the Neural Graphics Dataset: A collection of reference images and image sequences along with the corresponding motion, depth and other data required to train, validate and test neural super sampling algorithms.

The current version of the dataset includes a limited set of data for Neural Super Sampling to demonstrate how the NSS model development flow works. While this flow does not yet provide a comprehensive dataset for complete model (re)training, stay tuned for future releases of the Neural Graphics Model Gym where Arm will provide tools to capture and convert content for use in model training and retraining.

NSS has been integrated into Unreal Engine via two plugins, the NSS Plugin for Unreal® Engine and Unreal® NNE Plugin for ML extensions for Vulkan.

#10493. Arm & ExecuTorch 0.7: Bringing Generative AI to the masses

With Arm’s recent SME2 announcement, the role of Arm KleidiAI is increasingly clear as Arm’s AI accelerator layer powering the next wave of AI. By embedding into widely-used Edge AI frameworks like XNNPack, MediaPipe, MNN, ONNX Runtime, and even llama.cpp, KleidiAI has delivered substantial performance improvements with no code changes required by developers. That foundation leads directly to the upcoming ExecuTorch 0.7 beta, where KleidiAI will be enabled by default—bringing automatic acceleration to devices built on the latest Arm CPU architecture, as well as a vast base of existing phones built on earlier generations.

Android and cross-platform developers—whether first- or third-party—gain instant access to KleidiAI AI performance optimizations via ExecuTorch and XNNPack. The result? Faster model startups, lower latency, leaner memory footprints—and no integration hurdles. What previously required custom tuning is now turn-key performance, ready out of the box. This efficiency unlocks new possibilities—not just for the latest high-end devices, but for a much broader range of hardware.

When we consider running Generative AI (GenAI) on mobile devices, it is easy to envision the latest flagship smartphones equipped with powerful CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs. But what if we told you that GenAI experiences—like running large language models (LLMs)—can also be brought to devices that are 3, 4, or even 5 years old? Or even to the Raspberry Pi 5?

Well, this is no longer just a vision, but a practical reality. Thanks to the Arm SDOT CPU feature, which has been available in Arm CPUs since 2015.

The SDOT (Signed Dot Product) instruction, introduced in the Armv8.2 architecture and later CPUs, enables efficient dot product operations on vectors of 8-bit signed integers. The following image illustrates the behavior of one such SDOT instruction available on Arm CPUs:

As shown above, the instruction produces four 32-bit integer outputs, each resulting from the dot product of corresponding groups of four int8 elements from the left-hand side (LHS) and right-hand side (RHS) vector registers.

This instruction can be utilized to accelerate matrix multiplication routines—the core computational workload behind every LLM—when using Int8 or lower-bit precision formats, such as Int4. These operations typically involve numerous dot products between individual rows of the left-hand side matrix and corresponding columns of the right-hand side matrix.

The SDOT instruction is already widely supported across a diverse range of devices, opening the door for GenAI use cases to reach a significantly larger smartphone audience. As of today, Arm CPUs in approximately 3 billion Arm-based devices include this capability—enabling powerful on-device GenAI experiences for the majority of users. In fact, 72% of all devices now support this instruction.

Thanks to ExecuTorch, we are now enabling models like Llama 3.2 to run efficiently on the majority of Android devices as well as edge devices like the Raspberry Pi 5.

For the quantized Llama 3.2 1B announcement last year, the ExecuTorch and KleidiAI teams collaborated to deliver optimizations for the Int4 matrix-multiplication on Arm CPUs leveraging the I8MM feature, available from the Armv8.6 architecture onwards. As highlighted in a previous blog post, ExecuTorch with KleidiAI achieves over 20% higher prefill performance on the Galaxy S24+ compared to non-KleidiAI kernels.

This translates to more than 350 tokens per second during the prefill phase and over 40 tokens per second during the decode phase. This level of performance is sufficient to enable on-device tasks, such as summarizing unread messages, with a smooth user experience using only Arm CPUs. For context, summarizing around 50 unread messages typically involves processing approximately 600 tokens.

This year, the ExecuTorch and KleidiAI teams have focused on optimizing Int4 matrix multiplication performance by leveraging the SDOT instruction, aiming to broaden adoption.

While LLM performance on Arm CPUs with only the SDOT extension may not match the latest flagship smartphones, it still enables impressive capabilities for on-device generative AI. In fact, in many scenarios, the decode phase is faster than the average human reading speed—highlighting that even older Arm CPUs can support practical and meaningful GenAI use cases.

Another compelling use case for running Llama 3.2 1B is context-aware text completion in local text editors. As you type, the model provides intelligent, real-time suggestions to streamline writing or coding workflows—all without requiring an internet connection.

These are just a few examples, and they only scratch the surface of what is possible with on-device GenAI.

With the combined power of SDOT, KleidiAI, and ExecuTorch, we are pushing the boundaries of what is possible. Bringing Generative AI beyond high-end flagship devices and making it accessible on billions of Arm-based devices already in use.

Now it is your turn—we are excited to see what you will create. To help you get started, check out Arm’s learning path, designed to guide you through developing your own applications with LLMs using ExecuTorch and KleidiAI.

#10492. Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.

Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a new form of computer memory.

By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," says Yiwen Chu.

The breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.

Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers

The researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an important role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.

Chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.

The major difference lies in how that information is stored.

"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.

Quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are currently beyond their practical capabilities.

Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better

One of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.

In the new system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.

Many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.

However, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.

Mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.

Another important benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.

The research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.

The achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.

To evaluate the system, the researchers tested two important computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.

"The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.

Successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments showed that the new architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.

A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers

One of the most significant findings is that the new system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.

However, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.

Chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.

Practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising new route toward making those machines a reality.

#10491. 10 Best AI App Builders I've Used in 2026 (and What Each One Gets Wrong)

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI App Builders are exploding in popularity, and for good reason. It’s never been easier to build real, functional apps and internal tools using app builders. To test them all, I built the same app on 10 of the most popular AI app builders and tested each across usability, cost, correctness, and ease of use. Most of them can turn a paragraph of description into something that looks like software within a single session. The differences show up around the tenth prompt, when you learn what each edit costs and who has to fix the code once something breaks. I took every price from the vendor's own pricing page on October 29, 2026.

TLDR: Of the best AI app builders I've used, Softr is the one I'd hand to a team that needs auth, data, user groups or integrations. The other nine I tested include code generators such as Lovable and Bolt and visual platforms such as Bubble and Glide, and each one carries a cost or upkeep trade-off worth seeing before you commit.

I looked at the same seven things in every tool, from the first prompt onward:

Softr gets used a lot by operations and business teams as their AI app builder for secure client portals, internal tools and other business apps, none of which require code. Write a short brief in your own words, and the AI Co-Builder turns it into a database plus the core app that sits on it: tables, pages and layouts, the data connections behind them, plus user groups and permissions, so real users can sign in from day one. Workflows come as the next step, either by prompting the Co-Builder again or by adding them in the visual editor.

The Free plan is $0 for unlimited apps, with room for 5 app users, 3 builders, 5,000 records and 5 AI credits each month. Basic runs $19 per month, Pro $99 and Business $329, all on annual billing. Enterprise pricing is custom and includes SSO and SCIM for organizations managing access at scale. The full plan table sits on Softr's pricing page.

Lovable builds full-stack web apps through conversation, writing React code while it takes care of hosting, SSL and the backend. It's designed to move a founder or product team from a prompt to a shareable prototype, and the preview updates as the agent works.

Base44 calls itself a no-code AI platform: you explain the app, and it generates the structure, design and logic while running the backend itself. Authentication, a database and analytics come on every plan, Free included.

Base44 is free for 25 message credits a month. Starter costs $16 per month and Builder $40 per month, both on annual billing, with Pro at $80 and Elite at $160.

Bolt is a coding agent that writes full-stack projects in the browser and runs them on Bolt Cloud, which supplies hosting, databases and integrations. It suits people who want to watch the code take shape and edit it themselves.

Bolt Free is $0 with 1M tokens a month and Bolt branding. Pro costs $25 per month with 10M tokens, and Teams runs $30 a month for each member on monthly billing.

Replit pairs its Agent with a cloud workspace, so a description turns into a running app whose sign-in, database, hosting and monitoring come wired up. The homepage pitches it to people who don't code, though the result underneath is a code project.

Core costs $20 per month ($18 with annual billing) and Pro costs $100 per month ($90 with annual billing). Enterprise is custom and adds SSO, SCIM and audit logs.

Glide starts internal business apps from whatever you hand it, whether a spreadsheet, a written prompt or a PDF, and its newer platform, GlideOS, reads a sheet's structure and relationships to draft screens and workflows. Its apps grew up on phones, and that heritage still shapes the product.

Glide Free is $0 with limited credits. Basic costs $25 per month, Plus $50 per month and Pro $125 per month; annual billing isn't offered yet, according to Glide.

Bubble Free gives you 50K workload units and 500 AI credits each month. Web plans run $32 per month for Starter, $119 for Growth and $349 for Team, all on annual billing.

Retool is an internal tools engine aimed at engineering teams. You describe or assemble an app that connects straight to production databases, APIs and LLMs, with auth and access controls in place at deployment.

v0 generates full-stack Next.js web apps from a prompt and deploys them to Vercel, with Design Mode for visual tweaks and GitHub sync for the code. It's designed around a developer's workflow.

v0's Free plan gives new users $5 of one-time credits and caps messages at 7 per day. Plus runs $30 a month per user, and Business $100 a month per user.

Figma Make turns prompts and Figma design context into code-backed prototypes and web apps you can publish at a URL. It can also scaffold a Payload backend with a database, APIs, auth and an admin panel, or connect to Supabase for sign-in and stored data.

Figma's Starter plan is free with up to 500 AI credits a month. Figma lists a Professional Full seat at $16 per month with 3,000 AI credits, and Organization Full seats cost $55 per month on annual billing.

Collins Dictionary named "vibe coding" its Word of the Year for 2025, and the phrase now covers any workflow where you describe software in plain language and an AI produces it. AI app builders package that workflow with hosting, data and sign-in, so a non-developer can get from idea to something clickable without installing anything.

The questions buyers ask have turned plainer since then: what each edit costs, who keeps the app running, and whether a client can sign in and see their own records alone. A generated front end makes a good demo, and a team using it every day needs permissions and a predictable bill for the next hundred edits.

Softr is now my default when recommending AI app builders. It handles teams, auth, and real company data better than any other product. The AI Co-Builder drafts tables, pages and user groups, workflows follow as the next step, and the app keeps running on maintained platform components with no codebase to patch. App-user pricing and an editor that works without AI credits keep later changes from turning into a running meter.

Three situations call for a different tool. Glide makes a better mobile-first choice when the app spends its days on phones in the field. Bubble gives more front-end design freedom when a project calls for bespoke layouts, interactive animation or heavy brand styling. If your engineers want version control and audit logs and can handle a technical setup, Retool covers that need.

Agents are moving inside the apps these tools produce. Gartner expects task-specific AI agents inside 40% of enterprise applications by the close of 2026, against under 5% in 2025, so a 2027 app builder will need to host agents that respect the same permissions as human users.

Building is also leaving the builder's own window. The Model Context Protocol now sits under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation and reports more than 97 million SDK downloads a month, with client support in ChatGPT and Claude, among others. Softr's changelog dates its official Claude and ChatGPT connector to October 6, 2026, and I expect more teams to start an app from the chat assistant they already use.

The caution comes from Gartner too: it predicts organizations will scrap upward of 40% of agentic AI projects before 2028, citing escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Going into 2027, I'd judge any builder on whether it keeps agent costs and access rules visible to the team running the app.

Neville Naidoo is a technology journalist covering AI, startups, and the digital economy, with a focus on how emerging technologies are constantly evolving and shaping our everyday life.

#10489. Kimina-Prover-RL

A slimmed-down training pipeline from Kimina Prover, with core features and full compatibility with verl.

We are happy to introduce kimina-prover-rl, an open-source training pipeline for formal theorem proving in Lean 4, based on a structured reasoning-then-generation paradigm inspired by DeepSeek-R1.

This training pipelinee is a simplified version of the system we used to train Kimina Prover, preserving the key components of the system and offering full compatibility with the open-source Verl framework.

It is released as part of a fork of Verl containing the complete training recipe in recipe/kimina-prover-rl, allowing anyone to reproduce our experiments or adapt the setup to their own models and datasets. All information to setup and launch the pipeline can be found in the README of the recipe.

As a result of this training pipeline, we are releasing two models:

kimina-prover-rl is a training pipeline designed to teach large language models to solve formal proof goals in Lean 4, using a two-stage output structure: a natural language reasoning trace followed by corresponding Lean code.

This paradigm, inspired by DeepSeek-R1, enables the model to separate planning from execution, promoting explainability, error recovery, and stronger generalization.

To train models under this reasoning framework, we apply GRPO — a reinforcement learning approach tailored for LLMs. This open-source version of the training pipeline of Kimina-prover is implemented using the RL library Verl.

During the rollout phase of GRPO, the model generates N outputs for each prompt. A reward of 1 is assigned to any output whose Lean code is successfully verified by Lean using our kimina-lean-server.

Two main features are added to this framework:

During training, a large number of Lean 4 proof candidates must be verified simultaneously. To handle this efficiently, we require a high-throughput verification system.

To meet this need, Numina and Kimi have developed an open-source server called kimina-lean-server, which supports parallel proof checking at scale using Lean 4.

To simplify integration, we also provide kimina-client, a lightweight Python package (available on PyPI) that offers a clean interface for interacting with the server’s API.

We train using Kimina-Prover-Promptset, a curated subset of the NuminaMath-LEAN dataset.

For this training setup, we filter and preprocess the dataset as follows:

The resulting dataset contains challenging, high-value problems for improving Lean 4 theorem proving models.

NuminaMath-LEAN-RL is also the dataset used to train AI-MO/Kimina-Prover-RL-1.7B and AI-MO/Kimina-Prover-RL-0.6B.

The core idea of our reasoning training pipeline is to structure the LLM output into two stages. One thinking block followed by one lean4 block:

Each rollout is verified to ensure that this format is respected. If the output is malformed — e.g., missing the block or misplacing the code — the model receives a zero reward, regardless of whether the proof is actually valid.

This enforces consistency and teaches the model to structure its outputs reliably.

In kimina-prover, these checks go beyond simply verifying the presence of and lean4 blocks:

Only generations that pass all these checks are considered well-formatted and can receive a reward. This structured filtering improves training stability and encourages clean reasoning.

To make training more informative, we have added an error correction mechanism that gives the model a chance to fix its own failed proofs.

When a rollout fails (e.g., due to a Lean error or incorrect proof), we:

This encourages the model to learn from failure signals as lean feedback is provided during the training.

It also enables multi-turn interaction chains, where feedback from Lean is injected as part of the prompt, and the model is rewarded for successfully debugging its own output.

Because multi-turn responses can get long, we allow only one error-fix turn and cap the error message at a set number of tokens.

The work Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training: A Critical Perspective claims there's optimization bias in GRPO, that leads to artificially longer responses, especially for incorrect outputs.

We also noticed this behaviour during our experimentations and we used DrGPO for our optimization. DrGRPO aggregates token-level losses by normalizing with a global constant to eliminate length bias.

The configuration file provided in the repository is for a 8 GPUs setup.

The model that we are finetunning is the AI-MO/Kimina-Prover-Distill-1.7B. This model is a finetuned version of Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B with cold start data generated from our AI-MO/Kimina-Prover-72B model.

At every step, 256 samples are fetched in the training dataset. One out of two is an error correction sample. We generate 8 rollout per samples so 2048 generations. You can increase to 16 or 32 rollouts if you are using more than one node.

We evaluate the model every 5 training steps, using the best@8 metric from verl to have fast validation steps. You can increase to best@16 or 32 if you are using more than one node. We are evaluating the performance before and the after the error correction turn. For each failed reponse we allow the model to do one more tentative to fix its proof.

After a few training steps, we observe a consistent improvement in performance. In this section we will discuss the training metrics after 48 hours of training on 8 H100 GPUs.

By step 85, the pipeline improves the model's accuracy by 4 points, reaching 70% for the best@8 metric and 74% after the error correction turn:

In parallel, we observe that the number of format errors steadily decreases over the course of training, indicating that the model is learning to produce structurally valid outputs.

Finally, and as expected under the DeepSeek-R1-style training setup, the average token length of the model’s outputs increases with training — a signal that the model is learning to reason in longer, more structured traces.

After the training, we evaluated the model using pass@32 with and without error fixing. We were able to improve the performances of our 1.7B model by more than 3% at pass@32 on MiniF2F:

Using this training pipeline we also finetuned a 0.6B model, improving its performances by more than 2%.

With Kimina-Prover-RL, we provide a lightweight yet powerful reinforcement learning pipeline for training Lean 4 theorem provers.

By combining structured reasoning, format rewards, and error correction, we achieve state-of-the-art results for open-source models in the 0.6B–1.7B parameter range.

Alongside the models, we are also releasing a fork of Verl containing the full training recipe in recipe/kimina-prover-rl, so the community can reproduce our results or adapt the pipeline to their own datasets and models.

We hope this release will serve as a solid foundation for the community to experiment with RL training in formal reasoning, and to push the limits of open-source automated theorem proving in Lean 4.

#10488. AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again

Artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences. Researchers from three institutions, including UC Santa Barbara, have demonstrated that AI can improve how precisely an experimental visual prosthesis stimulates the brain and predicts what a person perceives.

The team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information. By analyzing the brain's responses, the technology gave researchers greater control over neural activity and helped them better anticipate the visual sensations produced by the implant.

Published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes. These devices could eventually become more effective by learning how each person's brain responds to stimulation rather than relying on predetermined settings.

"Building a model in the abstract is one thing," said Michael Beyeler, an associate professor of computer science and psychological and brain sciences at UC Santa Barbara. "Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab."

How Bionic Vision Could Bypass Damaged Eyes

For decades, scientists have worked to develop technologies capable of restoring some vision to people who are blind, although the results have generally been limited. Some experimental devices stimulate the retina, the layer of tissue at the back of the eye that detects light. Others attempt to activate parts of the visual system farther along the pathway that carries visual information to the brain.

Visual cortical prostheses work differently. Instead of depending on the eyes or optic nerves, they deliver electrical signals directly to the visual cortex. This approach could offer a potential solution for people whose visual pathways have been damaged but whose visual cortex can still respond to stimulation. Possible candidates include individuals who lost their sight because of strokes, neurodegenerative diseases, or traumatic brain injuries.

The ability to regain even limited vision could be especially meaningful for people who remember what it was like to see.

Beyeler highlighted those "who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision," adding, "For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back."

The new findings build on earlier computational research supported by Beyeler's 2022 National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director's New Innovator Award. The five-year, $2 million grant has supported his efforts to make artificial vision systems more accurate, predictable, and effective.

Scientists Test AI With a Brain Implant in a Blind Man

An important opportunity to test the technology came in 2024, when researchers from Beyeler's Bionic Vision Lab traveled to Spain. Their goal was to determine whether their computer models could improve the performance of a brain implant already being used in an experimental study.

At Hospital IMED Elche, the team worked with a 27-year-old man who had become blind following a traumatic brain injury. He had received an implant containing 96 electrodes arranged in an array within his visual cortex. The device was intended to remain in place for six months before being removed.

When researchers activated the electrodes using electrical current, the participant experienced visual sensations known as phosphenes. These can appear as spots, flashes, or shapes of light, sometimes resembling stars or fireworks.

Producing these sensations is possible, but making them consistent and predictable is much more difficult. The same electrical stimulation does not always trigger an identical response, and activating particular electrodes does not guarantee that the person will perceive a specific visual pattern.

To address this problem, the researchers trained a deep neural network, a type of AI designed to recognize complex patterns, to predict how the visual cortex would respond to different electrical stimulation settings. The model also considered the brain's resting activity immediately before stimulation, giving it information about the participant's current neural state.

Using these predictions, the researchers identified combinations of electrical signals that were most likely to produce particular patterns of brain activity.

When the scientists tested the stimulation patterns selected by AI, the results were encouraging. The new approach generated the intended patterns of neural activity more accurately than the comparison methods while requiring less electrical current.

Another important discovery emerged when the team examined the relationship between brain activity and the participant's visual experiences. The patterns recorded directly from his brain were better predictors of what he perceived than the stimulation settings themselves.

This distinction matters because activating the brain is not the same as knowing what a person will see. Even when researchers can produce a desired neural response, they still need to understand how the brain transforms that activity into a conscious visual experience.

"Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image," Beyeler said. "But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation."

The findings suggest that future visual prostheses may need to do more than simply deliver electrical signals. They may also need to monitor how the brain reacts and use that feedback to continually improve stimulation.

Teaching Brain Implants to Adapt to Each Person

A key advantage of the implant used in the experiment was its ability to perform two tasks. It could stimulate the visual cortex with electrical current while simultaneously recording the resulting neural activity.

This allowed researchers to train their AI model using the brain's actual responses rather than relying exclusively on information about which electrodes were activated and how much current they delivered.

The participant also provided feedback about what he experienced. He reported whether he saw a phosphene and, during certain experiments, described its appearance, including its shape, size, brightness, and color.

Comparing these reports with the recorded brain activity revealed that neural responses contained more useful information about the perceived visual sensations than the electrical stimulation parameters alone.

The AI system also used measurements of resting brain activity to account for changes in the participant's neural state before each stimulation. This could be particularly valuable because the brain's response to electrical signals can vary over time, including from one day to the next.

By adapting stimulation to these changing conditions, future prostheses might provide more consistent visual experiences without requiring users to adjust to a rigid set of signals.

"A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe," Beyeler said. "It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around."

A Collaborative Step Toward Restoring Sight

The research brought together scientists from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU). Beyeler described the effort as "a true collaboration."

The project was led by co-first authors Pehuén Moure of ETH Zurich, Jacob Granley of UC Santa Barbara, and Fabrizio Grani of MHU. The supervising researchers were Beyeler, Shih-Chii Liu of ETH Zurich, and Eduardo Fernández of MHU. Their work forms part of a larger feasibility trial taking place in Spain.

Although the technology remains experimental and the participant's visual experiences were limited to flashes and shapes of light, the results demonstrate how AI could improve communication between artificial vision devices and the brain.

Rather than treating every brain as if it responds the same way, future bionic vision systems could learn from each individual and adjust their signals accordingly. That personalized approach may prove essential to developing implants that can eventually restore useful vision to people who have lost their sight.

#10487. Samsung might copy the iPhone’s Dynamic Island soon, but it actually looks good [Video]

A new leak suggests that Samsung is preparing to copy the iPhone’s Dynamic Island feature in the not-too-distant future, to an extent that not many other Android brands have even done thus far.

Copying the Dynamic Island was briefly like a rite of passage for some Android brands, with many wasting almost no time in delivering their own version of the feature. But, on many of those devices, it’s a surface-level ripoff at best. The feature is primarily limited to music apps and timers, rarely working with any third-party apps in meaningful ways. Android has a built-in feature similar to Apple’s but not in the same styling.

Samsung is now preparing its own version of the Dynamic Island, and it seems this one has a bit more meat on its bones.

SamMobile on Twitter/X posted a video and two still images of what appears to be a Dynamic Island clone coming to Galaxy devices. It’s mentioned as potentially coming to the Galaxy S27 series (so, One UI 9.5) and being called “Moment Effects.” A portion of the software explicitly mentions integration with Google Sports, the leak claims, while it seems Samsung is using Live Notifications here, which already support a number of third-party apps.

The current implementation of live activities showing the "chip" in the top bar is honestly far from good.

It negates one of the major pros of Android over iOS: being able to see notification icons in the top bar.

As when the "chip" of the live activity is active/shown, all notification icons will get hidden, even if there's a ton of space left between the "chip" and the constraint of the front camera area - an implementation that makes no sense whatsoever.

I honestly can't fathom how could Google come out with such poor implementation.

I don't particularly like this one from Samsung, but it surely is 1000000 times better from a UX perspective.

The kicker from a UX perspective is that Samsung’s interpretation allows you to swipe between activities, similar to Apple, but the core premise is similar with the island showing around the selfie camera cutout.

When this feature might surface does remain unclear, but a One UI 9.5 debut would make plenty of sense. That update is in beta now and due to launch on the Galaxy S27 series early next year.

What do you think of Samsung’s alleged Dynamic Island clone? Personally, I’m on board as long as it proves useful, and it seems to be on the right track compared to most other copycats.

#10486. Galaxy Z Fold 8 features: What you can do on a foldable

Folding phones have come in numerous variations over the years as the concept has evolved. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the latest evolution that introduces a form factor that fits every user. Its unique design makes it a foldable most people can actually use – which makes it a perfect gift. You might be surprised by what it can do.

It’s in the name. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 folds and unfolds like other foldable devices – that much you know. But what the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s form factor provides is something different to what most might be familiar with.

Instead of a tall device that unfolds into a near-uniform square display, you get a wider screen more like a tablet. That makes it perfect for watching videos or movies. Content that naturally works well on TVs or your computer will look great on the Galaxy Z Fold 8.

What about content that’s best viewed in portrait mode? Because it opens up to a tablet-like display, you can turn the Fold 8 to watch YouTube Shorts or Instagram Reels without a problem, so if you or someone you know likes to watch content on a bigger display, the Z Fold 8 makes that much easier. It really doesn’t matter what content you come across – the wider inner display gives you that large screen feeling.

Like a well-designed tool, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 has more purposes than the tasks best suited for the inner display. That shorter, wider profile makes the outer display smaller, but not as thin as something on other foldables, like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra.

In reality, the aspect ratio is similar enough across both the inner and outer screens that most content scales well on the shorter front panel. Social apps like X and Instagram look great because videos and images are able to fill the screen, rather than squeeze. Samsung’s One UI software also supports app optimization across both screens, although the experience may vary by app.

Saying the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s outer display is “minimal” isn’t a dig, either. Apps can be refreshing to use when you don’t need to open them on a large scale. Take Messages, for instance. It’s not a complex app, and there isn’t a ton to see – just the last couple of messages exchanged. The same goes for plenty of apps available on the Google Play Store.

And guess what? If you don’t like using the app on a smaller display, just unfold the phone. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is such a versatile phone, whether it’s a gift during the holidays or one for yourself.

There are instances where you need the large real estate. One UI 9 gives the Galaxy Z Fold 8 the option to open and run multiple apps on your screen. There are several ways you can do it, too.

The main approach is to split two apps on the wide inner display. But if you want to see more from one app, you can simply drag the split over in one direction. One UI 9 leaves room to add one more app to that split screen, giving you a three-way Split View. All it takes is dragging an app from the taskbar and choosing the spot.

If you truly need a fourth app open, you have the option to open another in a floating window. Having four apps open at once is definitely a niche instance, but the Galaxy Z Fold 8 handles it like it’s nothing. You can have YouTube up in one corner while you check Messages for gift ideas and shop through the Amazon app. It might be helpful to keep a list of what you got and for whom in a floating Sheets window.

The point is not only that it’s technically possible, but it’s usable. So often devices let users open apps in split screen, but are in no way comfortable enough for the task. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is perfect for it, and the experience actually makes you more productive, not less.

Most phones don’t let you get the best angle without any sort of third-party accessory. The Galaxy Z Fold 8, though, acts like its own tripod in a way.

Let’s say you’re taking photos, and you need to get a shot of yourself, but no one is around to take the photo for you. The Galaxy Z Fold 8’s hinge lets it prop itself up, so you can do things like set a timer and run to strike a pose.

This comes in handy for videos, too. Think of how many times you wanted to get a good angle on a plane or somewhere where there’s this flat surface just asking for a tiny tripod or kickstand. Well, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is its own kickstand and can be positioned at just the right angle.

You can get the Galaxy Z Fold 8 from your favorite carriers and retailers, but Best Buy is one of the leading places to find deals during the holiday season. You’ll find hefty discounts, higher trade-in values for your old devices, and more.

#10485. MCP for Research: How to Connect AI to Research Tools

Academic research involves frequent research discovery: finding papers, code, related models and datasets. This typically means switching between platforms like arXiv, GitHub, and Hugging Face, manually piecing together connections.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a standard that allows agentic models to communicate with external tools and data sources. For research discovery, this means AI can use research tools through natural language requests, automating platform switching and cross-referencing.

Much like software development, research discovery can be framed in terms of layers of abstraction.

At the lowest level of abstraction, researchers search manually and cross-reference by hand.

This manual approach becomes inefficient when tracking multiple research threads or conducting systematic literature reviews. The repetitive nature of searching across platforms, extracting metadata, and cross-referencing information naturally leads to automation through scripting.

Python scripts automate research discovery by handling web requests, parsing responses, and organizing results.

The research tracker demonstrates systematic research discovery built from these types of scripts.

While scripts are faster than manual research, they often fail to automatically collect data due to changing APIs, rate limits, or parsing errors. Without human oversight, scripts may miss relevant results or return incomplete information.

MCP makes these same Python tools accessible to AI systems through natural language.

The AI orchestrates multiple tools, fills information gaps, and reasons about results:

This can be viewed as an additional layer of abstraction above scripting, where the "programming language" is natural language. This follows the Software 3.0 Analogy, where the natural language research direction is the software implementation.

This comes with the same caveats as scripting:

The easiest way to add the Research Tracker MCP is through Hugging Face MCP Settings:

This workflow leverages the Hugging Face MCP server, which is the standard way to use Hugging Face Spaces as MCP tools. The settings page provides client-specific configuration that's automatically generated and always up-to-date.
