#10449. Fine-tune Any LLM from the Hugging Face Hub with Together AI

The pace of AI development today is breathtaking. Every single day, hundreds of new models appear on the Hugging Face Hub, some are specialized variants of popular base models like Llama or Qwen, others feature novel architectures or have been trained from scratch for specific domains. Whether it's a medical AI trained on clinical data, a coding assistant optimized for a particular programming language, or a multilingual model fine-tuned for specific cultural contexts, the Hugging Face Hub has become the beating heart of open-source AI innovation.

But here's the challenge: finding an amazing model is just the beginning. What happens when you discover a model that's 90% perfect for your use case, but you need that extra 10% of customization? Traditional fine-tuning infrastructure is complex, expensive, and often requires significant DevOps expertise to set up and maintain.

This is exactly the gap that Together AI and Hugging Face are bridging today. We're announcing a powerful new capability that makes the entire Hugging Face Hub available for fine-tuning using Together AI's infrastructure. Now, any compatible LLM on the Hub, whether it's from Meta or an individual contributor, can be fine-tuned with the same ease and reliability you expect from Together's platform.🚀

Here's all it takes to start fine-tuning a HF model on the Together AI platform:

That's it! Your model will be trained on Together's infrastructure and can be deployed for inference, downloaded or even uploaded back to the Hub! For private repositories, simply add your HF token with hf_api_token="hf_xxxxxxxxxxxx".

As seen in the example above, when you fine-tune a Hugging Face model on Together AI, you actually specify two models:

Think of the base model as a "training template." It tells our system how to optimally allocate GPU resources, configure memory usage, set up the training pipeline, and prepare the model for inference. Your custom model should have a similar architecture, approximate size, and sequence length to the base model for optimal results.

As seen in the example above, if you want to fine-tune HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct (which uses Llama architecture), you'd use togethercomputer/llama-2-7b-chat as your base model template, because they share the same underlying architecture.

The integration works bidirectionally. Together AI can pull any compatible public model from the Hugging Face Hub for training, and with the proper API tokens, it can download models private repositories as well. After training, your fine-tuned model can be automatically pushed back onto the Hub if you've specified hf_output_repo_name, making it available for sharing with your team or the broader community.

In general, all CausalLM models under 100B params are intended to work. For a comprehensive walkthrough on how to choose base and custom models and much more, read our full guide!

This integration solves a real problem many of us have faced: finding a great model on Hugging Face but not having the infrastructure to actually fine-tune it for your specific needs. Now you can go from discovering a promising model to having a customized version running in production with just a few API calls.

The big win here is removing friction. Instead of spending days setting up training infrastructure or being limited to whatever models are officially supported by various platforms, you can now experiment with any compatible model from the Hub. Found a specialized coding model that's close to what you need? Train it on your data!📈

For teams, this means faster iteration cycles. You can test multiple model approaches quickly, build on community innovations, and even use your own fine-tuned models as starting points for further customization.

Beta users and early adopters of this feature are already seeing results across diverse use cases.

Slingshot AI has integrated this capability directly into their model development pipeline. Rather than being limited to Together's model catalog, they can now run parts of the training pipeline on their own infrastructure, upload those models to the Hub, and then perform continued fine-tuning of those models using the Together AI fine-tuning platform. This has dramatically accelerated their development cycles and allowed them to easily experiment with a broad variety of model variants.

Parsed has demonstrated the power of this approach in their work showing how small, well-tuned open-source models can outperform much larger closed models. By fine-tuning models on carefully curated datasets, they've achieved superior performance while maintaining cost efficiency and full control over their models.

Common usage we're seeing from other customers include:

The most significant advantage teams report is speed to value. Instead of spending weeks setting up training infrastructure or months training models from scratch, they can identify promising starting points from the community and have specialized models running in production within days.

Cost efficiency is another major benefit. By starting with models that already have relevant capabilities, teams need fewer training epochs and can use smaller datasets to achieve their target performance, dramatically reducing compute costs.

Perhaps most importantly, this approach gives teams access to the collective intelligence of the open-source community. Every breakthrough, every specialized adaptation, every novel architecture becomes a potential starting point for their own work.

As expected with a large feature of this nature, we're actively improving the experience based on real usage, so your feedback directly shapes the platform!

Start with our implementation guide for examples and troubleshooting tips. If you run into issues or want to share what you're building, hop into our Discord, our team is on there and the community is pretty active about helping each other out.

If you have any feedback about fine-tuning at Together AI or want to explore it for your tasks in more depth, feel free to reach out to us!

#10447. The 10-person board that voted to reinstate Nvidia’s CEO is also now under scrutiny

Jensen Huang has been under a spotlight for weeks, but after the 11-day period of disorder that included the resignation and reinstatement of the Nvidia executive, the company’s board is joining him at the center of scrutiny.

The 10-person board voted unanimously to rehire Huang as Nvidia’s president, CEO and a fellow board member, writing in an announcement Monday that the decision emerged after discussions with Huang and “input from senior levels of the United States government.” President Donald Trump said he believes his intervention was crucial to the reinstatement.

Just six days earlier, the board was singing a different tune. Board members had unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation following his admission that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The board did not intend to reinstate him, Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones said at the start of a quarterly earnings call.

“To bow to pressure to bring someone back who has hurt the reputation of the company is crazy,” said Kathleen Day, a lecturer at Johns Hopkins Carey Business School.

The board’s stunning reversal has spurred questions about its independence and what Trump’s role means for the meeting of business and politics.

Concerns swirl about corporate governance and Trump’s intervention

Nvidia’s board includes both business leaders with longstanding ties to the company and a group of more recent additions who have experience at big-name companies including Taco Bell, PepsiCo and Eli Lilly.

Some experts have called for the board to resign in the wake of the havoc.

Day, who has expertise in financial crises and corporate governance, emphasized that the board has a duty to represent shareholders, not the CEO.

“The shareholders should demand a new board,” she said.

Corporate governance experts say long tenures for board members can compromise their independence. Under the rules of the New York Stock Exchange and the Nasdaq, companies are required to have a majority of directors who are independent.

“Traditionally, it’s a good practice” to limit how long people can sit on a board, said Nada Kakabadse, professor of policy, governance and ethics at the University of Reading’s Henley Business School. “They should be eight years maximum. Four years, plus another four years if they’re performing well. But beyond that, they really become not independent anymore, right?”

It’s not unusual for U.S. tech bosses to stuff their boards with allies or high-profile figures who might not be aware of what’s happening at the company, Kakabadse said.

American business has a culture of “leader heroes” — entrepreneurs who founded companies and are seen as the only ones who can steer them through tough times, she said. But at some point, the companies can get so big that “you need proper corporate structure, you need proper governance.”

Many people are also questioning what “input” the company received from senior government leaders and why it persuaded the board to make a complete turnaround.

“The board should have listened to the president’s request and stuck to its position that it was time to find a new CEO,” said Peter Cohan, an associate professor of management practice at Babson College. “In my opinion, by giving in to Trump, the board is endangering the company. That’s because Huang has seen that he can do anything he wants, and he will get away with it.”

The idea of an independent board of experts looking out for the long-term interests of the company and its shareholders “sort of goes out the window” if the sitting president “essentially tells them what to do,” said Daniel Kinderman, a professor of political science and international relations at the University of Delaware.

“This is really the mark of crony capitalism, right?” he said.

Kinderman said the episode might “open the door a little bit more for more aggressive actions on behalf of elected representatives” in their relationships with businesses.

Lawmakers call for accountability from the board

The Nvidia saga has made waves in Washington, particularly in conversations around export controls. Huang’s affair raised questions about Nvidia’s compliance with those restrictions. The reinstatement has renewed fervor on Capitol Hill for more transparency from both Huang and the board.

Elected officials from both parties were quick to respond to the reinstatement with criticism and skepticism.

Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the incoming chair of the Senate Banking Committee, said the decision to bring Huang back was “reckless.” She wrote in a statement Monday that it does not change the fact that Huang, Nvidia executives and the company’s board “still owe Congress answers.”

Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, a New York Democrat, called for both Huang and the board to testify publicly to Congress. “A boardroom vote does not resolve a national security risk,” she said in a statement Monday.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who is investigating Nvidia in connection with Huang’s affair, said Tuesday in an interview with CNBC that the president’s intervention “does not bode well for enforcement of the law by the federal government without fear, without favor.”

The California Department of Justice said Thursday that it is asking Nvidia whether its advanced chips or confidential information may have gone to China and whether Nvidia misled investors and the public.

Some members joined the Nvidia board in the 1990s

Two board members, Mark Stevens and Tench Coxe, joined the board in 1993 when Nvidia was founded. Stevens and Coxe were both previously venture capitalists who made early investments in Nvidia.

Two other long-serving board members, Jones and Brooke Seawell, are the former chief executive and chief financial officer, respectively, of Synopsys, which makes chip-design software and counted Nvidia as its first customer. Jones joined Nvidia’s board in 1993, while Seawell joined four years later.

Stephen Neal, who’s designated as the board’s “lead independent director,” joined in 2019. He’s the chairman emeritus of Cooley LLP, Nvidia’s longtime law firm, and has advised the company in “various governance matters,” according to his bio.

Other board members have less of a direct link to Nvidia.

Melissa Lora, former president of Taco Bell International, spent 31 years at the fast food company and joined Nvidia’s board in 2023. Aarti Shah, formerly a senior vice president and chief digital officer at pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly, joined in 2020.

John Dabiri, an engineering professor at the California Institute of Technology whose lab researches fluid mechanics, was added to the board in 2020. Dawn Hudson was the NFL’s chief marketing officer and a former CEO of Pepsi-Cola’s North American division who’s been on the board since 2013. Suzanne Nora Johnson was a vice chairman at Goldman Sachs who joined the board in July.

None of the board members provided comment in response to requests from The Associated Press.

This story corrects that Shah joined the Nvidia board in 2020, not 2021.

—Kaitlyn Huamani and Kelvin Chan, Associated Press

#10446. Tricks from OpenAI gpt-oss YOU 🫵 can use with transformers

OpenAI recently released their GPT-OSS series of models. The models feature some novel techniques like MXFP4 quantization, efficient kernels, a brand new chat format, and more. To enable the release of gpt-oss through transformers, we have upgraded the library considerably. The updates make it very efficient to load, run, and fine-tune the models.

In this blog post, we talk about all the upgrades in-depth, and how they become part of the transformers toolkit so other models (current and future) can benefit from them. Providing clean implementations of new methods in transformers also allows the community to quickly understand and adopt them. Frameworks such as MLX, llama.cpp or vLLM can use the transformers code as a reference to build their own implementations.

Best part: Most of these features should work across all major models within transformers!

A kernel is a specialized, compact program that runs on accelerators to execute tasks like matrix multiplications, activations, or normalizations. In eager PyTorch, operations trigger individual kernels sequentially, which is straightforward but can incur extra memory transfers and launch overheads. PyTorch 2.0's torch.compile with backends like TorchInductor addresses this by automatically fusing and optimizing kernels, delivering 2–10× performance gains.

In addition, the community has created custom kernels for frequent combinations of operations, not just individual PyTorch ops like matmul. For example, Flash Attention was created to optimize the critical attention block that defines the transformers architecture, and is present in many models including most LLMs. By carefully combining all the attention operations inside a single kernel, memory transfers are minimized, memory use is reduced, and speedups can be achieved.

The problem is that all these various kernels are available in separate libraries, which creates a dependency bloat if they were to be added to the transformers library. Furthermore, these kernels are not just Python code, they consist of low-level cuda code, glued together with C++ and exposed through a Python layer. This means they have to be compiled in the target system, which in turn requires whatever build system is required by each kernel library.

The kernels package solves this problem by downloading pre-built binaries of supported kernels from the Hub. You just indicate the kernel you want to use, and kernels will look for a version compatible with your system and download it on first use.

GPT-OSS, a Mixture of Experts (MoE) model, is a big user of Kernels from the Hub. It leverages several custom kernels:

Behind the scenes, the decorators (1 and 2) simply point to community-contributed kernels. For example, RMSNorm comes from liger_kernels, while the MegaBlocksMoeMLP kernel comes from megablocks. Depending on your device (CUDA or ROCm) and whether you’re training or running inference, the right kernel is pulled in automatically.

This design is both specific and general: the RMSNorm liger kernels are already being reused across multiple models, and the MoE kernel could be applied to future MoEs as well.

Because kernels pulls code from the Hub, you have to opt-in to this feature by passing use_kernels=True in your model instantiation, as shown below. We enable INFO logging in the example so you can easily verify that downloadable kernels are in use.

These kernels are not compatible with mxfp4, so inference will happen in bfloat16 if you use them. Please, benchmark your system for the best combination in memory and throughput that suits your project!

Running a quick generation yields log messages like

Figure 1 shows that, in the system we tested, these kernels work best for larger batch sizes. We always recommend to benchmark any performance-related changes as closely to your production conditions as possible.

You can explore and play with the benchmarking script here

OpenAI gpt-oss models use attention sinks, which improves quality and facilitates the use of longer contexts. The vLLM team added this feature to the latest version of Flash Attention (Flash Attention 3), and the resulting custom kernel is available on the Hub. Currently, this kernel is compatible with the Hopper architecture. If you have one, this is the way to enable it:

Large language models are memory-hungry. Quantization reduces memory footprint by storing weights (and sometimes activations) in lower-precision formats. For reference, FP32 uses 32 bits per number and BF16 uses 16. By reducing bit width, we trade some precision for smaller models and faster memory movement.

If you want a visual primer on quantization trade-offs, Maarten Grootendorst’s article is excellent: A Visual Guide to Quantization.

MXFP4 is a 4-bit floating format with E2M1 layout: 1 sign bit, 2 exponent bits, and 1 mantissa bit, as shown in Figure 2. On its own, E2M1 is very coarse. MXFP4 compensates with blockwise scaling:

This blockwise scheme lets MXFP4 keep range while using very few bits. In practice, GPT-OSS 20B fits in roughly 16 GB of VRAM and GPT-OSS 120B fits in roughly 80 GB when MXFP4 is active, which is the difference between “cannot load” and “can run on a single GPU.” The catch is that matrix multiplies now have to respect block scales. Doing this efficiently at scale requires dedicated kernels.

transformers now includes native support for MXFP4, leveraging optimized triton (MXFP4) kernels for enhanced performance. This builds on the community-driven kernel distribution discussed earlier, utilizing pre-compiled kernels from the Hub to simplify deployment.

To check if a model supports MXFP4, inspect its configuration:

If 'quant_method': 'mxfp4' is present, the model will automatically use the MXFP4 pathway with Triton kernels when supported.

Thanks to this pull request, you can fine-tune gpt-oss models and save them directly to the Hub in MXFP4 format, streamlining deployment with optimized performance.

If these constraints are not met, transformers falls back to a higher-precision path (bfloat16 is used by default), which requires about 4× the memory of MXFP4.

The snippet loads GPT-OSS twice on CUDA: once with Mxfp4Config(dequantize=True) (memory intensive) and once in the default quantized path (memory efficient). Figure 3 shows the amount of used VRAM after each load so you can visualize the savings.

Efficient MXFP4 requires kernels that understand 32-element blocks and their scales during GEMMs and fused ops. This is where Kernels from the Hub comes in again. transformers automatically pulls in the MXFP4-aware Triton kernels from the community repository when you load a model that needs them. The repository will appear in your local cache and will be used during the forward pass. For the MXFP4 kernels one does not need to use the use_kernels=True parameter like before, it is set to default in transformers.

Quick sanity check with the Hugging Face cache CLI, after running gpt-oss-20b on a GPU compatible with the triton MXFP4 kernels:

This indicates the MXFP4 kernels were fetched and are available for execution.

Let's run some benchmarks and see how well the MXFP4 kernels perform. In Figure 4, we see that the MXFP4 kernels are even better than the custom MoE and RMSNorm kernels for larger batches.

You can explore and play with the benchmarking script here

Tensor Parallelism (TP) splits tensors inside a layer across multiple GPUs (as shown in Figure 5). Each GPU multiplies its shard in parallel, and then partial results are collected using all-gather or all-reduce operations. This reduces per-GPU memory and keeps all GPUs working on the same layer, which improves throughput as sequence length or batch size grow. TP is communication-intensive and generally works best on a single machine with fast intra-node links.

transformers implements TP directly in from_pretrained. You can start with the predefined plan:

If you don’t have the infrastructure to run the above, you can just spawn a process on our GPUs using Hugging Face Jobs!

hf jobs is available for all Hugging Face PRO & Enterprise users.

Under the hood, tp_plan="auto" selects a predefined sharding recipe for each layer and wires the necessary collectives. You can inspect the active plan with print(model._tp_plan) if you want to verify what is being sharded.

Use TP when the model is too large for one GPU and you want parallel compute, not only memory placement. TP tends to scale throughput with more GPUs, especially for long sequences or larger batches.

If you are curious about how TP differs from device_map="auto" (memory placement), this short Stack Overflow answer explains the distinction and when to use each.

To learn more about TP, here are two must-read resources:

Expert Parallelism (EP) shards experts inside MoE layers across GPUs. Each token is routed to one or a few experts, so only those experts run their feed-forward pass. Since experts are independent MLPs, we can place different experts on different ranks and exchange only the hidden states for the routed tokens. This keeps the matrix multiplies intact on each rank and replaces tensor slicing with routing and collectives.

Run with multiple processes using torchrun. EP is enabled via the distributed configuration and works with GPT-OSS MoE layers out of the box in transformers.

When you enable Expert Parallelism, Tensor Parallelism is also activated. This means you enjoy the best of both worlds!

Many recent LLMs use sliding window attention, or a combination of sliding and global attention layers, as a means to save memory and reduce those expensive quadratic matmuls that grow with sequence length. However, the dynamic KV cache implementation in transformers used to continue to allocate space according to sequence length, without looking at the individual attention layers. You could always optimize memory using compilation (meaning, fixed shapes), but that's a separate scenario altogether.

transformers now has a DynamicSlidingWindowLayer and a config‑aware DynamicCache. If the model config declares sliding‑window or hybrid attention (both sliding and global attention layers are used), the cache stops growing past the window for the sliding layers. If you don’t pass the config, behavior stays as before (full, ever‑growing KV as sequence length grows).

For models that only use sliding window layers, such as Mistral 7B, cache memory stops growing when the sequence reaches the window size (4096, in this case). This makes sense, because the sliding layers can't look past the previous 4K tokens anyway.

OpenAI gpt-oss alternates between sliding and global attention layers, which results in total KV cache memory being halved, as we'll see, as sequence length increases. This provides us with:

The optimized cache is set by default, that means you don't have to make any changes to your existing code. If you want to create the DynamicCache explicitly here is how you would do it:

Figure 6 showcases how much of a difference it makes for us to use the Dynamic KV Cache with sliding window attention.

A typical autoregressive generation process looks like Figure 7. You input the prefill tokens, and the model predicts each new token one after the other until it predicts the EOS (End of Sequence) token.

Let’s see what the generation process looks like when we pass a batch of inputs. In Figure 8 you notice that some generations finish off earlier than the others. This mismatch of length underutilizes the GPUs.

This type of batching sequences is called static batching. While this is simple and easy to understand, it inherently comes with inefficiencies. Only after each sentence is completely generated can we move on to the next batch.

To bypass this issue, we use dynamic batching (also known as continuous batching). Instead of waiting for all the generation to finish, we schedule incoming requests to the completed generations. That way, as soon as a generation in a batch is complete, we prefill the batch with the next request. The process looks like Figure 9.

Transformers supports continuous batching with the generate_batch API. This is not meant for production-grade model serving –frameworks like vLLM and SGLang are great at that–, but can be very helpful for evaluation and experimentation. Here is an example script that runs CB end to end on Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507.

We have also performed a benchmark between Continuous Batching and Static Batching with 100 samples. In Figure 9, we note that CB is quite faster than SB.

You can play around with the benchmark here: SB, CB

When you load a large model into your GPU, PyTorch needs to reserve GPU memory for each layer’s weights. Each of these requests (per layer) takes time, and for multi-billion-parameter models it can mean thousands of tiny memory allocations, adding up to a long wait before the model is ready. Instead of asking the GPU for new memory every single time, it can hold on to a big chunk once and then hand out slices from it quickly.

PyTorch allocators can do exactly this. The catch is that the allocator only gets fast after you’ve given it some memory to work with. If you don’t “stock the pantry” first, you still end up doing many slow trips to the market. This PR (🎉 #36380) taught transformers to pre-stock the pantry before it starts copying model weights.

You have to make no changes to your existing code, as this is default behaviour in transformers. If you use device_map="auto" or provide your own device map, your model will now load faster automatically. If you’re running with Tensor Parallel (tp_plan="auto") and torchrun you also benefit from companion changes that make multi-GPU loading smarter.

transformers moves quickly and it is community-first. The library evolves at the pace of the field because contributors shape it in the open. Pieces added for new models become part of the toolkit and are reused in future integrations.

This velocity enables day-zero integrations like the GPT-OSS series. As the stack becomes increasingly PyTorch-first, it trims bloat and doubles down on the PyTorch paths that matter in practice. The result is a cleaner core that unlocks new capabilities through community kernels, quantization, and parallelism plans, while also standardizing model definitions so that architectures supported in transformers are a reference and extend across the wider ecosystem.

This post is a one-time snapshot of a process we repeatedly iterate on towards the same direction: serve the needs of the community. To be up to date with the latest additions to transformers, check the docs and release notes. And please, keep sharing your feedback and releasing your models in transformers for the community to enjoy 🤗

#10445. I love YouTube on TV, but we desperately need better watchlist controls

Managing a YouTube watchlist shouldn’t be as frustrating as it is, especially on the most-used app in my life. Google’s premier streaming app has too many issues with resurfacing content; in my opinion, this is now a major problem that needs to be fixed.

Aside from my YouTube watchlist gripes, it’s no secret that moving from a web browser to the TV is ultimately still a frustrating experience.

Lots of things I love about watching videos on my laptop or PC just don’t translate well to when I’m sat on my sofa holding a remote trying to find something to watch after wrapping up for the day. One thing I’m getting annoyed with is how YouTube scales on TV and Android TV boxes because you’re given less choice and arguably poorer recommendations for content due to the constraints in place.

Understandably, you can’t compress the layout too much on a TV as you’re typically sat a few feet away and all aspects of the interface need to be legible. I would still like to tweak it, though, if that were possible.

Maybe we could get proper sections for content, like how Netflix and other streaming platforms offer categorized areas where you can search for “comedy” or “horror”. I’m almost certain that, with Google’s insane investment and massive AI push, where every video is already analyzed hundreds of times, that wouldn’t be too difficult to do.

The problem now is that the sidebar menu is just too broad. Gaming covers basically everything. Then each line of videos accounts for one title, but requires search and previous watch data to populate. I find myself often fighting with recommendations on my TV, whereas on desktop it’s not as much of a problem.

That leads me to my biggest problem with YouTube, and it’s the, frankly, embarrassing watchlist or “Watch later” controls.

I can’t fault that it works, but right now the watchlist function is like something out of the early 2000s due to the lack of flexibility that I touched on above. As my YouTube consumption has increased 20x over the past four or five years, managing what I want to come back to or might have missed the first time around is starting to become a bit of a chore.

I’ve tried using playlists to save things, but things get messy very quickly because of how cumbersome it is to a) create a playlist on TV and b) how playlists are organized by default.

Google TV isn’t perfect, but it’s where I keep my biggest TV and movie watchlist outside of YouTube. Yes, YouTube is mostly for user-generated content, but I would take something as basic as Google TV’s interface baked into YouTube somehow. Add in categorization and auto-clear.

The Watch Later section has become an unwieldy place that I never really want to go unless I desperately have to. I’m constantly losing videos that I hoped to come back to or have an affinity for.

Videos don’t clear automatically, nor do you know when they were added. Yes, I’ll give credit that you can sort by a few options, but that’s the bare minimum. The process of moving things around is slow and takes multiple taps. Watch Later is also hidden compared to other services. It’s under your account, then beneath “Liked videos,” which is below any you may have uploaded yourself.

On a TV, the process is so annoying I just avoid it altogether. You go to the sidebar menu > Library > Watch later. It should be front-and-center on a TV. It’s almost unforgivable in my eyes because even your watch history is given greater prominence. I simply cannot understand that decision.

I’m not always a huge fan of AI being shoehorned into apps and services, but this is one of those areas that has been left to rot for a while and could get a big uplift from adding in a little bit of Gemini. Even if it were just an enhanced search function or more tools for organizing.

With YouTube TV effectively taking over regular broadcast television and being the world’s biggest streaming platform, I’m shocked by how so many areas of the platform remain in a consistently neglected state.

A little bit of spit and polish, and maybe I’ll start using this section again. For now, though, I’ll stick to texting myself links of stuff I want to watch. The ball is in your court, Google.

#10444. Logging AI Prompts and Responses in Java Without Leaking Sensitive Data

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Picture this. A customer writes to your support chatbot: "Hi, I'm Asha, my card ending 4111 was charged twice, call me on 98400 12345." Your Java service wraps that message in a prompt, sends it to a model, and logs the whole thing so you can debug it later. Congratulations, you now have a customer's name, phone number and card details sitting in a plain text log file that half the engineering team can open.

This happens more often than people admit. Logging AI calls is genuinely useful, but prompts and responses are some of the most personal text your application ever touches. Here's how to keep the usefulness and drop the risk.

A regular web request is easy to log: URL, status code, time taken. AI calls are messier.

The output changes from run to run. If a user says "your bot gave me a wrong answer yesterday", the only proof of what happened is what you sent and what came back at that moment. You can't just replay it and expect the same result.

Prompts are also built, not typed. The final text is usually a template, a few retrieved document chunks, some chat history and the user's message stitched together. When something looks off, the bug could be in any of those pieces, and only the assembled prompt shows you which one.

Then there's cost. You pay by the token, so without per-call records you can't say which feature is burning money. And quality drifts over time as models get upgraded and templates get edited. Old logs are your only baseline.

So yes, you need these logs. The real question is what goes into them.

Before writing any masking code, agree on what counts as sensitive. In most business apps that means:

Names, emails, phone numbers and home addresses

Card numbers, bank details and government ID numbers

Health, legal or job-related details people mention in free text

Internal material like contract wording, pricing rules or source code

The first three groups follow patterns, so they're easy to catch. The last two don't, and that's where most teams get caught out. Keep that in mind, because it shapes the design below.

The safest sensitive value is the one that never reaches the log. So split what you record into two buckets.

The first is metadata: a request ID, a hashed user or tenant ID, model name, prompt template name and version, token counts, latency, retry count, error type and estimated cost. None of this is personal, and it answers most day-to-day questions.

The second is content, meaning the actual prompt and response text. You only need this when you're investigating quality, and even then you rarely need all of it. A sensible default is to log metadata for every call and masked content for a small sample, maybe five percent, plus every failed call.

Here's a mistake that's easy to make: letting the log appender clean things up afterwards. By then the raw text may already be in a buffer, an async queue or a crash dump. Mask first, then log.

The cleanest way is one small component that every AI log call has to pass through:

public interface PiiMasker {     String mask(String input); }

Nothing else is allowed to write raw prompts. One chokepoint is much easier to review and test than masking sprinkled across fifty classes.

For structured data like emails, cards and tokens, regular expressions do the job well:

public class RegexPiiMasker implements PiiMasker {     private static final Map RULES = new LinkedHashMap<>();     static {         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("[A-Za-z0-9.%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}"), "[EMAIL]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,19}\b"), "[CARD]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("\b(?:\+?\d{1,3}[ -]?)?\d{10}\b"), "[PHONE]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("(?i)bearer\s+[A-Za-z0-9.~+/=-]+"), "Bearer [TOKEN]");     }     @Override     public String mask(String input) {         if (input == null || input.isBlank()) return input;         String result = input;         for (var rule : RULES.entrySet()) {             result = rule.getKey().matcher(result).replaceAll(rule.getValue());         }         return result;     } }

A few small choices matter here. The patterns are compiled once, not on every call. The order is fixed, because a card number can otherwise get half eaten by the phone rule. And the replacement labels such as [EMAIL] keep the sentence readable, so whoever debugs it later can still follow what the user was asking.

Regex won't catch a name like "Asha Raman" or an address buried mid-sentence. For those you have a few options, and they work best together.

You can run a named-entity recognition model that tags people, places and organisations, then mask anything above a confidence threshold. You can do exact replacement of values you already know, such as the customer's name from the current session. Or, best of all, you can mask at the field level while building the prompt. If your code knows that customer.getEmail() is going into the template, swap in a placeholder right there instead of trying to spot it afterwards. Knowing beats guessing every time.

Plain redaction can remove too much. If the same email shows up five times in a conversation, five identical [EMAIL] tags hide the fact that it was one person.

The fix is consistent pseudonyms. Turn each real value into a short token using a keyed hash, so the same email always becomes something like EMAIL_7f3a. You can still follow the thread, but nobody can read the original from the log. Use an HMAC with a secret from your secrets manager. A plain unkeyed hash of a phone number can be brute-forced in minutes, because there just aren't that many phone numbers.

One warning: if you also store a lookup table to reverse the tokens, that table is now sensitive data too. Most teams are better off with one-way tokens.

Free-text log lines are hard to search and easy to leak through. Write one JSON record per AI call with clearly separate fields:

log.info("ai_call",     kv("requestId", requestId),     kv("model", model),     kv("promptVersion", "support-reply-v4"),     kv("inputTokens", usage.inputTokens()),     kv("outputTokens", usage.outputTokens()),     kv("latencyMs", elapsed),     kv("promptMasked", masker.mask(prompt)),     kv("responseMasked", masker.mask(response)));

Now dashboards for cost and latency never need to touch the text fields at all. You can also keep the two kinds of data for different lengths of time: metadata for a year, masked content for a couple of weeks. Put the request ID into your logging framework's MDC so every line belonging to one call, including retries and tool calls, carries the same ID.

Streaming trips people up. Tokens arrive in tiny pieces, and a card number can be split across two chunks, which means masking each chunk on its own will miss it. Collect the full response in a buffer, mask it once the stream ends, and log that. If the stream dies halfway, run the partial buffer through the same masker.

Tool calls are the other trap. When the model calls one of your Java methods, the arguments and return values are often the most sensitive thing in the whole exchange: order details, account balances, addresses. Treat them as part of the prompt and response. Log the tool name, duration and outcome by default, and log arguments only after masking.

Masking lowers the risk but never removes it, so surround it with some ordinary discipline:

Give content fields a short retention period. Old prompt archives are liabilities.

Limit who can read AI logs. Debugging a model doesn't mean someone needs to read customer messages.

Encrypt log storage and the pipeline that feeds it.

Log the hashed user ID so you can find and delete one person's records when they ask.

Allow verbose logging in development with fake data, and enforce strict settings in production through configuration, not through people remembering.

A masker that quietly stops working is worse than having none, because everyone assumes the logs are clean. Write tests for it:

@Test void masksEmailAndCardNumber() {     String raw = "Contact me at asha@example.com, card 4111 1111 1111 1111";     String safe = new RegexPiiMasker().mask(raw);     assertFalse(safe.contains("asha@example.com"));     assertFalse(safe.contains("4111"));     assertTrue(safe.contains("[EMAIL]"));     assertTrue(safe.contains("[CARD]")); }

Build a small set of messy, realistic samples: numbers with odd spacing, mixed languages, addresses inside sentences, text pasted from spreadsheets. Run them in your CI pipeline, and add a new case every time a leak turns up. A scheduled job that scans stored logs for patterns that should never appear makes a good safety net too.

A few I'd watch for. Logging raw text at debug level and assuming production never enables it; debug flags get switched on during incidents, so mask at every level. Masking only the user's message while forgetting retrieved documents, system prompts and tool results. Letting SDK exceptions carry the full request body into the logs. Leaving wire-level HTTP logging on in production, which bypasses your masker completely. And treating masking as finished once it ships, when every new prompt template can bring new kinds of data.

Every AI call writes a structured metadata record with a request ID

All prompt and response text goes through a single masker first

Streams are masked after assembly, and tool arguments are masked too

Content logging is sampled, short-lived and access-controlled

Tests cover the masker, with a regression case for every past leak

Client libraries aren't dumping raw payloads into the logs

Good logs turn an AI feature from a black box into something you can actually debug, price and improve. The same logs can also expose the people who trusted you with their details. The way through is fairly plain: record metadata for every call, push all content through one well-tested masker, use pseudonyms when you need to follow a conversation, handle streams and tools carefully, and keep retention short. Set that up before launch, not after the first incident, and you get visibility without regret.

#10443. Digital Duty of Care Act passes in Australia. Opposition say the law is ‘authoritarian’

Australia’s Parliament on Wednesday passed online safety laws that could expose tech giants to multibillion-dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harms.

The United States and the Australian opposition party warned that the legislation would lead to censorship of lawful speech.

The Digital Duty of Care Act requires Big Tech to proactively reduce the risk of harm before it occurs, according to an Australian government statement.

Australian online law falls in line with EU and British legislation

The legislation is similar to the European Union’s Digital Services Act, passed in 2022, and the United Kingdom’s Online Safety Act passed a year later.

The legislation became law in the House of Representatives, where the center-left Labor Party government commands a majority, by 97 votes to 43.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told Parliament the law would stand as a “powerful instrument to protect our children and our society from online harms by placing the onus on the tech platforms to ensure a safer online environment.”

“This is a victory for our children and young people. The dangers were unforeseen when the digital world was young,” Albanese said. “But now that the digital world has matured, they can be easily recognized and they can be remedied.”

Opposition leader vows to repeal ‘authoritarian’ law

Opposition leader Angus Taylor told Parliament he would repeal the legislation if his conservative Liberal Party wins elections in 2028. Taylor described the legislation as “authoritarian.”

“This bill is a blank check for political censorship,” Taylor told Parliament. “The bill is an attack on free speech that is absolutely central to our democracy.”

The government struck a deal with the minor Greens party on Tuesday to get the legislation through the Senate, where no party holds a majority.

“Today, the safety and wellbeing of Australians and their children have finally been put ahead of Big Tech’s bottom line,” Greens chief negotiator Sarah Hanson-Young said in a statement after the bill passed the Senate by 36 votes to 23.

“My message to Big Tech companies is, it’s time to make your platforms safe or we will see you in court,” she added.

The Australian legislation sets minimum safety standards for online services, including games, apps and artificial intelligence chatbots, requiring them to protect Australians from seriously harmful material and conduct, the government said.

The Greens’ amendments include increasing maximum penalties for breaches from 109 million Australian dollars ($72 million), as the government originally proposed, to 5% of a tech company’s global revenue.

U.S. Ambassador to Australia David Brat said on Tuesday the then-proposed laws would “impose disproportionate compliance burdens on American companies relative to competitors.”

“Vaguely defined ‘harms,’ backed by penalties of up to 5% of global revenue, will push platforms to censor lawful speech,” Brat posted on social media.

—Rod Mcguirk, Associated Press

#10441. McDonald’s has found a new way to sell burgers to people who don’t want to stop playing video games

McDonald’s to gamers: We are so hip.

Ahead of the highly anticipated release of Grand Theft Auto VI last week, the fast food giant announced that U.S.-based gamers can now place an order on Discord to be delivered by Uber Eats. And to demonstrate just how hip the septuagenarian company is, the announcement appealed directly to gamers with text speak—it’s littered with derivatives of “u” in lieu of “you.”

“McDonald’s is showing up on Discord to make it a little easier to get ur McDelivery order when breaking from ur servers just isn’t an option,” the company said in a press release. 

Yes, that’s verbatim from the Chicago-based company—the sort of appeal that could well remind some people of the “How do you do, fellow kids?” meme featuring actor Steve Buscemi from an episode of 30 Rock. Surprisingly, the announcement didn’t elicit many jeers from the Reddit crowd of Discord users, where many people drew comparisons to now-defunct collaborations between fast food chains and gaming consoles that similarly let gamers seamlessly order food. 

Hype around the end of a 13-year wait for a new edition of the popular game surely warranted being a little cringey. The company didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment from Fast Company regarding how popular the new ordering option has been thus far, but The New York Times reported that both DoorDash and Uber Eats experienced double-digit spikes in orders in the hours after the game was released. 

MCDONALD’S LATEST MOVES

Even if it’s only a marketing ploy, the Discord ordering optionality illustrates just how much McDonald’s wants to show up for customers. Earlier this month, company executives revealed plans to introduce new value-oriented meal bundles next year to appeal to cash-strapped customers.

And its nearly decade-long collaboration with Uber Eats is nothing to scoff at. Earlier this month, the two companies announced that their nearly decade-long partnership will expand delivery to 14 new markets, adding to its existing 30-country market.

In a more buttoned-up press release intended for investors, Mason Smoot, senior vice president of global franchising and delivery, said its home delivery option—dubbed McDelivery—is a $20 billion-plus global business each year.

Even though the company has been trying for more than a year to overcome a challenging market with its U.S. customers, it’s been making a wide range of attempts to lure them back—and that’s seemingly resonating with investors. 

While McDonald’s shares are still down for the year, they’ve surged more than 14% in the past month. During that same period, the broader S&P 500 Index has slumped nearly 8%.

#10439. Ozempic is changing the way Americans shop and eat, even if they’ve never taken it

The new class of drugs led by Ozempic and Wegovy don’t just have transformative effects on the people who take them – they’re reshaping the lives around them too.

Patients prescribed GLP-1s are eating less and drinking less, but those behavioral shifts are trickling down to people in their life who aren’t taking the medications themselves. Nearly one in four U.S. consumers have adjusted the way that they shop, eat, and drink based on knowing other people who take GLP-1s, according to a new survey from market research firm Escalent. 

The survey homed in on a group that the market research group calls “echo consumers,” which refers to people who don’t take a GLP-1 themselves but are changing their habits based on others in their social circles who do. The survey included data from 315 U.S. and 335 U.K. respondents who haven’t taken a GLP-1 drug but know someone who does and report changes to their own behavior based on those social connections.

“Much of the attention surrounding GLP-1 medications has focused on the people taking them, and those living in their households,” Escalent Europe Managing Director Melissa Bane wrote. “… For retailers, food and beverage brands and restaurants, that’s a significant consumer group whose changing habits have gone largely unnoticed.”

Among the echo consumers, 42% reported exercising more, 36% said they consume more wellness products, and 27% are drinking less. When eating out, 49% said they are ordering less at restaurants when eating with someone taking a GLP-1, while 21% are opting for alternative activities instead of socializing while eating and drinking. Almost one in five say they have picked different gifts for GLP-1 users they’ve shopped for, and many say they are buying different food and drinks to bring along to social gatherings in light of smaller appetites and friends and family who aren’t drinking as much.

Industry-shifting numbers

While the new survey only offers a small snapshot of consumer behavior, GLP-1 medications are clearly causing some seismic cultural shifts that we’re only beginning to understand. In the U.S., a massive 11% of the population are currently prescribed GLP-1s and 15% say they have tried them for weight loss before. That huge swath of Americans is already walking, running, and cycling more, buying fewer sweet treats, spending less on groceries, and drinking less alcohol.

Habit shifts among GLP-1 users alone already represent a massive amount of change for industries to adapt to across just a few short years. Beyond those consumers, Escalent’s survey suggests that there are 1.7 times as many people shifting their behavior in light of the widespread use of weight management drugs than there are GLP-1 users. If similar numbers play out in future research, that’s an even more massive chunk of the population suddenly eating, drinking, and buying differently than they did prior to the advent of drugs like Ozempic, Wegovy, and Zepbound.

“For Echo Consumers, a box of chocolates or a bottle of wine may no longer be the gift of choice, and social occasions could increasingly revolve around activities rather than going out for food and drink,” Bane said, calling the changes a “major shift” that will be even more evident during the holiday season. 

“Brands, retailers and hospitality businesses will need to find ways to adapt their offerings to reflect changing demand as these habits continue to spread through social networks.”

#10438. Introducing the Palmyra-mini family: Powerful, lightweight, and ready to reason!

The team at WRITER is thrilled to announce the release of three new open models in the Palmyra-mini family. These models are designed to be powerful, lightweight, and highly performant for their size (1.5B to 1.7B), making them ideal for a wide range of applications with efficient inference.

The "thinking" models have been trained with a Chain of Thought (CoT) approach, which improves their reasoning abilities. We're excited to see what the community will build with these new models!

GGUF and MLX quantizations are also available for your convenience:

palmyra-mini: Our non-reasoning improved base model, delivering a score of 52.6% on Big Bench Hard (get-answer)(exact_match), making it a fantastic all-rounder for a wide variety of generative tasks.

palmyra-mini-thinking-a: This variant is your go-to for complex logical challenges. Trained with a Chain of Thought (CoT) approach, it achieves an impressive 82.87% on GSM8K (strict match), demonstrating its powerful reasoning capabilities. It has the highest overall average score on benchmarks relative to other models in the release.

palmyra-mini-thinking-b: Pushing the boundaries of problem-solving, this model scores a solid 92.5% on AMC23. It's a great choice when you need a model that can "think" its way through demanding tasks. This has the highest average benchmark scores in the benchmarks AIME24,AIME25, GPQA, HMMT25, HLE, MMLU_PRO,MATH500, LCB relative to the other models in the release.

We're releasing both pass@1(avg-of-1) and pass@1(avg-of-64) results. Benchmarking methodology (sampling parameters: temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95): Pass@1(avg-of-1) scores:

GSM8K through MBPP: collected using lm_eval framework. AIME24 through HMMT25: collected using lighteval framework.

Pass@1(avg-of-64) scores: collected using nemoskills framework.

Since all the base models are Qwen architecture the inference should be runnable on popular inference frameworks such as vLLM, SGLang, TRTLLM, TGI.

For palmyra-thinking-b the base model was https://huggingface.co/nvidia/OpenReasoning-Nemotron-1.5B. We ran RL fine tuning and observed that it's capable of improving performance. While Reinforcement learning improved single-shot accuracy (pass@1), it reduced sampling diversity, leading to a drop in majority@64 performance compared to the SFT base model. This highlights a trade-off between accuracy and diversity, and we believe transparency around these findings will spark further research along mode collapse, small model performance and other areas.

Through this work, we've tried to push the boundaries of what's achievable with small parameter models, and we're excited to see how the community will continue advancing inference efficiency without sacrificing performance quality.

#10436. Major League Baseball sues players’ union ahead of lockout next week

Major League Baseball sued its players’ association in federal court on Wednesday, asking that its contemplated lockout next week be declared legal and trying to head off any attempt by the union to decertify and challenge the work stoppage with an antitrust case.

In a 38-page complaint filed in U.S. District Court in Manhattan, MLB and the corporate entities owning its 30 teams sued the Major League Baseball Players Association and the eight players on the union’s executive subcommittee, including record-setting pitcher Tarik Skubal.

“MLB brings this action to keep the dispute over the next collective bargaining agreement (‘CBA’) at the bargaining table, where federal law says it belongs,” the lawsuit says. “MLB has a reasonable and imminent fear that the Union will attempt to use the threat of antitrust liability to derail the collective bargaining process altogether in favor of antitrust litigation.”

Baseball’s five-year labor contract expires at 11:59 p.m. Dec. 1 and owners are expected to immediately impose a lockout, which would be the sport’s 10th work stoppage since 1972. Owners have proposed a salary cap for the first time since 1994, when players fought off the proposal with a 7 1/2-month strike that led to the first cancellation of the World Series in 90 years.

Owners asked for a declaratory judgment determining a lockout doesn’t violate antitrust laws and doesn’t amount to an unreasonable restraint of trade. They asked for a ruling that the federal courts lack jurisdiction to enjoin a lockout and for an order that the players be defined as a legal class, which if granted could block individual lawsuits.

“The lawsuit filed today by MLB is completely frivolous,” the union said in a statement. “We will respond appropriately, but MLB’s decision to run to court in the middle of negotiations rather than bargain in good faith is incredibly disappointing.”

Among the lawyers representing MLB are former Solicitor General Paul D. Clement and Keker, Van Nest & Peters, which worked on behalf of the union in litigation against government seizure of drug tests.

“Today’s filing is a defensive measure simply intended to keep the parties at the bargaining table to work towards a new collective bargaining agreement and a full 2027 season,” MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said in a statement. “We believe the union is preparing to follow the playbook its new leadership has used against other major professional sports leagues by pretending to ‘disclaim’ its status as the players’ bargaining process.”

Caplin referred decertification as a “nuclear option,” mirroring union head Bruce Meyer’s description of the salary cap proposal as a “nuclear bomb.”

—Ronald Blum, AP baseball writer

#10435. How to Build a Unified Lead Tracking Pipeline for Web Forms and Phone Calls

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A visitor clicks a search ad, submits a quote request, and calls your sales team ten minutes later. The form integration creates a CRM contact. The phone platform records a call. By Friday, the marketing report shows two leads, while sales remembers one conversation that turned into a deal.

Both systems captured something useful. The problem is that neither record explains how the two interactions belong together.

A unified tracking pipeline gives forms and calls a common event format, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to CRM outcomes. It also needs to survive a less tidy reality: repeated callbacks, missing campaign data, delayed updates, and a CRM that occasionally refuses requests.

This tutorial builds the core of that pipeline with JavaScript and PostgreSQL. We will capture campaign parameters, define a shared event contract, and persist events alongside the work needed to deliver them. Provider authentication and CRM requests belong in adapters around this core, using the documentation for the services you choose.

Before writing an endpoint, decide what you are counting. A phone call can produce several status callbacks. A person can submit two forms. An existing customer can contact sales about a new purchase.

Use separate identifiers for these different things:

This separation prevents two common mistakes. Deduplicating by call ID alone can discard later status updates. Counting every callback as a lead inflates demand.

For this implementation, each event is unique within a tenant and source. A tenant is the business whose data you are processing; the source identifies a website or provider account. The same provider event ID can therefore appear in two accounts without causing a collision.

Keep the original interactions even after you connect them to one contact. The form and the call are both useful evidence. Your reporting layer decides whether they represent one opportunity.

Campaign parameters are easiest to capture when the visitor first arrives. Waiting until the form submission can lose them if the visitor has already moved to another page.

Google's campaign URL documentation explains the roles of utm_source, utm_medium, and utm_campaign. The following helper reads those fields and a few optional ones, without copying the entire query string:

const params = new URL(url).searchParams;

"utm_source", "utm_medium", "utm_campaign",

return Object.fromEntries(keys.flatMap(key => {

The browser's URLSearchParams interface handles query parsing and decoding. It saves you from writing string-splitting code that breaks on encoded characters.

Run this helper through your site's existing consent and attribution flow. Where storage is permitted, associate the result with an opaque attribution reference in your backend and retain that reference through the visit. A later form submission sends the reference; the server resolves it within the correct tenant and visitor session. The form must still work when attribution storage is unavailable.

Keep first-touch and current-touch records separately if you need both. Overwriting the first campaign every time someone returns makes the eventual report answer a different question.

Treat campaign labels as untrusted input. Visitors can edit query strings and hidden fields. Validate them on the server, escape them when displayed, and never use them as authorization or as the sole evidence for commission payments. Avoid putting names, email addresses, or other personal information in UTM values.

Missing tags also need careful handling. An empty UTM object only tells you that no accepted UTM values were captured. Classifying a visit as direct, organic, or referral requires additional evidence and an explicit attribution rule.

Forms carry browser context naturally. Phone calls need a bridge between the number dialed and the marketing interaction that prompted the call.

There are two useful levels of precision. A number assigned to one campaign can identify that campaign. Dynamic number insertion can support a more detailed association by displaying tracking numbers according to a visitor or session mapping. That association depends on the provider's number allocation and expiry rules.

Providers differ in how they implement this, and in what they expose beyond it, such as keyword-level reporting or conversation analysis. If you are still choosing one, this comparison of attribution software with call tracking is a useful starting point. At the integration boundary, check which event identifiers, attribution fields, delivery mechanisms, and authentication options your configured product exposes.

Keep that provider-specific work in an adapter. Its job is to turn an authenticated notification into your event contract and resolve any attribution reference supported by the provider's data. The application schema below is an internal contract; each provider adapter translates its documented payload into that contract.

Store the basis of a match with the attribution record. For example, session_match, campaign_number, and unknown make different levels of evidence visible to reporting. If a number has been reassigned, use the mapping valid when the call occurred, not whichever mapping happens to be current when the callback arrives. If the evidence is ambiguous, leave the association unresolved.

Caller ID is a separate issue. A shared office number, a withheld number, or an outdated contact record can make automatic identity matching unreliable. A confirmed CRM contact ID or an authenticated account provides a stronger link. Treat a matching phone number as a candidate for reconciliation rather than proof that two records belong to the same person.

A shared event envelope lets the rest of your application work with a small, predictable vocabulary. Here is an illustrative call event:

"occurred_at": "2026-11-06T10:14:00.000Z",

The event ID identifies this occurrence. The interaction ID groups it with other events for the same call. contact_ref can remain empty until you have enough evidence to connect the interaction to a contact.

Keep contact details in a controlled contact store and campaign details in an attribution store. The references above point to those records; they are not credentials and must not grant access on their own.

The following factory checks the shared envelope. Each adapter still needs its own validation for provider fields and the contents of data.

"form.submitted", "call.started", "call.completed",

export function makeEvent(input, trusted) {

const ids = [trusted.tenantId, trusted.source,

if (ids.some(id => typeof id !== "string" ||

throw new TypeError("Invalid event identifiers");

throw new TypeError("Unsupported event type");

const time = Date.parse(input.occurredAt);

if (typeof input.occurredAt !== "string" ||

new Date(time).toISOString() !== input.occurredAt) {

throw new TypeError("Expected a canonical UTC timestamp");

attribution_ref: input.attributionRef ?? null,

Resolve trusted from server configuration and the authenticated integration. Never let a submitted tenant_id choose whose records a webhook can write. Resolve contact and attribution references within that same tenant.

For a form, issue a submission ID and reuse it when retrying the same submission. Generate a new one when the visitor deliberately starts another inquiry. Preserve the originally accepted timestamp as well. For a phone event, prefer the provider's stable event ID. If the provider documents a sequence number, a call ID plus that sequence can identify an occurrence within a provider account.

Twilio's call resource documentation provides a concrete example: call progress callbacks include a SequenceNumber, and separate HTTP requests can arrive out of order. Preserve that sequence in the adapter. A late “ringing” event should remain in the history without replacing a newer terminal state.

Authenticate before calling this factory. Use the provider's supported validator and the exact request representation it requires. Twilio's webhook security guide describes signature validation, including the importance of the request URL and payload. Other providers may use different mechanisms. Public form endpoints need their own input limits, abuse controls, and appropriate CSRF protection.

Consider a failure between these two operations: the application saves an event, then crashes before scheduling its CRM update. The event exists, but nothing is waiting to deliver it.

A transactional outbox addresses that gap. Save the event and a delivery task in the same database transaction, then let a worker process the task. AWS explains this dual-write problem in its transactional outbox guidance.

Here is a compact schema. received_at records ingestion time, while the envelope retains the event's original occurred_at value.

received_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),

PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, source, event_id)

id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,

available_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),

FOREIGN KEY (tenant_id, source, event_id)

REFERENCES lead_events (tenant_id, source, event_id)

The ingestion function below accepts a pg pool and a normalized event. Install pg in your Node.js project, save the function as persist.mjs, and initialize the pool using your application's database configuration.

export async function persistEvent(pool, event) {

const key = [event.tenant_id, event.source, event.event_id];

const values = [...key, JSON.stringify(event)];

await client.query("BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED");

ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, source, event_id) DO NOTHING

WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND source = $2 AND event_id = $3

const error = new Error("Event ID reused with new data");

INSERT INTO crm_outbox (tenant_id, source, event_id)

return { inserted: inserted.rowCount === 1 };

PostgreSQL's INSERT documentation defines the conflict handling used here. The unique key makes duplicate detection hold across application processes. A duplicate with the same normalized payload creates no second task; reuse of the key with different data raises a conflict for investigation.

This depends on immutable event bodies. Do not add a fresh receipt timestamp, random identifier, or current CRM status to the normalized payload on each delivery. Store later enrichment separately or emit a new event. Otherwise an ordinary retry will appear to be a conflicting event.

The function deliberately uses one database client throughout the transaction, as required by the node-postgres transaction documentation. Parameter values are passed separately from SQL, following its parameterized query guidance.

After this function commits, acknowledge the notification using the response expected by the sender. An identical duplicate should also receive a successful acknowledgement. If persistence fails, return the appropriate failure response and rely on the configured retry or reconciliation process. A success response sent before durable storage can turn a temporary database failure into a missing event.

For voice integrations, distinguish an informational status callback from a request asking your application how to handle a live call. They can require different response bodies, as explained in the Twilio webhooks FAQ.

The outbox gives you durable work to process. It does not make a remote CRM operation happen exactly once.

Imagine the CRM saves an update, but the worker crashes before setting processed_at. When the task runs again, the same request may reach the CRM twice. Design for that case explicitly.

Use a stable external identifier for each contact, opportunity, and activity, and check which deduplication guarantees the destination supports. HubSpot's contacts API documentation, for example, describes upserts using unique properties. Support for a contact upsert does not automatically make every associated activity or workflow idempotent. Verify the behavior of each operation you send.

If the destination cannot deduplicate a create request and a timeout leaves its result uncertain, reconcile that operation before repeating it. A local “sent” flag alone cannot prove whether the remote write happened.

The worker should claim due tasks, commit a recoverable lease, and perform network calls outside the database transaction. A lease allows another worker to recover work after a crash. When multiple workers poll the outbox, PostgreSQL's SKIP LOCKED behavior can help claim separate rows, but the lease and its recovery logic still need to be implemented.

Retry transient failures with increasing delays and jitter. Respect the destination's rate-limit instructions. Send persistent validation failures to a review queue with a useful error category, and provide a way to replay them after correction. The schema above is the ingestion foundation; a production worker needs lease fields, failure details, and a retry policy appropriate to its destination.

Also preserve ordering where it changes meaning. If two events update the same contact or opportunity, process them serially or reject stale updates using a stored version. A historical event should not move a won opportunity back to an earlier stage.

Once both channels reach the CRM, connect them to the result the business cares about. A form submission is an inquiry. A completed phone call is a technical outcome. Neither alone establishes that a lead qualified or a purchase happened. If agents record call dispositions, such as whether a call was qualified or transferred to a closer, that field is a richer signal than call completion status alone.

Have the CRM or the system that owns the transaction emit explicit outcome events, such as lead.qualified and deal.won. Include the internal opportunity ID and the original outcome time. Model reversals or cancellations explicitly if they affect revenue reporting.

Then choose the unit behind each metric. For a report about opportunities acquired during a particular month, a qualification rate can use qualified opportunities divided by all opportunities in that acquisition cohort. Counting qualification events received during the month would answer a different question and could include older inquiries.

Deduplicate opportunities before calculating channel totals. A person who submits a form and calls about the same purchase should retain both interactions, while the opportunity receives credit according to your chosen attribution rule. Label that rule in the report so first-touch and last-touch numbers are not compared as though they measure the same thing.

Measure data quality alongside performance. Track unresolved attribution, duplicate deliveries, ingestion failures, and the age of the oldest pending outbox task. Once several sources and destinations feed the same reports, a data observability platform can watch these signals across the whole pipeline instead of relying on checks inside a single worker. An apparently quiet campaign may actually have a broken integration.

Operational logs should contain enough context to investigate failures without becoming another customer database. Use internal references and error categories, and avoid dumping webhook bodies into logs. The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet provides guidance on excluding or protecting sensitive values.

A successful form submission proves little about retries or missing data. Before connecting production traffic, test the cases that could distort reporting or lose an inquiry.

Run database cases against PostgreSQL with separate connections so the tests exercise actual constraints and transaction behavior. Use the provider's test tools or signed fixtures for webhook authentication. Test CRM retries against a sandbox with the destination's real duplicate-handling rules.

Start rollout with one form and one phone source. Trace a known inquiry from its captured campaign through its interactions to its CRM outcome. Reconcile event totals against the source systems over the same time window, allowing for delivery delays. Expand once that path is explainable and failures are visible.

The same adapter pattern extends to inquiries that start offline, such as leads collected at a trade show and exported as a CSV or XLSX file. Import each row as a form.submitted event with the event as its source, a stable row identifier as event_id, and the original capture time as occurred_at. Because the outbox treats an identical event as a duplicate, re-importing the same export won’t create a second CRM task.

What is a unified lead tracking pipeline?

It is a workflow that converts inquiries from different channels into a shared data model, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to business outcomes. Forms and calls keep their own interaction records, while contacts and opportunities provide the relationships needed for reporting.

Can I connect a phone call to a website visit?

Sometimes. Dynamic number insertion can provide a session or visitor association when the provider's mapping is available and valid. A campaign-specific number usually supports campaign-level attribution. If the caller uses a saved number, switches devices, or calls after a mapping expires, the available evidence may be less precise.

Handle duplicate delivery and identity resolution separately. Stable event IDs and a database constraint prevent repeated notifications from producing repeated work. Connecting several interactions to one contact or opportunity requires a separate matching policy, with ambiguous cases left unresolved until there is enough evidence.

Should a completed call count as a conversion?

Only if that is the conversion your report explicitly measures. A completed call does not establish that a prospect qualified or bought something. Keep technical call status separate from CRM outcomes and use the latter when reporting qualified demand or revenue.

Do I need a message broker for this architecture?

You can begin with PostgreSQL and an outbox worker if that setup meets your throughput and latency needs. A broker becomes useful when several consumers need independent delivery, or when buffering and scale justify the additional operations. In either case, retries still require idempotent consumers.

What happens when tracking consent is unavailable?

Keep the inquiry flow usable and apply your site's existing consent rules to optional attribution collection and storage. Accept permitted form or call data, leave unavailable attribution empty, and avoid reconstructing a visitor identity through fingerprinting. Reports should expose that missing context instead of inventing a campaign match.
