Getting a GPU in the current climate can be a tricky affair, with rising prices and demand through the roof. That's why this offer on a Gigabyte Eagle RTX 5070 Ti with a free Gigabyte Aorus X870E Elite motherboard might be one of the better bundled GPU offers you see this holiday season, at $1,469 for the pair. Both the GPU and the motherboard are fairly no-frills, but will deliver performance where it counts and will help you save a couple of dollars on a brand-new PC build.

With free Gigabyte X870E Aorus Elite Wi-Fi 7 Motherboard

The Gigabyte Eagle RTX 5070 Ti comes equipped with 16GB of GDDR7 Memory, 8960 CUDA cores, and offers a core clock of 2542 MHz. The card comes with Gigabyte's Hawk fans in a 2.5-slot design.

The free Aorus X870 Elite motherboard comes with support for up to 5 DIMM slots, offers 3x PCIe 5.0 NVMe slots, and one PCIe 4.0 m.2 slot with a suite of I/O and Wi-Fi connectivity.

The utilitarian design of both parts in this bundle will suit any PC build out there, though if you wanted to shell out for a fancier GPU, you'll have to pay a higher price. As far as we've seen, you can also grab this deal alongside Gigabyte's Gaming and Windforce RTX 5070 Ti models, if you wanted a slightly higher-end cooler attached to your silicon.

The motherboard itself hosts the AM5 socket, meaning it'll fully support any of AMD's latest CPUs, and has plenty of slots and ports across a total of four m.2 slots (four PCIe 5.0, one PCie 4.0), a Realtek connectivity chipset with Wi-Fi 7 support, and full USB-4 ports on the rear. — Sayem Ahmed

This year's Apple MacBook Air has dropped to $999 across multiple storefronts, including Amazon and Best Buy, this Black Friday. The M5 Air is our go-to everyday laptop for most people, as its premium build quality, trackpad, and solid battery life make it a no-brainer for people who want a step up from the MacBook Neo, with a little more computing heft for everyday tasks, if you can stomach the display's notch, of course.

The M5 MacBook Air offers 512GB of storage, a 13-inch Retina display, and a 10-core CPU and 8-Core GPU with 16GB of unified memory that can take on pretty much all everyday tasks with ease.

We reviewed this model of MacBook Air earlier this year and said that it offered great value if you're looking for a premium ultraportable device. At under $1000, the deal only gets better. If you're doing serious multitasking work regularly, then the M5 MacBook Air is a worthy upgrade, or a better pick than the MacBook Neo deals that we've seen floating around recently.

Of course, you get additional frills like MagSafe Charging, solid speakers, and a pretty-much unmatched trackpad, to boot. Despite its place as Apple's mid-range laptop option, it's a solid pick that will suit most people for everyday computing tasks. — Sayem Ahmed

If you own an Apple device, it's likely that you have — or want — a set of AirPods. Sure, you can pair any old set of Bluetooth earbuds with an iDevice, and they'll probably work fine. But every time you run into a cut corner or software feature that doesn't work seamlessly on those buds, you'll curse yourself for not going with the Apple option. And non-techies will be even less tolerant of those pitfalls, which is why AirPods are a perennially solid gift idea.

If you or a loved one could use an AirPods upgrade, now is a great time to grab a new pair. Amazon has Apple's latest AirPods Pro 3 buds on sale for just $149, a new all-time low price.

Apple's AirPods Pro 3 seamlessly fit into your personal Apple device ecosystem. The third generation boasts improved active noise cancellation and fitness tracking tech.

Apple claims the AirPods Pro 3 are twice as effective at canceling noise as their predecessors thanks to upgraded ear tips and stronger active noise cancellation. In the event you have hearing loss, these buds can double as hearing aids, too.

If you forget to charge your Apple Watch before a workout (or just don't have one, period), the Pro 3s can link up with your iPhone to monitor your heart rate and activities instead. And if you frequently misplace your wireless earbuds, the AirPods Pro 3 support Apple's Find My and Precision Finding features, making them harder to lose.

If you want (or need) advanced wireless earbuds that are easy to live with and easy to love, this is a great deal on a solid pair. — Brandon Hill

If you have a Thunderbolt 5 Windows PC or Mac, investing in a good docking station is critical to supporting a large variety of accessories and monitors. This is especially true for ultrabooks, which often are limited to two external ports that must be shared between charging and connectivity. With that said, Wavlink's WL-UTD58 Thunderbolt 5 docking station is a perfect solution for adding I/O ports and is on sale for $179 (versus a list price of $219.99).

The Wavlink WL-UTD58 is a Thunderbolt 5 docking station that provides three downstream Thunderbolt 5 ports, SD and microSD slots, four USB-A ports, and a 2.5 GbE port.

First of all, it is pretty well stacked with ports:

I previously tested the WL-UTD58-M version of this dock, which is identical, save for the inclusion of an internal M.2 slot for a PCIe 4.0 SSD. It offers good overall performance and easily accessible ports. My main gripe with the dock is that the Thunderbolt 5 port for connecting to the host machine is on the front of the unit instead of the back. — Brandon Hill

When you need a small, pocketable router to carry with you for work or vacation, the TP-Link TL-WR3602BE is one of the best options on the market. And Amazon is currently selling the device for $83.49, a $36.50 discount off its MSRP.

The TL-WR3602BE is a pint-sized dual-band Wi-Fi 7 router that is perfect for those who are frequently on the road and need to connect multiple devices.

The TL-WR3602BE, which we reviewed last year, is compact, measuring just 5 x 3.7 x 4 inches and weighing roughly 8 ounces. But don't knock that small size: it still provides dual-band Wi-Fi 7 coverage (2.4 GHz + 5 GHz) and includes a 2.5 GbE WAN, GbE LAN, and a USB-C port for power. Although the TL-WR3602BE includes a USB-C power adapter in the box, its miserly power requirements let you power it from a USB power bank.

The router also offers several operating modes, including the ability to share a paid Wi-Fi connection on an airplane (this would be a handy place to leverage the aforementioned power bank) or in a hotel room. And you can even tether your smartphone to the router via USB or connect to a USB cellular modem. — Brandon Hill

When you're always on the go, be it on vacation or airport/hotel hopping for business, having a battery bank in your laptop bag is a must. Anker is one of the best-known names when it comes to chargers, adapters, cables, and power banks. The company’s 25,000 mAh Laptop Power Bank is now priced at just $91.19, which is a 32 percent discount over its normal going rate.

The Anker Laptop Power Bank is a 25,000 mAh power bank with 165-watt charging support, dual built-in USB-C cables, a USB-C port, and a USB-A port. It also has an integrated

That $91 goes a long way, as you get three USB-C ports, each supporting a maximum of 100 watts of power to a single device. The power bank can simultaneously charge four devices and has a 25,000 mAh capacity. A built-in LCD shows battery status and power stats, while an integrated retractable USB-C cable serves as a carrying strap. — Brandon Hill

Looking for a gaming mouse that looks as good as it performs? The Logitech G502 X Plus should be on your shortlist. It's currently on sale in both black and white variations for just $119.99 at Amazon, down 25% from its retail price of $159.99.

This right-handed contoured gaming mouse features 13 programmable buttons, dual-mode scrolling, a reversible/removable DPI switch button, and up to 130 hours of battery life (with the pretty lighting turned off).

The G502 X Plus is a large, right-handed contoured gaming mouse with a thumb rest, 13 programmable buttons, and 8 RGB zones. It uses Logitech's Hero 25K optical sensor and has an adjustable (and removable) DPI shift button, as well as a dual-mode scroll wheel that lets you switch between smooth free-scrolling and precise notched scrolling with the press of a button.

It also has hybrid optical-mechanical switches in its primary buttons, with optical for speed and low-latency, and mechanical for improved battery life. It gets up to 130 hours with the lighting turned off, but that drops to around 37 hours with the lighting turned on. Our Logitech G502 X Plus review has the full details but this is the best price we've seen this mouse in months. — Ben Stockton

The Samsung P9 is one of the best microSD Express cards you can buy right now, withultra-fast sequential read speeds of up to 800 MB/s. Those speeds mean it's a great option for installing games and playing them on your Switch 2 without gameplay lag. Write speeds aren't shared, but in this class and capacity, you can usually expect up to 300 MB/s.

All in all, though, installing this card will triple your Switch 2's internal storage. Not a bad option if you've got a huge backlog of games to play. — Ben Stockton

Give your Switch 2 the storage boost it needs. With fast speeds and respectable endurance, the P9 Express from Samsung is one of the best microSD Express cards you can get.

With the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time rerelease on everyone's holiday wishlist, now's the time to think about upgrading your Switch 2 storage with a decently-sized MicroSD Express card. Luckily, this Samsung P9 Express card with 512GB storage is now just $92.99, a huge 38% discount on its usual price.

Sure, you could spend hundreds of dollars on a new gaming mouse, with all the top features. You don't need to, though. There are competition-ready options for much less money that'll give you a good experience for gaming. For example, there's the Logitech G305 Lightspeed wireless mouse, and this ol' reliable in black is down to only $26.99 on Amazon.

Sporting a 12K sensor, a 99g weight, and a 250-hour battery rating on a single AA battery, Logitech's G503 wireless isn't an ultra-light 8K polling elite gaming mouse. But it solid experience while gaming and working. Unless you're playing competitive titles on an elite level, it just might be all the gaming mouse you really need.

While the G305 Lightspeed is getting on in years (our review of the G305 Lightspeed dates back to 2020), it's still a good option for gamers on a budget. We praised it for its 12K DPI sensor, along with its reliable wireless connection. The build quality is good, although it'll feel a little small if you've got big hands. There's no rechargeable battery included, so you'll need to keep some AA batteries close by. That does give you the convenience to get up and running again in seconds, though.

Smart, simple, and powerful. There are several colors on offer here, but the cheapest is in a (very bright) blue for $25.48. The black, the most understated, is $26.99. Not a bad option for a gamer on a budget. — Ben Stockton

There's a new record low for the Razer Huntsman Mini 60% gaming keyboard on Amazon right now. This wired keyboard is just $65.54 right now, a discount that saves you 50% compared to its original $129.99 list price.

You're able to pick up this board with either clicky or linear optional switches, but only the linear version is on sale right now. The clicky one isn't in stock on Amazon, although you can pick it up for $65.54 over at Best Buy instead.

The Razer Huntsman Mini 60% Wired is a mechanical keyboard with Razer's optical linear switches, offering adjustable actuation points and Razer's Snap Tap feature.

With these Razer's optical switches, you're able to use its Snap Tap functionality to rapidly swap between two key presses, as well as rebind commands to different actuation points on the key press. The keyboard is mostly made out of plastic, though Razer uses an aluminum top frame to give it a bit of a premium flair.

If you've got limited desk space, this Razer Huntsman Mini isn't a bad option, offering good performance at a budget price with its smaller 60% layout. — Ben Stockton

Woot, Amazon's budget-friendly offshoot, has a deal on the Nintendo Switch 2 that knocks $30 off the current list price. This family friendly gaming console is on sale for just $469 right now. There are no games included with this package, but you can put those savings towards a copy of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time re-release.

The Switch 2 is Nintendo's latest flagship game console.

There are no bells and whistles to think about here. You're just saving some cash on one of the hottest game consoles. Ocarina of Time is bound to have increased demand, so if you want to pick up this handheld before the holidays, this Woot! deal is one of the best ways to do it.

We've reviewed the Nintendo Switch 2 ourselves, and it's a console that impressed us, thanks to its boost in performance compared to the OG switch, along with better graphics fidelity, larger screen, and backward compatibility. It's not going to beat the PS5 Pro, but if you love Nintendo, and don't already own one, put this Switch 2 in your basket. — Ben Stockton

The best upgrades for your setup are often the ones that deal with a quality-of-life issue. For me, that would be getting under my desk to turn my PC on or off. If you're facing the same issue, and want to save your knees, you might want to pick up this cheap, external PC power button for just $6.79.

OwlTree's remote power switch is just a power switch, but it's a big, inviting button with a spiffy blue LED ring to indicate system status. It also has a nice, long 5.7-foot (174cm) cable for flexibility and comes with a header splitter so you don't have to add any extra cables to your build. Best of all, it's just $6.99.

Less than a coffee for a button that'll make your life a whole lot easier. These things aren't just about being comfortable, though. If you read the kind of reviews on these kind of products, a common use case is for open bench rigs or for embedded builds that needs a flexible power button location. They're also useful for placing your PC somewhere out of reach.

The header cables will plug into your motherboard, so installing them is easy, and it comes with a 5.7-foot cable for flexibility. There's also a header splitter so you can connect it up to your existing setup without affecting your case. functionality. For $7, it's an obvious one: if you're building, just buy it. — Ben Stockton

No less than four members of the Tom's Hardware team have invested in this very screwdriver set from Hoto with their own money. There's a reason why: it's great. In fact, it's a must-buy if you're setting out to build or expand your toolkit, especially if you're a PC builder or maker. Right now, you can pick up the Hoto NEX 01 Pro for $28.48.

The Hoto NEX O1 Pro is a magnetic precision screwdriver powered by a 1,500 mAh battery, allowing you to drive over 1,000 screws on a single USB-C charge. It weighs 250g, features three different torque settings, and includes 25 ultra-hard screw bits, rated for 60HRC hardness on the Rockwell scale.

This portable kit is perfect for any seriously small screws you might be dealing with. The 3.6V driver itself features a 1,500mAh battery that reportedly allows you to drive over 1,000 screws from a full charge. It uses USB-C for charging via the supplied cable, so no need to worry about finding some AA batteries, with a total charge taking just 150 minutes from start to finish.

It’s ultralight, too, and weighs just 250g, with a durable case for your bits. The included 25 bits offer a myriad of choices, from Pozidrive, slot, Torx, Hex, security bits and many more. All of your 1/4 inch bits will also work with the Hoto, so you can get to work on that PC build or any IKEA furniture you buy over Black Friday.

The Hoto NEX O1 Pro is also fully adjustable, with three separate torque settings, along with a sensor that can quickly stop driving when you release control. The Hoto also features a circular LED that helps you get the job done, even in a dark environment, and is fully magnetic, so you won't lose any tiny screws along the way. If you don't already own one, the sub-$30 price tag here makes it an essential Black Friday purchase. — Ben Stockton

The Deco BE63 is an excellent mid-range, tri-brand Wi-Fi 7 mesh router that we reviewed last year. Thanks to Black Friday, you can grab a Deco BE63 two-pack for just $279.99 or you can pick up the three-pack for $369.99.

The mesh system is capable of 574 Mbps on the 2.4 GHz band, 4,324 Mbps on the 5 GHz band, and 5,188 Mbps on the 6 GHz band. For wired connectivity, you'll find four 2.5 GbE ports and one USB 3.0 port per node.

The Deco BE63 is a mid-range, tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router with four 2.5 GbE ports, 10 Gbps of combined throughput, and coverage of 5,800 square feet.

The Deco BE63 is a mid-range, tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router with four 2.5 GbE ports, 10 Gbps of combined throughput, and coverage of 5,800 square feet.

It's only possible to set up and manage TP-Link Deco routers using a smartphone app, so that's something to consider if you prefer a desktop browser. That said, the Deco app is easy enough to use, with simple menus and plenty of features to manage your network remotely. Performance is the BE63's strength, though, managing close to 2 Gbps throughput in our short-range iPerf3 tests.

Either the two or three-pack Deco BE63 will be good options for your home or office, but go for the bigger three pack if you have a bigger space to work with, as it'll cover you for 7,600 square feet. — Ben Stockton

This is absolutely an act-fast deal, as we are positive it will not last long. This deal has already gone up in price not once, but twice this week. Earlier this week, we highlighted a great deal on Apple's MacBook Neo, which is $100 off and back to its original launch price of $599. This is also better than the previous $50 discount to $649, so if you missed out the first time, this deal is now better! The $599 price gets you 256GB of storage and 8GB of RAM, and is available in all four of Apple's vibrant colors.

You can also snag the 512GB version for $699, a $100 discount.

Apple's base MacBook Neo has an A18 Pro chip, 256GB of storage, and 8GB of RAM. A solid alternative with a more powerful SoC.

The A18 Pro chip in the MacBook Neo is solid for single-core productivity performance excelling in single-core performance, though the 8GB can be difficult for serious multitasking. For people working on basic tasks, this is going to be sufficient.There have been a handful of other deals on the Neo so far this week. We saw the base model drop to $599 (in citrus only) at one point, while the upgraded 512GB model with Touch ID dropped to $699 (in blush) at another. It's possible we'll see more color-specific price drops, but it's not a guarantee, and $649 isn't bad given the RAM situation. — Andrew E. Freedman

You don't have to spend a fortune to upgrade your setup. Sometimes, the simplest (and cheapest) options can win the day, like this $9.89 Cazoo headphone holder for your desk. It'll hold your headphones and cables and charge your devices, with three USB ports (two USB-C, one USB-A) and 20W PD included.

This Cozoo device ships with both 3M tape and screws for mounting under your desk, as well as cable tie-downs to help make the setup as tidy as possible.

This quirky device combines an under-desk headphone hook and a 20W PD USB charger with one USB-C and two USB-A ports. It can bring a bit of extra convenience and tidiness to your setup, especially if desk space is tight.

The brand might be unfamiliar to most, but this is an obvious impulse buy for a techie, especially for less than $10. It solves a simple problem (where do you stick your headphones?) and has dual use, keeping your headphones and other devices like your phone charged up. — Ben Stockton

A splash of light is sometimes all that we need. No fancy buttons, rotating dials, apps. Just press a button and you have some light. The Olight IMINI 2 flashlight goes one better, because there are no buttons, and it's on sale for just $11.99 right now.

This compact and easy to use flashlight provides 50 Lumens of light, without the need to fiddle around for a button. Just unclip, and your flashlight is ready to light your way.

All you need to do to switch it on is to remove the flashlight from its magnetic holder; when you put it back, it turns off. It's as easy as that. The magnetic cap holds the flashlight firmly in place and the flashlight itself is made from aluminum, with a decent grip to reduce the chance of losing it. The base of the flashlight is magnetic, too, so you can stick it inside a PC case as you work on it.

You'll charge it using a USB-A cable that plugs into the port. This is a simple, quick and easy upgrade for your toolbox and one that you'll always reach for when you're buying and upgrading your PC. — Ben Stockton

The Keychron K10 HE keyboard is on sale for $115.99, which is back at the lowest price we've seen it on Amazon. This is a full-size gaming board with a wood frame on the side, along with backlit RGB keys. The RGB is a little less OTT than other models, though, instead going for a classic, rather understated design. It's a magnetic board, too, with magnetic hot-swappable switches.

Jump into the future of keyboards on the cheap (for Hall Effect) with the Keychron K10 HE full-size keyboard. Priced at $115.99, you'd be hard-pressed to find a better deal on full-size Hall Effect keyboard.

You're getting double-shot PBT keycaps here, and underneath them are Gateron double-rail magnetic switches. These give you a lightening-fast response time with a 0.1mm press sensitivity, along with adjustable actuation points for per-key customization. This gives you full flexibility over the entire board.

You've got two options on sale, with the all-black and all-white options at the same $115.99 price: a great deal on a full-size Hall effect keyboard. — Ben Stockton

Anker has carved a name for itself in the portable power bank business, and it's a familiar option for Amazon buyers. Right now, you can pick up its laptop power bank, with a huge 25,000 mAh battery capacity, for just $91.19. That's a 32% discount compared to its usual list price.

The Anker Laptop Power Bank can supply up to 165 watts when two USB-C ports are in use. It also features a retractable USB-C cable and another integrated cable that doubles as a carrying strap.

$91 is enough to get you a power bank with three USB-C ports, including one retractable cable, each capable of 100W each, with a USB-A port capable of 33W. If you're using more than one USB-C cable, you can output a maximum of 165W between them or 133W if you’re using one USB-C port and the USB-A port. If you max out the power bank by using all four ports simultaneously, you’re limited to 130 watts maximum output.

This will let you power up a smartphone, laptop, portable game console, and more, with up to 100W each to supported devices. If your laptop can push that far, it'll carry on charging your laptop until it depletes. It's also capable of charging up itself with a 100W-charger, gaining 30% in 22 minutes.

There's also a built-in display that lets you see charge, device temperature and battery health. If you're on-the-go with plenty of devices in your bag, this is the kind of battery pack you'll want at your disposal. — Ben Stockton

Our favorite gaming chair isn't a typical racing-style chair, but it's not an office one, either. It's this collab between Herman Miller and Logitech G. The Vantum, ergonomic but "built for gamers" with gaming features like an adjustable neckrest, lumbar support and forward-leaning alignment is on sale right now for $768.07 right now, down from $1,155, with an extra 5% off thanks to a Black Friday promo code.

Features an "active, forward leaning alignment," adjustable lumbar support, and passively-adaptive thoracic support. It has a foam-padded seat cushion and a mesh suspension backrest for breathability, as well as an adjustable neck rest.

The Vantum is a seriously premium chair. It has a mesh backrest and a padded cushioned seat, along with 4D armrests with padding. As you can imagine, it scored well in our Herman Miller x Logitech G Vantum review, thanks to its lightweight but comfortable design, with the adjustable lumbar support similar to the functionality you'd see in the company's pricier Herman Miller task chairs.

While the chair doesn't offer full recline, its tilt mechanism is pretty comfortable, as is the passively-adaptive thoracic support. This Black Friday discount means you can save $386.93, as long as you use the SAVE5 code at checkout to get the full discount. — Ben Stockton

The Logitech Yeti Orb is the spiritual successor to the classic Blue Snowball microphone — it's a unique-looking, ball-shaped microphone that sits on top of a sturdy desktop tripod stand and sounds great out of the box. It's our favorite budget-priced gaming mic and it's on sale right now for an even more budget-friendly $39.99 at Best Buy — $30 off its MSRP of $69.99.

This round, ball-shaped desktop mic features a cardioid polar pattern and sounds great out of the box. It comes with a desktop stand and has customizable RGB lighting, and can be mounted at two different angles.

The Yeti Orb is a simple, stylish microphone that comes with a plastic desktop tripod stand in the box. It has the Blue Snowball's iconic ball shape, with two mounting points — so you can mount it straight on, or at an angle, depending on whether you're mounting it on the included stand or on a boom arm. There are no on-mic controls or ports (other than its USB-C port), so you won't be able to adjust the mic's gain or plug in a headset for zero-latency monitoring, and for that reason it's not really a mic for serious streamers. But it does have customizable RGB lighting, which indicates whether the mic is recording, and it sounds great right out of the box — so while you can tweak the settings using Logitech G Hub (which comes with Blue Vo!ce), you don't have to. It's a great mic for casual chatting and streaming, and this is a great price to get it at. You can read my full review of the Logitech Yeti Orb here. — Sarah

Corsair's wireless MMO / MOBA-focused gaming mouse features 16 programmable buttons, including 12 in a side array, and sports Corsair's 33K Marksman S optical sensor. It also has native integration with Elgato's Stream Deck platform, so you can map Stream Deck commands directly to the buttons.

If you're looking for a mouse with tons of buttons, look no further than Corsair's Scimitar line — the Corsair Scimitar Elite SE Wireless is currently on sale for just $69.99 at Best Buy, which is 50% off its retail price of $139.99. And if you don't need a wireless mouse, the wired Corsair Scimitar RGB Elite is down to $49.99 at Amazon, which is 44% off its retail price of $89.99.

The Scimitar RGB Elite mouse from Corsair features 17 programmable buttons, including 12 located on the side panel, the left/right primary mouse buttons, two DPI switch buttons above the scroll wheel, and the scroll wheel's center click. You can slide the 12-button side panel to fit your hand size.

The Corsair Scimitar Elite SE Wireless is an MMO / MOBA-focused gaming mouse with an adjustable 12-button side panel — it doesn't swap out, like the side panel on the Razer Naga V2 / V3 Pro, but it does move forward and back (it comes with a hex tool so you can adjust it to where you want and lock it in). It doesn't move a ton, but it's a nice accommodation for people who find that the giant gaming mice that dominate the market don't have buttons in quite the right places.

The Scimitar Elite SE Wireless sports Corsair's Marksman S 33K sensor, which has a maximum resolution of 33,000 DPI and a maximum speed of 750 IPS and can handle up to 50 G's of force. It's a heavier mouse — 4.02oz / 114g, but weight isn't that big of a deal in the MMO / MOBA community. Also, it's integrated with Elgato's Stream Deck platform, so you can program Stream Deck functionality directly to the mouse's buttons. You can read my full review of the Corsair Scimitar Elite SE Wireless here. — Sarah

The 9800X3D might not be the fastest gaming CPU on the market but it's still the best option owing to its speed and power draw. Now, at Amazon, it just crashed to an all-time low of $369, thanks to a coupon you can apply before checking out.

The Ryzen 7 9800X3D is a potent gaming 8-core, 16-thread desktop CPU. It has a massive 96MB L3 cache for gaming performance, with clock speeds of up to 5.2GHz.

The 9800X3D really needs no introduction, but in case you aren't familiar, this is one the best gaming CPUs around. IT isn't quite AMD's fastest — the 9850X3D takes that crown — but this chip draws significantly less power while still being very close in terms of performance. The industry leading 3D V-Cache means the CPU is much less reliant on your slower RAM, drastically boosting frame rates.

This deal is not likely to be around for long, so move fast if you want one to start an AM5 build or upgrade your existing rig. - Stephen Warwick

This TKL mechanical keyboard features hot-swappable switches and a built-in Stream Deck with 12 LCD keys, a 2.75-inch screen, and 2 rotary knobs.

The Corsair Galleon 100 SD is a keyboard with an integrated Stream Deck — it's a mechanical keyboard with a TKL layout, plus a 2-knob, 12-key Stream Deck that has all the functionality of Elgato's Stream Deck platform. Although I still lament the lack of a true 10-key numberpad, I have to admit that the Corsair Galleon 100 SD has been my daily driver for the better part of the past year. Who knew an integrated Stream Deck was so useful?!

Of course, at $350... it's definitely not cheap. But right now it's down to $259.99 at Best Buy — $90 off its retail price, and a pretty good deal when you consider you're getting both a keyboard and a Stream Deck in one.

The Galleon 100 SD is a pretty premium keyboard, with a nice-looking design, double-shot PBT keycaps, a pass-through USB port, and a hot-swappable PCB. It comes with only one switch option: Corsair's MLX Pulse (purple) switches, which are "thocky and linear" — and they sound pretty good, though they're definitely linear. The case has six layers of sound-dampening foam and it's a great-sounding keyboard overall, especially for a mainstream gaming keyboard.

The Stream Deck features 12 LCD keys that are the same size and shape as typical Stream Deck keys. There's a 2.75-inch LCD screen above the keys, which is divided into quadrants that are controlled by the two notched, clickable rotary knobs at the top. The Stream Deck is a true Stream Deck, so it has all the functionality of Elgato's platform, and can be easily programmed with the Stream Deck software. The keyboard also comes with a soft-touch plastic wrist rest, two USB cables, and a handful of other accessories in the box. You can read my full review of the Corsair Galleon 100 SD here. — Sarah

The Turtle Beach Atlas Air lives up to its name — this wireless, open-back headset is lightweight and airy in both comfort and sound. Although its all-plastic design didn't feel quite up to the $179.99 price point it debuted at, the comfort and audio quality was enough for us to recommend it — and now it's down to just $119.99 at Amazon for Black Friday.

The only wireless open-back gaming headset on the market is incredibly light and comfortable and sounds great. It has a detachable, flip-to-mute boom mic, dual-mode wireless connectivity, and gets about 50 hours of battery life.

The Atlas Air is a wireless, open-back headset, which means the sound isn't closed in. While this does mean that people around you can hear what you're listening to, there are several benefits to an open-back design — specifically, you don't get the same listening fatigue you get when listening to a closed-back headset, because the sound can escape instead of reverberating inside your head. For gamers, it also allows for a wider soundstage and a more immersive environment. As long as you don't work in close quarters, an open-back headset is a nice option if you don't want to commit to speakers.

The Atlas Air has a lightweight, plastic build, with a mesh suspension headband and floating earcups. It's extremely lightweight — just 10.61oz / 301g — and it basically feels like you're wearing nothing. It sports 40mm dynamic drivers with a frequency response range of 20 - 40,000 Hz, and it sounds surprisingly good: it has a nice, wide soundstage and a slightly bass-heavy sound profile, and it did especially well with picking up details in layered audio environments, such as cities and jungles. It's probably not the headset for those looking to gain advantage in shooting games — the directional sound is fine, but a closed-back headset will help you zero in on footsteps and gunshots. But for the less competitive games, this is a great option, especially if you find other headsets hard to wear for long periods of time. You can read my full review of the Atlas Air here. — Sarah

The Razer Naga V2 Pro is one of my favorite mice of all time, because I can never have enough buttons on a mouse. This wireless mouse is aimed at MMO / MOBA players, but it can actually be used by just about anyone thanks to the three swappable side plates it comes bundled with. Naturally, this kind of versatility doesn't come cheap, but right now you can grab the Naga V2 Pro for just $129.99 at Amazon — $50 off its MSRP of $179.99.

The Razer Naga V2 Pro sports a customizable magnetic side plate, offering 12-, 6-, and 2-button configurations, Razer's Hyperscroll Pro wheel, fully wireless connectivity, and its Focus Pro 30K Optical sensor.

The Naga V2 Pro comes with three interchangeable side plates with 12-, 6-, and 2-button configurations. It's not the lightest mouse on the market — it weighs 4.72oz / 134g, but lightness is not what most MMO players are looking for. Instead, they're looking for comfort, and the Naga V2 Pro is a very comfortable mouse, with a contoured, ergonomic right-handed shape and a rest for your ring finger. It sports Razer's Focus Pro 30K optical sensor, which has a maximum sensitivity of 30,000 DPI and a maximum speed of 750 IPS and can handle up to 70 G's of acceleration. It also has a customizable tilt wheel, which can be tuned in Razer's Synapse software.

I used this mouse for two years straight, until I recently replaced it with the Razer Naga V3 Pro — more because my Naga V2 Pro was starting to look a little worse for the wear, not because it wasn't still a fantastic mouse. You can read my full review of the Razer Naga V2 Pro here. — Sarah

The HyperX Cloud III wired gaming headset is one of the most comfortable headsets we've ever tested — it's almost exactly the same as the HyperX Cloud III S Wireless, just, well, wired. It has a premium build with a steel headband and curved aluminum forks, large over-ear earcups with leatherette-covered memory foam padding, and a leatherette-covered padded headband. It's sleek and understated, with a detachable boom microphone, and it's fairly lightweight at just 10.86oz / 308g. And it's currently on sale for $39 at Walmart — down $60.99 from its MSRP of $99.99.

The HyperX Cloud III is a wired gaming headset with a detachable microphone. It features 53mm drivers and virtual surround sound support.

The Cloud III wired gaming headset is basically the most comfortable headset we've tested in recent years. It's fairly adjustable, with earcups that tilt and are independently height-adjustable (they don't pivot, but the forks allow for some lateral movement and the headband is very flexible). The memory foam padding is thick and soft enough to wear comfortably over glasses, and the clamping force is practically perfect — enough that it won't fall off if you tilt your head back, but not much stronger than that. Add this into the weight and you have a headset that you can wear for hours and hours at a time without needing a break.

The headset sports HyperX's angled 53mm dynamic drivers, which have a frequency response range of 10 - 21,000 Hz — slightly outside the typical frequency response range of most gaming headsets, and nicely tuned to give you a neutral audio profile that still brings plenty of bass. This is the wired version, and it comes with an analog cable that can plug into a USB cable extension, which gives you plenty of length for when you're sitting at a PC while still being able to plug into any standard 3.5mm jack. It was already a good deal at its starting $100 price point, and at $39 it's absolutely worth it.

You can read my full review of the HyperX Cloud III wired gaming headset here. — Sarah

The quirky G3S case from Wokyis might be pushing the limits of practicality (not to mention copyright infringement), but it sure is cute and nostalgic. It’s a plastic shell that tips your Mac Mini (M6, M5 Pro, and M4 models) on its side and turns it into a tiny Power Mac G3 tower.

Whether you were a Mac fan in the late 90s or not, there’s a whole lot of nostalgia in this design. It’s available in four colors and is currently 50% off, taking it down to $19.99 at Amazon.

This ABS plastic Mac Mini case is pure nostalgia and not all that practical, but there are benefits to tipping Apple’s smallest Mac up on its side.

Aside from the throwback 90s looks, tipping the Mac Mini on its side like this actually lets you press the power button without lifting up the mini PC. Plus, if your desk space is cramped, putting the system on its side will free up some room. -- Matt Safford

If you're in the market for a current-gen RTX 50-series card that won't set you back thousands of dollars, then this might be the deal for you. Newegg is selling the cheapest RTX 5060 you can buy right now at $439.99, an $80 saving. While that's a far cry from the MSRP of $299, GPUs are very expensive these days, so this is about as good as it gets for 1080p gaming.

Get an RTX 5060 with 8GB of GDDR7 VRAM, clock speeds of 2550 MHz, 3840 CUDA cores, and a free GPU holder.

At 1080p, the RTX 5060 can put out more than 60 fps, making it perfect for entry-level gaming. It also supports Nvidia's DLSS technologies, so you can squeeze out more frames or even try your hand at 1440p.

This specific version of the RTX 5060 is Zotac's AMP series, with core clocks of 2550 MHz, with the same speed listed for its boost clocks. It has 3840 CUDA cores, and 8GB of GDDR7 VRAM with a 128-bit memory interface. While this won't blow titles out of the water at 4K, this is budget gaming performance at a time when GPUs are becoming increasingly more expensive. - Stephen Warwick

Buying a PC on Black Friday doesn't have to mean spending the Earth. If you want a budget build, this Intel Core i7 14700F rig from Cyberpower is a fantastic cheap option for 1080p gaming. With an RTX 5060 Ti 8GB, this should be brilliant for entry-level gaming and could even be pushed to 1440p with Nvidia's DLSS technology.

The CyberPower Gamer Xtreme prebuilt PC offers a 20-Core Intel i7 14700F CPU, RTX 5060 Ti GPU, 16GB of DDR5 memory, and 1 TB of storage, wrapped up in a white case, and flush with glowing RGB fans.

As you can see from our testing data, in our 19-game testing suite, the RTX 5060 Ti 8GB is good for average frame rates of 72 fps. This drops to around 46 at 1440p without any help from frame generation.

The CPU in this build is Intel's i7 14700F with 20 cores and 28 threads, boasting boost clocks of up to 5.4 GHz- a great processor for productivity and gaming.

Aside from the potent 20-core CPU and GPU for 1080, you also get 16GB of DDR5 RAM and a 1TB SSD. Windows 11 Home comes as standard, and the motherboard supports Wi-Fi 6 and Bluetooth 5.3. There are also ports aplenty. - Stephen Warwick

Samsung's P9 Express microSDXC is one of the top storage solutions for Nintendo Switch 2. With transfer speeds of up to 800 MB/s and similar sequential read speeds, this is a speedy storage solution for your handheld.

The Switch 2 ships with 256GB of internal storage as standard, so a 512GB expansion will triple that capacity for storing games and files. While not quite its lowest-ever price, there's a great deal on this card, 38% off at Amazon, now just $92.99.

The Samsung P9 is a microSD Express card that offers great performance and reliability for its price. The 512GB model is currently priced at its original MSRP of $99.99.

The P9 Express comes with Dynamic Thermal Guard technology to stop your card from overheating while in use for smoother gameplay. It also has a three-year warranty and can be used with microSD UHS-I devices such as tablets and drones, too.

The 256GB model is also on sale, an arguably better value. At 44% off, it's less than half the price of the 512GB model. In theory, buying two would get you the same amount of storage for $89, provided you don't mind swapping cards around.

The Samsung P9 is a microSD Express card that offers great performance and reliability for its price. The 256GB model is currently priced at its original MSRP of $44.99.

With SSD and flash storage prices through the roof thanks to AI, this is a solid deal on a great Nintendo Switch 2 card. - Stephen Warwick

I use the Gateron Oil King Ghost Pro switches on my own keyboard, and they're a go-to linear switch for a good reason. The heavier 50gf operating force is heavier than a standard Red-style switch, leading to a deep sound and more pronounced feedback while typing, particularly if you're a heavy typer.

The Oil King Ghost Pro switches are linear key switches for a mechanical keyboard with a 50gf operating force.

These switches are an upgraded version of standard Oil Kings, with the new Ghost name noting the passthrough channel for lighting. The switches themselves are the same, and they come factory lubricated, so they sound great out of the box. You can use the switches with any standard 3-pin or 5-pin PCB — Jake Roach

This hefty Lenovo Legion gaming laptop is the first RTX 5090-powered laptop we've seen under $4,000. This is a huge spec with a 240Hz OLED display, 24GB VRAM GPU, a massive 24-core Intel Core Ultra 9 290HX CPU, 32GB of DDR5 RAM, and a 1TB SSD.

The 16-inch Lenovo Legion Pro 7i gaming laptop comes with an Intel Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus CPU, RTX 5090 (175W TGP) GPU, 32GB of DDR5 memory, and 1TB of storage. The OLED display offers a 240Hz refresh rate and a 2560 x 1600 resolution.

With its 24 cores and performance core boost clocks of up to 5.5 GHz, this is a fantastic mobile CPU for both work and play. Combined with the laptop RTX 5090, the best laptop GPU on the market, this will make light work of any title you can throw at it in the 2560 x 1200 resolution. That stunning OLED will really make games pop, too.

Also offers 1x Thunderbolt 4 port (USB-C), 1x 3.2 Gen 2 (USB-C), 1x USB 3.2 Gen 2 (USB-A), 2x USB 3.2 Gen 1 (USB-A), a 3.5mm headphone jack, 1x HDMI 2.1 port, and a 2.5 Gbps Ethernet jack, as well as Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4. While we haven't reviewed this specific spec, in our Lenovo Legion Pro 7i Gen 10 review, the laptop scored very well thanks to its exceptional OLED screen, aluminum chassis, and sharp webcam. - Stephen Warwick

Earlier this week, we highlighted a great deal on Apple's MacBook Neo, which is $100 off and back to its original launch price of $599. This is also better than the previous $50 discount to $649, so if you missed out the first time, this deal is now better! The $599 price gets you 256GB of storage and 8GB of RAM, and is available in all four of Apple's vibrant colors.

You can also snag the 512GB version for $699, a $100 discount.

Apple's base MacBook Neo has an A18 Pro chip, 256GB of storage, and 8GB of RAM. A solid alternative with a more powerful SoC.

The A18 Pro chip in the MacBook Neo is solid for single-core productivity performance excelling in single-core performance, though the 8GB can be difficult for serious multitasking. For people working on basic tasks, this is going to be sufficient.There have been a handful of other deals on the Neo so far this week. We saw the base model drop to $599 (in citrus only) at one point, while the upgraded 512GB model with Touch ID dropped to $699 (in blush) at another. It's possible we'll see more color-specific price drops, but it's not a guarantee, and $649 isn't bad given the RAM situation. — Andrew E. Freedman

In what might be one of the best gaming PC deals we've seen so far, this HyperX OMEN desktop at Best Buy, featuring Intel's Core Ultra 7 270K Plus and RTX 5080 GPU, is now just $2,699. The graphics card in this build alone currently retails for around $1,700, making this a really good value build.

Get an RTX 5080 PC with Intel Core Ultra 7 270K Plus, 16GB of RAM, and a 1TB SSD, with plenty of space to upgrade. Also features Wi-Fi 7.

The star of the show here is the RTX 5080, a fully-fledged 4K GPU that will take care of any title you want to play at high resolutions and settings. That's complemented by the Intel Core Ultra 7 270K, a much-improved Intel gaming CPU released not too long ago. With 24 cores, it performs extremely well in productivity tasks as well as gaming. While it can't quite match the X3D SKUs of AMD for gaming performance, it is still a very strong desktop CPU.

The supporting cast of the build is perhaps the only compromise. The 1TB SSD is fine to get you started, but 16GB of RAM is a little less than we'd like in a build of this caliber. Still, this is such a cheap build for an RTX 5080 that it will be worth the trade-off for some. Of course, if you already have some DDR5 RAM lying around, you could swap that in, or you could spend some of that $1,700 saving on an upgrade.

The build supports up to 128GB of memory, with 4 DIMM slots for future expansion. It also has two further SSD slots, as well as Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.0, thanks to the Intel Z890 motherboard inside.

This build will not be around for long, so move fast if you want to grab one. - Stephen Warwick

Whether you need to upgrade your boot drive or you’re attempting to rescue the laptop or gaming PC of a friend or family member, an SSD cloner can make a scary, potentially tedious job surprisingly easy. I know because I bought this cloner a couple of years ago (when it cost about $15 more) and moved someone’s existing OS from an extremely cramped 128GB drive onto a faster 512GB drive in less than half an hour. And now Rosewill’s SSD cloner is on sale for its lowest-ever price at Amazon.

With support for NVMe M.2 SSDs and offline cloning, this handy device makes it simple to move your files or OS from one drive to another. And with a 20 Gbps USB-C interface, it's also speedy in your OS of choice if you want to use software to clone or move your data between drives.

Keep in mind this device only supports M Key PCIe / NVMe drives, so it won’t work with SATA M.2 drives. But it can work both as a standalone drive or with software if you need to, say, resize the partition. The Rosewill cloner is also handy for checking the contents of M.2 drives you may have lying around. But if that's all you need, you can get a good tool-free enclosure for less than $20. -- Matt Safford

#10409. Why employees are ‘habit hugging’ at work

If you’re prone to hanging on to the way things always used to be done at work, you might be “habit hugging.” It’s where employees hold on to familiar routines even after new tools and processes have been introduced.

Habit hugging may be a sign of insecurity, or a form of self-preservation — finding stability and control in a working world that feels increasingly unfamiliar.

A new report by online learning platform TalentLMS, based on a survey of 1,500 US employees who had received training on a new tool, technology, process, or way of working in the previous 12 months, found that 65% of respondents said letting go of an old habit is harder than learning a new one. And only 41% consistently used a new way of working after they were trained on it. Meanwhile, 42% admitted they still used tools or processes their managers believed had been replaced.

Multiple industries are evolving and being disrupted by AI. Habit hugging could be a response to the pressure employees feel to continually adapt as everything changes around them. As uncertainty grows both inside and outside the office, sticking to what you know may offer a little comfort.

There’s a tension between employers demanding adaptability and employees being expected to maintain productivity throughout that change: The report found that 48% of respondents felt rushed to adopt new ways of working. Employers aren’t necessarily helping their workforce overcome their old habits when they expect them to adopt new systems without slowing down or making mistakes.

That pressure may also make employees reluctant to admit they’re struggling. The report found that 45% of respondents had avoided questioning a new way of working because they didn’t want to appear resistant. Among those who continued to use, or fell back on, old ways of working, 22% said they feared making mistakes or looking slow.

When workplaces demand this constant adaptation without creating the space for it, employees might prefer to stick to what they know. Sixty percent said their workplace prioritized results over the process of getting them, while just 41% said they felt they were given room to be less productive while learning something new.

There may also be a question of trust. Employees who have seen workplace initiatives and technologies come and go may be reluctant to embrace the latest change, particularly if they aren’t convinced it will last. They may prefer to future-proof themselves by leaning on the skills and systems they already know, rather than investing time in learning a new tool that could be forgotten about in six months.

That reluctance could be costing employers: The report found that 29% of employees said their company was investing in tools they’d stopped using.

But habit hugging isn’t necessarily an outright rejection of change. The report found that 73% of respondents mixed old and new ways of working to get the job done, suggesting employees may be finding ways to adapt without abandoning familiar routines altogether.

Rather than blindly embracing the latest systems, people may be finding their own ways of adapting to a future nobody is sure of.

We're thrilled to share that Scaleway is now a supported Inference Provider on the Hugging Face Hub! Scaleway joins our growing ecosystem, enhancing the breadth and capabilities of serverless inference directly on the Hub’s model pages. Inference Providers are also seamlessly integrated into our client SDKs (for both JS and Python), making it super easy to use a wide variety of models with your preferred providers.

This launch makes it easier than ever to access popular open-weight models like gpt-oss, Qwen3, DeepSeek R1, and Gemma 3 — right from Hugging Face. You can browse Scaleway's org on the Hub at https://huggingface.co/scaleway and try trending supported models at https://huggingface.co/models?inference_provider=scaleway&sort=trending.

Scaleway Generative APIs is a fully managed, serverless service that provides access to frontier AI models from leading research labs via simple API calls. The service offers competitive pay-per-token pricing starting at €0.20 per million tokens.

The service runs on secure infrastructure located in European data centers (Paris, France), ensuring data sovereignty and low latency for European users. The platform supports advanced features including structured outputs, function calling, and multimodal capabilities for both text and image processing.

Built for production use, Scaleway's inference infrastructure delivers sub-200ms response times for first tokens, making it ideal for interactive applications and agentic workflows. The service supports both text generation and embedding models. You can learn more about Scaleway's platform and infrastructure at https://www.scaleway.com/en/generative-apis/.

Read more about how to use Scaleway as an Inference Provider in its dedicated documentation page.

The following example shows how to use OpenAI's gpt-oss-120b using Scaleway as the inference provider. You can use a Hugging Face token for automatic routing through Hugging Face, or your own Scaleway API key if you have one.

Note: this requires using a recent version of huggingface_hub (>= 0.34.6).

For direct requests, i.e. when you use the key from an inference provider, you are billed by the corresponding provider. For instance, if you use a Scaleway API key you're billed on your Scaleway account.

For routed requests, i.e. when you authenticate via the Hugging Face Hub, you'll only pay the standard provider API rates. There's no additional markup from us; we just pass through the provider costs directly. (In the future, we may establish revenue-sharing agreements with our provider partners.)

We also provide free inference with a small quota for our signed-in free users, but please upgrade to PRO if you can!

#10407. Markdown to PDF in 2026: No-Install Methods and the Rendering Problems Nobody Warns You About

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Converting Markdown to PDF is easy until the document has real content: long code blocks, wide tables, images and non-Latin text are where most tools fall apart.

Pandoc with LaTeX is still the most powerful route, but it needs a large install and trips over Unicode and emoji unless you switch engines and fonts.

Browser-based approaches (print CSS, Chromium-powered converters, in-browser tools) avoid the install and give you HTML-quality rendering, as long as you control page breaks.

A handful of print CSS rules (@page, break-inside: avoid, break-after: avoid) fix the majority of ugly PDFs, whichever tool you use.

Choose the tool by the document: a quick README export, a long technical report and a multilingual document each have a different best option.

I write almost everything in Markdown: READMEs, release notes, client handovers, meeting notes. And at least once a week, someone asks for "the PDF version". Every time, the conversion looks fine on the first page and falls apart somewhere around page three: a code block split in half, a table running off the edge, an emoji replaced by an empty box.

SitePoint covered the classic route back in 2015 with Creating PDFs from Markdown with Pandoc and LaTeX. That approach still works. But a lot has changed since then, and today there are several ways to get a clean PDF without installing a TeX distribution. This article compares them, then goes through the rendering problems you'll actually hit, with a fix for each.

Pandoc is still the Swiss Army knife. The simplest command is:

By default, that goes through LaTeX, which means you need a TeX distribution installed (several gigabytes for a full one). The output is beautiful for prose and math, but LaTeX has strong opinions about layout, and customizing it means writing LaTeX.

Pandoc can also render through an HTML engine instead, which lets you style the PDF with CSS:

Best for: long documents, academic writing, math, automated pipelines.

Watch out for: install size, Unicode handling with the default engine (more on that below).

Render the Markdown to HTML (any previewer, a static site, a GitHub page) and print it to PDF. It's free and already installed everywhere, but you inherit whatever the page looks like on screen: navigation bars, sidebars, and page breaks wherever they happen to fall.

Best for: quick, one-off exports of short documents.

Watch out for: zero control over page breaks unless the page ships print CSS.

Extensions like Markdown PDF for VS Code, or CLI tools like md-to-pdf, render your Markdown to HTML and print it with a headless Chromium:

You get the same rendering quality as a browser, plus a config file for CSS, margins, headers and footers. The trade-off is a Node install and a downloaded Chromium.

Best for: developers who live in their editor or want CI-friendly exports.

Watch out for: the first run downloads a browser, and print CSS is still your job.

The newest option is tools that do the whole conversion inside the browser tab: you paste or drop the .md file, preview the actual pages and download the PDF. The good ones don't upload your file anywhere, which matters for client documents and internal notes.

Best for: people who don't want to install anything, non-developers on your team, private documents.

Watch out for: many online converters do upload your file to a server; check before you paste anything confidential.

Whichever method you pick, the same handful of problems show up as soon as the document is longer than a page. Most of them are fixed with print CSS, which works in Pandoc's HTML engines, Chromium-based tools and any HTML you print from a browser.

A 20-line function cut after line 3, with the rest on the next page, is the most common complaint. The fix is to ask the renderer not to break inside the block:

One caveat: a block longer than a full page has to break. For those, it's better to let it break cleanly than to push it to a new page and leave a huge gap.

On screen, a long line in a code block scrolls horizontally. On paper, there's no scrollbar, so it's simply cut off. Wrap long lines in print:

Tables with many columns overflow the page or get squeezed until every cell is one word per line. Three things help: a smaller font size for tables, a landscape page for the worst offenders, and avoiding breaks in the middle of short tables:

If a table genuinely needs eight columns, consider whether it should be a table in the PDF at all, or an appendix in landscape.

A heading alone at the bottom of a page, with its content on the next one, looks broken. This rule keeps a heading attached to what follows it:

Support for break-after: avoid varies between rendering engines, so test it with yours; when it isn't honored, a manual page break before the heading is the reliable fallback.

Markdown has no syntax for a page break. The usual trick is a raw HTML element that print CSS turns into a break:

Some converters also recognize a comment like , which has the advantage of staying invisible when the same file is rendered on GitHub.

Images are inserted at their natural size, so a 4000-pixel screenshot spills off the page. Cap them:

For blurry images, the problem is usually the opposite: a small screenshot stretched to page width. Export screenshots at 2x if they're going into a PDF.

This one is specific to the LaTeX route. With the default pdflatex engine, Unicode characters outside its supported set produce errors or simply vanish. Switch to XeLaTeX or LuaLaTeX and give it a font that actually contains the characters:

Emoji are harder still in LaTeX and often need a dedicated package. HTML-based renderers handle both far better, because they use the operating system's font fallback just like a web page does.

Internal links ([see setup](#setup)) and external links should stay clickable. HTML-based renderers usually keep both. If yours doesn't, check that headings get IDs (most Markdown parsers add them) and that the PDF engine preserves link annotations.

Put together, these rules make a solid starting point for any HTML-based route:

Save it as print.css and pass it to Pandoc (--css=print.css with an HTML engine), to md-to-pdf through its config, or include it in the HTML you print from the browser.

My rule of thumb after a lot of trial and error:

A quick README or notes export, no install, private content: an in-browser converter. Full disclosure: this need is why I built the free Markdown to PDF converter on AwesomeToolkit, and it's what I use for this case now. It renders real A4 or Letter pages as you type, has an option to keep code blocks and tables whole, adds page numbers and a table of contents, and the conversion happens in the browser, so the file isn't uploaded anywhere.

Documentation in a repo, exported in CI: md-to-pdf or Pandoc with an HTML engine, plus the stylesheet above.

Long reports, math, academic formatting: Pandoc with XeLaTeX, using a font that covers every script in the document.

Something you'll print once and forget: the browser's Print to PDF is fine.

Whatever you choose, the biggest quality jump comes from the print rules, not the tool. Ten lines of CSS turn "it looks fine until page three" into a PDF you can actually send.

Yes. Your browser's Print to PDF works on any rendered Markdown, and in-browser converters do the whole conversion in a tab. Check that the converter processes files locally if the content is private.

The default pdflatex engine has limited Unicode support. Use --pdf-engine=xelatex or lualatex and set a font that contains the characters with -V mainfont= (and -V CJKmainfont= for CJK text).

Markdown has no native syntax for it. Insert

where you want the break, or use the page-break comment your converter supports.

Add pre { break-inside: avoid; } to your print CSS. Blocks longer than a page will still break, which is expected.

With HTML-based renderers, usually yes, both external links and links to headings inside the document. Test internal links in particular, since they depend on headings having IDs.

#10406. How job hunting became an expensive cash suck

There’s an expense that’s easy to overlook when talking about the cost of living: getting and keeping a job. 

We tend to think of work as the thing that pays the bills, but commuting and the other costs associated with it come with a price tag of their own. In a recent TikTok video posted in October, content creator Char shared that she had just had to quit her job because she could no longer afford the commute. 

Char, who lives in the UK, said the amount of money she used to spend on a full tank of fuel now only filled her car halfway. And with fuel prices showing no sign of easing, she said, the commute was only going to get more expensive.

“I can’t afford to keep driving to work,” Char said. “I can’t afford to live. Something has to give.” 

And right now, she decided, that something was her job. She would have to search for a position closer to home. 

In the comments, people shared they had been in a similar position recently, also highlighting how everything else had hit them financially, such as grocery prices and rent.

Commuting costs are also affecting people looking for work. Some job seekers have shared online how the expense of traveling to interviews is becoming difficult to manage. One creator said in a recent TikTok that she can no longer afford the job hunt.

“Assuming you get past the 12,000 rounds of phone screens and Zooms, and you are invited to an on-site interview, what if you don’t have the money to commute?” she said.


Compound that with the fact many are interviewing at several different companies at once, she said, and the costs quickly rack up. 

The costs aren’t necessarily limited to getting from A to B. Job seekers may also need to pay for childcare, buy appropriate clothes, or cover other expenses associated with making a good impression. For those who have been unemployed for some time, and have to interview in person several times, they can easily end up hundreds of dollars out of pocket.

An Indeed/Harris Poll survey found that 84% of job seekers had spent money attending an in-person interview. Of those who had spent money, 30% said they spent at least $100 on their most recent interview.

Meanwhile, a 2026 Monster survey of 1,005 employed US adults found that 49% of workers had turned down a job opportunity because of commuting costs or the length of the journey. More than three-quarters (76%) said current gas prices increased their financial stress, and 68% believed employers should help with commuting expenses when employees are required to work on-site.

Commuting costs highlight a widening inequality between people who can afford to look for work and those who can’t. For example, job seekers with savings or financial support from their families may be better positioned to travel to interviews, pursue roles further afield, or absorb the costs of a lengthy search. For others, the price of getting to work limits the opportunities they can realistically pursue.

Work is supposed to be the most obvious way of providing financial security, but that isn’t necessarily the case anymore. For some, even getting their foot in the door is becoming something they have to budget for.

#10405. Here’s the best day to shop for travel deals—and it isn’t Black Friday or Travel Tuesday

Black Friday may have come early this year, but the best travel deals are still to come, according to data from Skyscanner—which found the best day to find discounts on travel isn’t Black Friday or Travel Tuesday.

While Travel Tuesday generates plenty of buzz, Skyscanner analyzed billions of proprietary flight data points and found Cyber Monday was the cheapest day to book flights. That day had “the lowest average price per seat” across the five-day Black Friday-to-Travel Tuesday sales period last year, according to Skyscanner, a global travel platform.

“Cyber Monday offered the lowest average fares, making it a day worth checking this year,” Lourdes Losada, Skyscanner’s director of the Americas, tells Fast Company. “Start comparing fares before the sales begin so you have a baseline, then monitor prices throughout the period. Knowing what your flight typically costs makes it easier to recognize a worthwhile offer without feeling pressured by a sale’s countdown.”

However, Travel Tuesday still had plenty of standout destination-specific savings, with average flights to Fort Lauderdale, Florida; Seoul; and Honolulu dropping 28%, 24%, and 15% respectively, compared with the previous 12-month average. This is an indication that there are strong deals across the entire period.

The destination that saw the largest surge in interest was Cabo San Lucas, the Mexican resort town in Baja California Sur. Searches for the location increased 444% across the full Black Friday-to-Travel Tuesday window, compared with the previous 12-month average.

Other destinations that Americans searched for on Travel Tuesday included Florence, Italy (interest up 163%); Edinburgh, Scotland (up 162%); Liberia (up 158%), Hanoi, Vietnam (up 147%); and Tokyo (up 132%).

Where did American travelers find the biggest Black Friday and Travel Tuesday deals? For travelers looking for savings by destination, the biggest average flight price drops were for Casablanca, Morocco (-30%); Lisbon, Portugal (-28%); Sydney (-21%); Seoul (-17%); and Honolulu (-16%). 

Skyscanner’s advice for shopping the deals

Skyscanner recommends travelers be flexible with dates, set a price alert, stay open to new destinations, and check for alternative departure or arrival airports near your home and destination.

The key takeaway is that travelers shouldn’t feel pressure to book on one day, since the entire five-day window provides opportunities that might otherwise be missed, according to Skyscanner.

“Black Friday can bring a lot of tempting travel offers and it can also be an overwhelming time to book,” says Laura Lindsay, travel trends and destination expert at Skyscanner. “The key is not to rush, stay open minded and focus on the trip that works best for your budget and plans.”

#10403. Are stores open on Thanksgiving Day 2026? Holiday hours for Walmart, Whole Foods, Costco, and more

Thanksgiving centers on gratitude, which is good for mental health, as scientific studies have proven.

The stress and anxiety of the holiday season can almost seem antithetical to these findings. It’s hard to be zen when wondering if the local supermarket is open because you need another cup of milk for the mashed potatoes.

Here’s everything you need to know about what is open and closed on Thanksgiving for those last-minute needs. We even threw in some fun facts so you can wow everyone at dinner with your wit and wisdom. 

Do other countries celebrate Thanksgiving?

The United States is not the only country that celebrates gratitude at the end of the year.

The first recorded Canadian Thanksgiving took place in 1578, which was more than 40 years before its American counterpart. In Canada, Thanksgiving takes place on the second Monday in October.

In Germany, Erntedankfest, a harvest of thanks, takes place in September or October, depending on the year.

In Japan, Kinro Kansha no Hi, Labor Thanksgiving Day, focuses on appreciation for workers. This celebration evolved from an ancient rice festival and takes place on November 23.

In Liberia, Thanksgiving falls on the first Thursday of November. A spicy roast chicken is the main dish, not turkey.

Is Thanksgiving a federal holiday?

Yes. In the United States, Thanksgiving takes place on the fourth Thursday of November and is a federal holiday.

Are banks open on Thanksgiving?

No, most are closed for the holiday, as is the Federal Reserve. Online banking and ATMs outside branches are good alternatives.

Is the stock market open on Thanksgiving?

No. Even the stock market takes a day off to be grateful for capital gains. Both the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq are closed.

Is the Post Office open on Thanksgiving? Is Mail delivered?

Unless you are getting your Hogwarts acceptance letter by owl, no mail will be delivered on Thanksgiving.

Physical post office locations operated by the U.S. Postal Service will be closed for the holiday. Online services and self-serve kiosks are your best bet in a pinch.

Are FedEx and UPS delivering on Thanksgiving?

No, FedEx locations are not open and it is not delivering or picking up on Thanksgiving.

Most UPS locations are also closed and the organization is not delivering or picking up. The only exception is UPS Express Critical service. 

Are schools open on Thanksgiving?

No. The majority of schools will not be in session due to the holiday. It is always a good practice to double-check with your child’s institution.

Are restaurants open on Thanksgiving?

Yes. Many restaurants will be open. Some will even feature a special menu for the holiday as certain families would rather make reservations than a turkey with all the trimmings.

Are retail stores open on Thanksgiving?

Only some retail stores will be open on Thanksgiving. Walmart, Target, REI, Kohl’s, Dick’s Sporting Goods, and Home Depot are just some of the chains that will be closed.

It is probably safer to focus on turkey instead of shopping on Thanksgiving. On Black Friday, however, all bets are off.

Are pharmacies open on Thanksgiving?

Some pharmacies will remain open on Thanksgiving. For instance, more than 4,000 Walgreens locations will be open. It is best to double-check your favorite location before you head out so you avoid getting headaches, even if they are just metaphorical ones.

Are grocery stores open on Thanksgiving?

Only some grocery stores are open on Thanksgiving. Do not go to Costco, Trader Joe’s, Sam’s Club, Aldi or Publix for last-minute meal supplies as you will find closed doors.

Kroger says stores will be open until 4 p.m. Whole Foods says most stores are open with modified hours, so check your local location.

What television specials are happening on Thanksgiving?

Since 1924, the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade has been delighting spectators with its big balloons, floats, and musical acts.

This year marks its 100th iteration (No parades took place from 1942 to 1944 because of World War II)). However, the parade will be postponed for the first time in its history. New York City is under a high-wind warning due to a nor’easter.

New balloons joining in on the milestone celebration include Bluey, Hello Kitty, Joe Cool and Woodstock, and Sorcerer’s Apprentice Mickey.

Natasha Bedingfield, Devo, Jimmy Fallon & The Roots, Mckenna Grace, Megan Moroney, Indigo Girls, JoJo, Wyclef Jean, Queen Latifah, Leslie Odom Jr., Anthony Ramos, Smash Mouth, and Teddy Swims are just some of the performers lending their talents to the parade route.

One controversial change is a single 10-minute Broadway medley featuring performers from nine Broadway shows. Historically, several shows have been able to perform their own numbers.

The Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is broadcast on NBC on Saturday, November 28, from 8:30 a.m. to 12 noon, across all time zones. It will also be available to stream on Peacock.
