#10401. Gaia2 and ARE: Empowering the community to study agents

In an ideal world, AI agents would be reliable assistants. When given a query, they would easily manage ambiguity in instructions, construct step-by-step plans, correctly identify necessary resources, execute those plans without getting sidetracked, and adapt to unexpected events, all while maintaining accuracy and avoiding hallucinations. However, developing agents and testing these behaviors is no small feat: if you have ever tried to debug your own agent, you’ve probably observed how tedious and frustrating this can be. Existing evaluation environments are tightly coupled with the tasks they evaluate, lack real-world flexibility, and do not reflect the messy reality of open-world agents: simulated pages never fail to load, events don’t spontaneously emerge, and asynchronous chaos is absent.

That’s why we’re very happy to introduce Gaia2, the follow-up to the agentic benchmark GAIA, allowing analysis of considerably more complex behaviors. Gaia2 is released with the open Meta Agents Research Environments (ARE) framework to run, debug and evaluate agents. ARE simulates complex real world-like conditions and can be customized to further study agents behaviors. Gaia2 dataset is released under CC by 4.0 license, and ARE under MIT license.

GAIA is an agentic benchmark published in 2023, with 3 levels of information retrieval questions requiring tools, web browsing, and reasoning to solve. In 2 years, the easiest levels have become too easy for models, and the community is coming close to solving the hardest questions, so it was time for an entirely new and harder agent benchmark!

Here comes Gaia2, a follow up to GAIA, going way beyond it in terms of capabilities studied!

Where GAIA was read-only, Gaia2 is now a read-and-write benchmark, focusing on interactive behavior and complexity management. Agents are now evaluated not only on search and retrieval, but also on instruction following over ambiguous or time-sensitive queries, in a noisy environment with controlled failures - reflecting real-world conditions more than any other simulated environment. We want to test how agents manage tools or APIs that sometimes do not work, plan successions of actions with very specific time frames, and adapt to new events - a whole new range of complexity!

To do this, we use the following task groups (thanks to 1000 brand new human-created scenarios):

In the spirit of GAIA, scenarios do not require specialized knowledge: humans should in principle be able to get 100%, which allows easy debugging for model developers.

Want to explore the benchmark? Check out our dataset, which you can better display in our demo here.

Gaia2 runs with ARE, an execution environment, where an agent of your choice has access to a combination of applications and associated pre-populated data.

For Gaia2, we created a smartphone mock-up environment, simulating what a human would use in their daily life. It contains real-world applications such as messaging (Email), utilities (Calendar, Contacts, Shopping, a FileSystem, …), and a chat interface to talk to the agent. All applications are also accessible to the agents through tool calling. Last but not least, the demo also contains a simulated persona’s history of conversations and app interactions.

All agent interactions are automatically recorded as structured traces during execution for deep dives and analysis: they include tool calls, API responses, model thoughts, timing metrics (e.g., response latency), user interactions, and so forth - and can all be exported as JSON.

For reference, we compare a range of large open and closed source models: Llama 3.3-70B Instruct, Llama-4-Maverick, GPT-4o, Qwen3-235B-MoE, Grok-4, Kimi K2, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude 4 Sonnet, and GPT-5 in all reasoning modes.

All models are evaluated using the same setup (a uniform ReAct loop for consistency, temperature of 0.5, generation limit of 16K tokens), with a combination of model-as-a-judge (Llama 3.3 Instruct 70B) and exact-match evaluation depending on the particular task. All 101 tools (and the general environment description) are provided in the system prompt.

Among the evaluated models, the highest-scoring model overall as of September 2025 is GPT-5 with high reasoning, and the best open source model is Kimi K2.

Some capabilities appear to be already close to solved by the best models: execution of simple tool calls and instruction following (execution), and overall search (as we could have guessed from current results on GAIA). The ambiguity, adaptability, and noise splits remain challenging for now for all models, and it’s interesting to see that performance on what were considered complex agentic tasks (instruction following and search) is not a good proxy for performance on closer-to-real-world tasks. Last but not least, the hardest split for all models at the moment is the time one: it’s very hard at this moment for models to correctly handle time-sensitive actions (though this could likely be mitigated by the use of specialised tools and better temporal reasoning). Detailed analysis of these results can be found in the paper.

However, we believe it’s important to push reporting beyond raw scores: if the model is correct but took several thousand tokens to reach the correct solution, or ran for several hours, it is “not as good” as a model which succeeded orders of magnitude faster. We therefore also normalize scores for cost, quantified as the average number of LLM calls and output tokens (which both define a cost-performance Pareto frontier). In the paper you’ll find score vs monetary cost and time.

If you want to evaluate your model on Gaia2, you can follow these steps:

First, install Meta's Agent Research Environment in your Python environment of choice (uv, conda, virtualenv, ...)

Then, run the benchmark for all configurations: execution, search, adaptability, time and ambiguity. Don't forget to upload all results to the hub with the hf_upload kwarg!

Run the oracle to get your aggregated score file

Finally, add all the relevant information about your model in the README, and share it on the leaderboard to centralize Gaia2 traces here!

Beyond benchmark scenarios, you can use Gaia2 apps and content in ARE to see if the model is able to correctly solve less verifiable tasks such as loading emails, writing follow-ups, adding events to the calendar or booking meetings - in sum, providing the perfect setup to evaluate your AI assistants through interaction!

You can also easily customise the environment, by 1) connecting your tools (via MCP or directly ) to test your agents on it; 2) implementing your own scenarios, including defining trigger or timed events (eg: after 2 minutes, the Mail app will receive a new email from Contact), to see how the agent is able to adapt to an evolving environment

(As the agents are by default json agents, they can’t mess up your machine, unless of course you connect them to external apps with unsafe rights. So, operate with caution when adding your own apps or using untrusted MCPs)

Here are several use cases that we’ve used ARE for:

We recorded 3 videos so you can check some of these use cases (but of course, we hope the community gets creative with ARE :hugging_face:). For these videos, we use the default demo described above, which contains the simulated life of Linda Renne, PhD student in machine learning.

To test how good the default model is at event organisation, let’s plan a birthday party!

We first ask the agent to text everyone in the Renne family about the user’s 30th birthday party on November 7. The default universe has 21 contacts in the list, including 5 Renne family members - Linda, the simulation “owner”, George and Stephie, her parents, Anna her sister, and Morgan her grandfather. The agent successfully goes through the contact list, finds the four family members, and texts them.

Next, we ask the agent to create a calendar invite and add them as invitees. The agent remembers the above context! It creates a calendar invite on the correct date and correctly adds the family members to it.

ARE also allows us to check the traces behind the actions taken by the agent. Upon opening the Agent logs tool on the left, we can see the system prompt, the chain of thought, multi-step actions taken with the tools called, and the outcomes as neatly organised logs. Everything can be exported as json if you want to consult things offline!

In this last example, we connect ARE to a remote robot arm via MCP, so it can gesture things to us, then ask the agent to answer our yes or no questions by waving the robot arm! Here’s what it looks like.

But these examples are only very simple starting points, and we’re really looking towards what you’ll build! (For more advanced users, you can even directly install and edit the Meta-ARE code here.)

Gaia2 and ARE are new research tools that we hope will empower anyone to easily build more reliable and adaptable AI agents - by allowing easy experiments, making real-world evaluation accessible to anyone, as well as improving trust through transparent, reproducible benchmarks and debuggable traces.

We’d love to see what you will do with this project!

Build environments and evaluate AI agents

#10400. Stop scheduling meetings over lunch

Ever wonder what happened to the front porch?

The front porch used to play an important role in everyday life. Neighbors who weren’t necessarily close friends saw each other, stopped to talk, and maintained a sense of community. Then daily life moved indoors. Air-conditioning made staying inside more comfortable, television pulled families into the living room, and backyard patios offered more privacy so you didn’t have to say “hi” to the overly talkative neighbor.

There was no single moment when the front porch disappeared. It just gradually became less central to the way people connected, and faded away.

The lunch break is headed in the same direction.

Technology has made it possible to collaborate across locations and time zones, while AI is helping work move faster than ever. But constant connectivity has also weakened the boundaries around the workday. An open hour at noon can quickly become another meeting or a chance to catch up on work.

Peer pressure plays a role too. Employees see colleagues and leaders eating at their desks or scheduling meetings over lunch with a polite, “Sorry, it was the only free time I could find.” Eventually, skipping lunch becomes an unwritten expectation rather than an individual choice. And when that behavior is rewarded with recognition and career growth, the expectation becomes even harder to challenge.

Yet lunch is one of the few natural opportunities during the workday to step away and connect with colleagues without an agenda. It also gives employees a chance to decompress, take a walk, and mentally reset before tackling the rest of the day. Leaders who want sustainable performance should make sure that opportunity doesn’t disappear.

5 ways to protect lunch breaks 

You don’t have to mandate how employees spend lunch. Some people want to eat with colleagues. Others prefer to take a walk, run an errand, or simply be alone. 

The point is to create a culture where stepping away feels like a normal choice. And it requires looking at the signals your workplace sends about availability, performance, and connection.

1. Create space that can’t automatically become another meeting

If every open block on a calendar is considered schedulable, lunch will always be at risk. Consider establishing meeting-free windows during the day so employees have protected time to recharge.

Adapt that approach for global and frontline teams instead of assuming the same time works for everyone. Employees across time zones and operating environments may need different windows, but the principle is the same: Build recovery into the work day.

2. Model the behavior you want 

Culture is a collection of the norms, values, and behaviors that employees see around them every day. And nothing is more important for building culture than what employees see from their leaders. If leaders are regularly scheduling meetings during lunch, it’s a signal that the break isn’t protected. New employees in particular pick up such signals, and quickly learn which behaviors are associated with success (and failure) in their new team or organization.

Your own calendar also sends a powerful message. Protecting and taking your lunch break is critical, as is extending the same respect to your team during their breaks. These small, visible behaviors speak louder than words.

3. Treat skipped lunches as an important signal

Understanding and measuring workplace culture requires listening in different ways. Surveys alone don’t cut it. Paying attention to skipped lunches can be part of that strategy. And while working through lunch might ultimately be a personal preference, when it becomes the norm, it tells you something about your organization.

If employees feel they can’t step away for even 30 minutes without falling behind, that’s a strong signal that the always-on mentality is rampant in your organization. Burnout in these cultures can be prolific, and workloads, staffing levels, and meeting demands should be questioned.

But consider the unwritten expectations, too. What happens when employees say no? Is their commitment to the team or organization questioned? Are they no longer seen as top performers?

4. Use lunch to make human connection easier

Lunch offers us much of what the front porch did: unstructured time together. No agendas, no project tasks, no scheduled meetings. Instead, employees have space and time to build connections and relationships within and beyond their immediate teams.

That’s especially important for younger workers. Gen Z employees have 47% increased odds of saying they can’t find community at work, and 32% increased odds of saying technology makes it difficult to disconnect from work.

This research demonstrates that while technology makes it easier to stay in contact, it doesn’t guarantee genuine relationships. Employees can be constantly reachable and still feel they don’t know their colleagues at all.

Lunchtime gives employees room for conversations that aren’t tied to a project, deadline, or key performance indicator. When we protect this space, we create organic opportunities to build relationships and communities that are much more difficult to develop through structured interaction.

5. Reward outcomes instead of constant availability

Employees pay attention to who and what is getting recognized. If you want to shift behavior, change what you reward. Recognition is a powerful tool for change management.

Focus recognition on the outcomes and behaviors you want to encourage. Make it clear that high performance doesn’t require employees to prove they’re always available. When organizations reinforce behaviors through integrated recognition, they see a 43% reduction in early warning signs of burnout.

The focus on outcomes becomes even more important as AI increases the speed and capacity of work. When employees can accomplish more in less time, resist the temptation to fill every available minute with more work. Be deliberate about rewarding strong outcomes rather than constant activity.

The case for keeping lunch on the calendar

As technology makes it easier to stay connected and accomplish more throughout the day, protecting time for a real break gets harder. 

Push back on that pressure by establishing clear boundaries and modeling them yourself. Giving employees permission to pause creates room to recover and connect, while reinforcing that performance doesn’t depend on always-on expectations.

How you approach lunch reflects the broader expectations you set for your workplace. By making breaks a regular part of the day, you can help establish healthier habits that become a lasting part of your culture.

#10398. In the AI era, dependability is the key to customer loyalty

Before I launched my own company, I worked as a web developer for a New York media company. One of my colleagues was a coding savant. They could build a webpage in mere hours, an incredible feat in the early aughts. They could identify bugs and rapidly come up with smart solutions. But they also frequently disappeared in the middle of the workday and took personal days with little to no notice. My colleague was reliable in their work, but not dependable day-to-day. Employees—and organizations—need both to provide real value.

In today’s fast-changing tech landscape, customer expectations are evolving. Customers expect businesses to be reliable and digital experiences to work as promised. At the same time, they’re becoming wary of the tech race. In a recent survey of about 3,500 U.S. consumers about their digital lives, 77% said tech companies focus more on outpacing the competition than on solving real user problems.

What separates leading organizations in the AI era is not reliability alone, but dependability at every step. Here’s how leaders and organizations can deliver on that promise.

Make every customer experience consistent

Having a product or service work the way you need it to is important. No doubt, customers take note. In the above-mentioned survey, three-quarters of consumers reported that new tech features improved their lives and that digital experiences were becoming more personalized. At the same time, fewer than 30% said they strongly agree with that sentiment.

The takeaway for businesses: There’s room for improvement. Where can businesses identify those areas for improvement? One strategy is ensuring that the entire user experience is 24/7 consistent. Every interaction along the customer journey, from initial inquiries to troubleshooting, should provide the same level of care and attention. Artificial intelligence can help make that possible.

Customized AI agents, for example, can respond to common inquiries around the clock. When faced with more complex or nuanced issues, they can escalate the matter to human representatives. This ensures customers can connect with your company whenever they need to, and without requiring employees to be always on.

Consistency also means ensuring customers receive the same information across channels, whether they’re perusing the website, DMing with a chatbot via an app, or speaking with an employee on the phone. 

For customers, the result isn’t just a reliable product or service—it’s feeling heard and seen. That’s where dependability makes a difference. Customers build trust when every interaction feels responsive and aligns with what the organization has promised.

Ensure every interaction feels like your brand

Every interaction between customers and your company is an opportunity to build a relationship—or weaken an existing one.

Especially in the age of AI, your company’s voice has to be cohesive, whether customers are chatting with an employee or a chatbot. As noted in Harvard Business Review, chatbots are becoming the frontline of customer interactions—and they can shape how customers perceive your brand, from its personality and values to its approach to customer service.

What’s more, the HBR article highlights research showing that people who interacted with a warm, supportive AI companion felt closer to the chatbot than to colleagues, acquaintances, and even friends. Users of a more task-oriented assistant, on the other hand, felt less connected to it than to their human relationships. 

The implication for brands: How AI communicates impacts the customer experience, as well as the kind of relationship customers believe they have with a company.

For starters, customer-facing AI tools should reflect your brand identity. With a chatbot, for example, you can begin by defining its personality; whether it’s a supportive coach, an empathetic companion, or a sophisticated advisor. Decide the kind of information it handles and when conversations should be handed off to a human. 

AI-powered chatbots should do more than just sound like your brand. They should deliver the kind of relationship that reflects your company’s mission and values. 

Anticipate customer needs and act on them

In the AI era, one of the biggest competitive advantages is anticipating customers’ needs, sometimes even before they’re aware of them. Consider a large language model like ChatGPT, which predicts what you might need next, encouraging users to continue engaging with it. For instance, you prompt ChatGPT to generate an outline; it does, then asks whether you’d like a draft introduction as well. Whether or not you say yes is your choice, but the option is there.  

Today’s companies can leverage AI to anticipate needs, streamline service, and resolve issues faster. AI-powered platforms like Chorus.ai can analyze customer interactions, synthesize sentiments, and flag recurring pain points. Then, your employees can better understand the customer experience and focus on developing solutions.

Looking forward, AI-powered tools like Thematic can identify emerging trends and themes, helping companies evolve their products and services to remain competitive. As the founder of a company that began with online forms and has continually expanded its offerings over the past two decades, I know firsthand the importance of adapting to changing needs and spotting market opportunities.

Importantly, AI is not error proof. Humans should always be kept in the loop to review decisions that impact the customer experience. Be transparent about AI use and jump in if and when AI falls short. That kind of behavior builds dependability and, on the customer side, reinforces loyalty.

#10397. What Is the Best UI design Tool? 8 Tools Compared by the Job They Do (2026)

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

The ideal UI testing tool is the one that discovers what your users discover first: broken layouts, usability issues that no longer work, and new accessibility issues in all the browsers your users use before a change goes into the repository. In 2026, most frontend teams don't rely on a single tool to do all of that. The best setups involve two layers: a test runner layer that launches the browser and monitors behavior, and a UI testing and review platform that visually checks the outcome and routes changes to the right stakeholders for sign-off.

Even with the right stack, it still relies on what your team needs to catch. Different teams will focus on different points: a QA team trying to automate checkout flows, a design system team defending shared components, and a single developer working on a tight budget will all be somewhere different. This guide is categorized by the job these UI testing tools do, then connects them.

Most "best UI testing tool" lists rank test runners and visual testing platforms against each other as if they were interchangeable. They aren't. UI testing covers four distinct jobs:

Functional testing: Does the UI respond correctly when a user clicks, types, or hovers?

Visual testing: Does the UI still look right across layout, color, typography, and spacing?

Accessibility testing: Can people using keyboards and screen readers use it, and did this change introduce new violations?

Cross-browser and device coverage: Does it work in Safari on mobile, not just Chrome on a developer's laptop?

There are also other levels of UI tests. Unit tests test the logic but don't interact with the UI. End-to-end (E2E) tests represent the full user journey in a browser but are difficult to set up, hard to troubleshoot when the bug is a visual detail, and can't practically test every state. Between the extremes of unit tests and E2E tests, component tests simulate each component's behavior in a real browser using fixed inputs, offering speed closer to unit tests and user-level coverage closer to E2E. Many teams maintain a thin layer of E2E tests for critical journeys, and they have component tests for the dozens of states a component may be in.

These tools are organized by job so you can stack them rather than choose one winner

These platforms sit on top of your test runner. They capture rendered UI, compare it to approved baselines, and give your team a place to review what changed.

Chromatic is a UI testing and review platform made by the Storybook team. It catches visual, interaction, and accessibility bugs in components and pages before they merge, and it gives developers, designers, and product managers one place to review UI changes and sign off. Chromatic's team is the core maintainer of Storybook, which has about 90,000 GitHub stars and 17 million weekly npm downloads, and a Vitest core maintainer on the team built Chromatic's Vitest integration. Chromatic is used by 45 Fortune 100 companies, including GitHub, Shopify, Microsoft, Adobe, the BBC, and monday.com.

Pricing: Free plan with 5,000 snapshots per month (Chrome only), unlimited projects and users. Starter is $179/month for 35,000 snapshots and adds Safari, Firefox, and Edge. Pro is $399/month for 85,000 snapshots. Enterprise is custom, with SSO, SCIM, SLA support, and data retention. TurboSnap snapshots count as 0.2 of a regular snapshot.

Trade-offs: Chromatic is strongest when your UI is built from components. Teams with no component tests can start from Playwright or Cypress E2E tests, but they'll get the most value once components are covered too. Snapshot usage also grows with each browser and viewport you add, so plan coverage before you scale it.

Best for: Design system teams, product teams that want designers and PMs to approve UI changes, React Native teams, and Vitest-first teams that want visual testing without baselines stored in the repo.

Percy is BrowserStack's visual testing platform. It captures screenshots from your existing tests, renders them across browsers and responsive widths, and highlights pixel differences for review.

Strengths: Framework-agnostic SDKs for Playwright, Cypress, Selenium, and Storybook. App Percy covers native mobile apps. The free plan includes 5,000 screenshots per month with unlimited users and projects.

Trade-offs: Percy is page-oriented, and each page rendered in each browser at each width counts as a separate screenshot, so usage climbs quickly with cross-browser coverage. Percy compares feature branches against a base branch, which teams with complex branching should test early. Reviewers see rendered screenshots rather than an inspectable copy of the code under test, so debugging a diff usually means reproducing it locally.

Pricing: Free tier, then paid plans with fixed screenshot allowances and overage.

Best for: Teams already paying for BrowserStack that want visual checks on page-level E2E tests.

Applitools Eyes uses Visual AI to compare screenshots the way a person would, with match levels that can ignore content changes and focus on layout. Its Ultrafast Grid re-renders captured page states across many browser, viewport, and device combinations.

Strengths: Mature AI matching, broad browser and device coverage, Figma and Storybook testing, accessibility testing, and an MCP server. Higher tiers add AI-driven functional testing and plain-English test authoring.

Trade-offs: Applitools is priced and packaged for enterprises. There's a free trial but no free plan, and the Starter plan is $667/month billed annually for 100,000 component checkpoints or 1,000 page checkpoints. Professional and Enterprise are custom-priced.

Best for: Large QA organizations with big cross-browser matrices and budget for a dedicated visual AI platform.

BackstopJS is a free, open-source visual regression testing tool released under the MIT license. You list the URLs, viewports, and CSS selectors to capture in a config file, and BackstopJS renders them in a headless browser through Playwright or Puppeteer, then compares the results against approved reference screenshots. The core workflow runs on three commands: backstop init, backstop test, and backstop approve.

Strengths: Completely free, with no screenshot limits. A built-in browser report shows reference and test images side by side with a visual diff inspector, and changes can be approved from there. Optional Docker rendering keeps screenshots consistent between laptops and CI; Playwright adds Firefox and WebKit, and click, hover, and keypress selectors capture interactive states. JUnit reports plug into existing CI pipelines.

Trade-offs: BackstopJS is self-hosted, so there's no cloud dashboard, shared team review, or pull request status checks out of the box. Reference screenshots are usually committed to your repository, and every page or component state you want to test needs its own URL and scenario in the config. Someone on the team also has to own the setup, CI integration, and maintenance.

Best for: Developers and small teams with no budget who are comfortable running and maintaining their own visual regression setup.

Test runners click, type, and assert. They're free and open source, and every platform above builds on them. On their own, they offer limited visual testing: built-in screenshot assertions store baselines in your repository, rendering can drift between laptops and CI, and designers have no review interface.

Playwright is Microsoft's open-source browser automation framework. It runs tests across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, with auto-waiting, trace viewer debugging and code generation, and supports JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, and .NET.

Visual testing: Playwright's toHaveScreenshot assertion compares screenshots against baselines stored in Git. It works, but baselines must be regenerated per operating system, and accepting a change means rerunning with an update flag.

Best for: Teams automating critical user journeys such as sign-up, checkout and login. Pair it with a platform like Chromatic for visual review across real browsers.

Cypress is an open-source testing tool that runs inside the browser, with time-travel debugging that shows the app at each step of a test. It supports both E2E and component testing.

Visual testing: Cypress has no built-in visual comparison and relies on plugins or a platform such as Chromatic, Percy or Applitools. Cypress Cloud, its paid service, adds recording, parallelization, flake detection and add-ons for accessibility and UI coverage.

Best for: Frontend developers who want fast feedback and an interactive test runner while they build.

Storybook is the open source workshop for building UI components in isolation. Each story captures one component state, and those stories double as test cases.

Testing features: Interaction tests with play functions and Testing Library, accessibility checks with the a11y addon, and a Vitest integration that runs stories as component tests.

Visual testing: Storybook doesn't diff screenshots on its own. Chromatic, built by the same team, is its visual testing and review layer.

Best for: Design system and component library teams, and any team practicing component-driven development.

Vitest Browser Mode runs component tests in a real browser instead of a simulated DOM, using Playwright or WebdriverIO under the hood.

Visual testing: Vitest's toMatchScreenshot assertion stores screenshots in the repository. For large projects, this can bloat the repo and baselines drift between machines. Chromatic can take Vitest Browser Mode tests with no code changes and run them in a stable cloud environment instead.

Best for: Teams already writing Vitest tests who want them to check how the UI looks without adopting a new framework.

Start from the problem your team is trying to fix:

"Shared component changes keep breaking other teams' screens." Test at the component level with Storybook or Vitest Browser Mode and Chromatic, so the change shows up on the pull request that caused it.

"Our Playwright tests pass, but the layout still breaks in Safari." Functional assertions don't check appearance. Add a visual testing platform that renders in Safari, such as Chromatic, Percy or Applitools.

"We turned off screenshot tests because of false alarms." Look for deterministic component states and flake controls such as Chromatic's SteadySnap, or AI matching such as Applitools.

"Designers find UI bugs after release." Choose a platform with a review and approval workflow, and make sign-off a required pull request check.

"AI coding agents keep inventing components." Give agents access to your real component library, for example through Chromatic's hosted MCP, and run every agent-built change through the same UI tests as human code.

"We have no budget." Use Playwright or Vitest screenshot assertions, self-host BackstopJS, or start on the free tiers of Chromatic or Percy.

A practical, well-covered setup for a React web app looks like this:

Unit tests in Vitest for logic and utilities.

Storybook stories or Vitest Browser Mode tests for every meaningful component state, with interaction tests on key components.

Chromatic running visual, interaction and accessibility tests on those components in Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge on every pull request, with designers assigned as reviewers.

A thin layer of Playwright E2E tests for sign-up, checkout and other critical journeys, also captured in Chromatic so page-level visual changes go through the same review.

This keeps most UI coverage in fast, deterministic component tests, while E2E tests confirm the journeys that matter most still work end to end.

Playwright is the best free tool for E2E UI testing, and Storybook is the best free tool for testing component states. For visual testing, For visual testing, Chromatic and Percy both offer free tiers of around 5,000 snapshots or screenshots per month, and BackstopJS is free to self-host.

UI testing is the broad practice of checking that an interface works for users, including functional, visual and accessibility checks. Visual testing is one part of it: comparing rendered UI against approved baselines to catch unintended changes in layout, color, typography and spacing.

No. Chromatic was built by the Storybook team, but it also runs visual tests from Vitest Browser Mode, Playwright and Cypress tests, and from React Native Storybook on iOS and Android simulators.

Playwright's toHaveScreenshot covers basic visual checks, but baselines live in your repo, rendering can differ between machines, and there's no review interface for designers. Teams with several reviewers or many browsers usually add a platform on top.

Most teams use both. Component tests cover individual UI states quickly and reliably, while a smaller set of E2E tests confirms that critical user journeys work across the whole app.

#10395. SyGra: The One-Stop Framework for Building Data for LLMs and SLMs

When we think about building a model - be it a Large Language Model (LLM) or a Small Language Model (SLM) - the first thing we need is data. While a vast amount of open data is available, it rarely comes in the exact format required to train or align models. In practice, we often face scenarios where the raw data isn't enough. We need data that is more structured, domain-specific, complex, or aligned with the task at hand. Let's look at some common situations:

You start with a simple dataset, but the model fails on advanced reasoning tasks. How do you generate more complex datasets to strengthen performance?

You already have a knowledge base, but it's not in Q&A format. How can you transform it into a usable question-answering dataset?

You've prepared a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) dataset. But now you want to align your model using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). How can you generate preference pairs?

You have a Q&A dataset, but the questions are shallow. How can you create in-depth, multi-turn, or reasoning-heavy questions?

You possess a massive corpus but need to filter and curate data for mid-training on a specific domain.

Your data lives in PDFs or images, and you need to convert them into structured documents for building a Q&A system.

You already have reasoning datasets, but want to push models toward better "thinking tokens" for step-by-step problem-solving.

Not all data is good data. How do you automatically filter out poor-quality samples and keep only the high-value ones?

Your dataset has small chunks of context, but you want to build larger-context datasets optimized for RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) pipelines.

You have German datasets but need to translate, adapt, and repurpose them into English Q&A systems. And the list goes on. The needs around data building never end when working with modern AI models.

This is where SyGra comes in. SyGra is a low-code/no-code framework designed to simplify dataset creation, transformation, and alignment for LLMs and SLMs. Instead of writing complex scripts and pipelines, you can focus on prompt engineering, while SyGra takes care of the heavy lifting. Key Features of SyGra:

Data is the foundation of AI. The quality, diversity, and structure of your data often matter more than model architecture tweaks. By enabling flexible and scalable dataset creation, SyGra helps teams:

Note: An example implementation can be found at https://github.com/ServiceNow/SyGra/blob/main/docs/tutorials/image_to_qna_tutorial.md

Few Example Task https://github.com/ServiceNow/SyGra/tree/main/tasks/examples

The journey of building and refining datasets never ends. Each use case brings new challenges - from translation and knowledge base conversion to reasoning enhancement and domain filtering. With SyGra, you don't have to reinvent the wheel every time. Instead, you get a unified framework that empowers you to generate, filter, and align data for your models - so you can focus on what really matters: building smarter AI systems.

#10392. Smol2Operator: Post-Training GUI Agents for Computer Use

TL;DR: This work shows how a lightweight vision–language model can acquire GUI-grounded skills and evolve into an agentic GUI coder. We release all training recipes, data-processing tools, resulting model, demo and datasets to enable full reproducibility and foster further research 🫡. Find the collection here.

Graphical User Interface (GUI) automation is one of the most challenging frontiers in computer vision. Developing models that see and interact with user interfaces enables AI agents to navigate mobile, desktop, and web platforms. This will reshape the future of digital interaction.

In this blog post, we present a comprehensive approach to training vision-language models for GUI automation through a multi-phase training strategy. We demonstrate how to transform a model with zero grounding capabilities into an agentic coder capable of understanding and interacting with graphical interfaces.

Rather than aiming for a SOTA model, our goal is to demonstrate the entire process, from data processing to model training, and, in doing so, show how to unlock GUI-grounding capabilities in VLMs.

GUI capabilities combine understanding of the interface and precise element localization. These abilities enable the model to translate high-level tasks into low-level GUI actions such as clicking, typing, …

Our approach leverages SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct as the baseline model, a small powerful vision-language model that initially has no grounding capabilities for GUI tasks. This makes it an ideal candidate to demonstrate the effectiveness of our training methodology. Through our two-phase training process, we first instill grounding capabilities in the model, then enhance it with agentic reasoning abilities using Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT).

We evaluate our approach on an established perception benchmark: ScreenSpot-v2, which tests the model’s ability to understand and locate elements within screenshots. Our process is inspired by the AGUVIS paper, and we leverage their carefully curated datasets to build upon their foundational work.

Evolution of ScreenSpot-v2 performance during the training phase of the base model SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct.

This section explains how we convert heterogeneous GUI actions format from multiple datasets into a single unified format. By standardizing function names, signatures, and parameters, we create consistent, high-quality data that forms the foundation for effective model training.

One of the primary challenges when working with multiple GUI automation datasets is the lack of standardization in action representations. Different datasets use varying function signatures, parameter naming conventions, and action taxonomies, making it difficult to train a unified model across diverse data sources.

We took the open-source datasets (xlangai/aguvis-stage1, xlangai/aguvis-stage2), originally used by AGUVIS, and implemented a comprehensive data transformation pipeline to create a unified action space. Our approach involved:

Here are real examples from our action conversion system (preprocessing/action_conversion.py) showing how we transform heterogeneous action representations into our unified format (grounding coordinates normalized to [0,1]):

Before (Original Action Dataset Formats):

This unification process was essential for creating coherent training data that allows the model to learn consistent action patterns across diverse GUI environments.

To maximize flexibility for different use cases, we developed the Action Space Converter (utils/action_space_converter.py), a tool that allows users to easily adapt from an action space to their own custom action vocabularies and naming conventions.

You can use this tool to transform one action signature (function names, parameter names, and parameter value changes, ...) into another:

This tool enables researchers and practitioners to:

The Action Space Converter is particularly valuable for preparing datasets for training, as it ensures consistent action vocabularies across different deployment environments while maintaining compatibility with existing automation frameworks.

Through this pipeline, we transform the open-source datasets xlangai/aguvis-stage1, xlangai/aguvis-stage2 into our unified action space (see here). The output of this process is released as two new fully formatted datasets: smolagents/aguvis-stage-1 and smolagents/aguvis-stage-2.

Phase 1 leverages the smolagents/aguvis-stage-1 dataset, which introduces GUI grounding by pairing low-level instructions with diverse executable actions (expressed in code form). For example, a user/assistant turn in smolagents/aguvis-stage-1 follows the structure:

Each sample links a screenshot with multi-turn user/assistant interactions, enabling the model to learn fine-grained action grounding across dialogue turns. During fine-tuning, the data collator masks everything except the assistant’s answers when computing the loss.

Before proceeding with full-scale Phase 1 training, we conducted comprehensive ablation studies to determine optimal training configurations

We experimented with different image sizes and coordinate representation systems to identify the optimal configuration for SmolVLM2:

Some SOTA GUI VLMs (e.g., Qwen-VL) appear also to use a different normalized range (0–1000), which was not tested in this experiment.

Table 1: Baseline on HuggingFaceTB/SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct (400k samples, aguvis-stage-1). Higher is better.

As demonstrated in our benchmark results, SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct base initially achieved 0% performance on perception benchmarks like ScreenSpot-v2. This complete lack of grounding capability provided us with a clean slate to evaluate the effectiveness of our training methodology.

From our experiments, we determined that:

Using the optimal configuration (1152px resolution with normalized coordinates), we trained for 2 epochs on the smolagents/aguvis-stage-1 dataset. The results were remarkable, +41% improvement over baseline on ScreenSpot-v2

This dramatic improvement demonstrates that our Phase 1 training successfully instilled fundamental grounding capabilities in the model, enabling it to understand and locate visual elements within screenshots.

Table 2: Baseline on HuggingFaceTB/SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct (2 epochs, aguvis-stage-1).

Whereas Phase 1 provided grounding capabilities, Phase 2 targets agentic reasoning, the ability to deliberate and plan before acting. This stage transforms the model from a reactive system identifying GUI elements into a proactive agent capable of executing complex, multi-step interactions.

Phase 2 uses the smolagents/aguvis-stage-2 dataset, which introduces agentic scenarios:

Explicit reasoning about upcoming actions

Context consistency across multiple interaction steps

High-level instructions require multi-step, low-level actions.

For example, the smolagents/aguvis-stage-2 chat message is like this:

Each sample links a screenshot with a system/user/assistant turn. During fine-tuning, the data collator masks everything except the assistant’s answers when computing the loss.

Starting from the Phase 1 checkpoint (1152 px resolution, normalized coordinates), we fine-tuned the model for two epochs on smolagents/aguvis-stage-2. The accuracy on ScreenSpot-v2 increased from 41% to 61%, indicating that explicit reasoning improves GUI grounding performance.

Table 2: Baseline on HuggingFaceTB/SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct after Phase 1 finetuning (2 epochs, aguvis-stage-1).

All training code, data processing pipelines, datasets and model are open-source!

Our experiments demonstrate that high-quality, reasoning-oriented data can substantially improve GUI grounding, even for small VLMs, using only supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Beyond raw performance gains, these results show that the GUI grounding capabilities are largely determined by the quality of the data. Carefully curated datasets teach models the structure and semantics of user interfaces, providing the grounding needed for accurate action prediction.

To support the development of GUI agents, we’re open-sourcing everything: our complete pipeline, datasets, and trained model. You can reproduce our results, experiment with different models and architectures, or adapt our approach to new domains. The future of agentic AI depends on researchers like you pushing these boundaries further!

While SFT excels at supervised tasks, emerging methods such as Reinforcement Learning (RL) or Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) help develop stronger reasoning capabilities and enable real-time adaptation. These advances point toward a new generation of GUI agents that learn and improve through interaction rather than relying solely on static datasets.

#10391. Build Live Video Chat With WebRTC: From First Call to Production Debugging

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Adding real-time video to a web app used to mean plugins, proprietary SDKs and a lot of money. Today every modern browser ships with WebRTC, a set of APIs that lets two browsers exchange audio, video and data directly. The catch is that WebRTC gives you building blocks, not a finished feature. This guide walks through those blocks in the order you actually need them, with the exact API calls you need, and then covers the production issues that tutorials usually skip.

A browser-to-browser call has four moving parts:

Start with the local preview. Browsers only allow camera access on HTTPS or localhost, so serve your page accordingly.

1.     Request a stream with navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia(), passing video constraints (an ideal width of 1280 and height of 720 is a sensible default) and audio constraints with echoCancellation and noiseSuppression enabled.

2.     Assign the returned MediaStream to the srcObject property of your local video element.

3.     Keep a reference to the stream, because you will add its tracks to the peer connection later.

Set the muted and playsinline attributes on the local video element. Without muted users hear themselves, and without playsinline iOS Safari opens the video full screen.

The peers need a way to find each other. A tiny Node.js server using the ws package is enough for development. Its whole job is to relay messages between the peers in a room:

1.     Create a WebSocket server (for example with the ws package) listening on its own port.

2.     Keep a map of room names to the set of sockets in each room.

3.     When a client sends a join message, store the room name on the socket and add it to that room's set.

4.     For every other message type, forward the raw message to the other sockets in the same room, and never echo it back to the sender.

5.     On disconnect, remove the socket from its room so stale peers do not receive messages.

In production you would add authentication, limit room size to two for one-to-one calls, and validate message types, but the shape stays the same.

Both sides create an RTCPeerConnection, add their local tracks and listen for the remote ones:

1.     Create a new RTCPeerConnection with an iceServers list that contains at least one STUN server.

2.     Loop over the local stream's tracks and call addTrack() for each one.

3.     In the ontrack handler, attach the first remote stream to your remote video element.

4.     In the onicecandidate handler, send every new candidate to the other peer through your signalling channel as a candidate message.

One peer creates an offer, the other answers, and both apply each other's descriptions. Candidates arrive asynchronously in the background.

1.     The caller runs createOffer(), applies it with setLocalDescription() and sends the description as an offer message.

2.     The callee applies the offer with setRemoteDescription(), runs createAnswer(), applies it locally and sends it back as an answer.

3.     The caller applies the answer with setRemoteDescription().

4.     Both sides pass every incoming candidate message to addIceCandidate().

If both peers might start a call at the same time, look up the "perfect negotiation" pattern on MDN. It assigns one side as polite and resolves offer collisions cleanly instead of leaving both peers stuck.

On a home network, STUN alone often works. On corporate Wi-Fi, mobile carriers and symmetric NATs it frequently does not, and the call silently fails to connect. A TURN server relays media when a direct path is impossible. The open-source coturn server is the usual choice.

In practice, your iceServers list should contain your own STUN URL plus a TURN URL with a username and credential, so the browser can fall back to the relay automatically when direct connectivity fails.

Generate short-lived TURN credentials on your backend rather than hard-coding them, and budget for bandwidth: relayed calls pass every frame through your server.

Users deny camera access, unplug headsets and switch from Wi-Fi to 4G mid-call. Catch NotAllowedError and show a clear explanation, listen for devicechange events, and use RTCRtpSender.replaceTrack() to swap cameras without renegotiating the whole call.

Listen to pc.onconnectionstatechange. When the state becomes disconnected, wait a few seconds before giving up, because it often recovers. On failed, call pc.restartIce() to try new network paths.

Use RTCRtpSender.setParameters() to cap the bitrate on weak connections, and read pc.getStats() to monitor packet loss and round-trip time. Showing a small "poor connection" indicator does more for perceived quality than any codec tweak.

Mesh calls, where every participant connects to every other, work for two or three people. Beyond that, upload bandwidth explodes. Group calls need a Selective Forwarding Unit (SFU) such as mediasoup, LiveKit or Janus, which receives each stream once and forwards it to the others.

Tutorials end at a working demo, but the fastest way to understand what production WebRTC looks like is to watch a real call from the inside. Chrome ships an internal diagnostics page that shows every peer connection the browser opens, and it works on any site that uses WebRTC.

1.     Open chrome://webrtc-internals in one tab and keep it open.

2.     In another tab, start a call on your own demo and find its RTCPeerConnection entry.

3.     Expand that entry and look at the ICE candidate pairs: you will see whether the call went direct (host or srflx) or through a TURN relay (relay).

4.     Open the stats graphs for the outbound video stream and watch the bitrate, frame rate and resolution adapt when you throttle the network in DevTools.

5.     Check the negotiated codec and how quickly the connection recovers when you switch Wi-Fi off and back on.

Once you can read your own call, repeat the exercise on a production service. Any browser-based product works, whether a meeting tool or a live video chat that pairs two visitors, because webrtc-internals shows the same data for every site. Expect differences from your demo: more candidate pairs, a relay candidate in the list and a bitrate that adapts faster. Seeing them makes the earlier sections concrete, from why TURN matters to how bandwidth estimation reacts to packet loss.

The one-to-one call above is the core of many products, from telehealth consultations and tutoring to customer support. The engineering challenges grow with the use case: random matching needs queueing and presence on the signalling server, public platforms need moderation and reporting, and global audiences need TURN servers in several regions.

Start with the minimal version, get it working across Chrome, Firefox and Safari on both desktop and mobile, and add TURN before real users arrive. Once the call is reliable, every other feature becomes a much easier problem.

#10390. Which 2026 Samsung Galaxy Tab should you buy?

Samsung has a huge lineup of Galaxy tablets to choose from right now, and they’re all a little different.

The Galaxy Tab S12+ is the Samsung tablet to choose for a premium mix of entertainment, creativity, and productivity. The Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra gives you an even bigger canvas, while the Galaxy Tab S11 brings flagship features to a more portable size. For everyday value, start with the Galaxy Tab S10 FE series or the affordable Galaxy Tab A11+.

Samsung’s tablet lineup covers everything from watching a show on the couch to sketching your next project or getting work done between meetings. The right choice comes down to what you want that extra screen to do.

With options across a wide range of price points, Samsung has a Galaxy tablet for different needs and budgets this holiday season.

Here’s a list of the main Galaxy Tab options available in 2026, from family-friendly entertainment to Samsung’s largest creative workspace:

Screen size is only one part of the whole story. The Galaxy Tab S11, S12+, and S12 Ultra have AMOLED displays that offer rich contrast for movies and photos, while the FE models provide useful everyday features at a more accessible price.

The Galaxy Tab S12+ is the sweet spot if you want a serious upgrade over a basic tablet without moving to Samsung’s biggest screen.

As we covered in our Galaxy Tab S12 launch story, it combines a 12.6-inch 120Hz AMOLED display with a MediaTek Dimensity 9500 processor, 12GB of RAM, and an included S Pen, with four months of complimentary Adobe Photoshop access and a six-month Notability trial, both of which support the stylus.

The S12+ is easy to use and appreciate in daily life. It puts reference material beside your notes during a course, sketch ideas for a presentation, while making it easy to settle into a movie after finishing your email. It has room to spread out without requiring the Ultra’s larger footprint.

The Galaxy Tab S12+ also offers a 5G version, making it worth considering if you regularly work away from Wi-Fi.

Buy the Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra when the screen itself is the upgrade you’ll enjoy every day.

The Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra is made for creative professionals and families seeking premium entertainment. It moves naturally between focused creative work and immersive movie nights at home.

Its 14.6-inch AMOLED display gives photos, drawings, and multiple app windows more breathing room. Picture reviewing a document while keeping your handwritten notes visible, or drawing with reference images alongside your canvas.

The Ultra shares the S12+’s Dimensity 9500 processor but offers configurations up to 16GB of RAM and 1TB of storage. It’s available for $1,399.99, but last year’s Tab S11 Ultra is on sale during Black Friday for just $899.99.

Both S12 tablets ship with Android 17-based One UI 9 and seven years of OS and security updates. Photoshop comes pre-installed with a four-month access offer, giving you a way to explore S Pen-assisted photo editing.

The Ultra is especially appealing with a keyboard at a desk; Samsung’s Ultra Book Cover Keyboard Slim is the perfect companion to the S12 Ultra, and is on sale for $146.99 during Best Buy’s Black Friday Deal event.

Yes, the Galaxy Tab S11 is the premium Galaxy tablet to choose when portability comes first.

Our Galaxy Tab S11 launch coverage highlighted the return of Samsung’s smaller flagship tablet, with a Dimensity 9400+ processor, 12GB of RAM, and an included S Pen. Its 11-inch AMOLED screen makes it an attractive companion for reading, travel, and handwritten notes.

The Galaxy Tab S11 is the sort of tablet you can bring to a meeting or pull out on a train without needing a large work surface. You still get premium display quality, just in a size that’s easier to carry, and it comes in at a lower price.

A discounted Tab S11 Ultra can also be worth considering if you want a 14.6-inch screen. Compare the actual price with the S12 Ultra rather than dismissing an older flagship automatically.

The Galaxy Tab S10 FE and FE+ are compelling choices for people who want an included S Pen without flagship pricing.

Choose the 10.9-inch FE for a study companion that travels easily. Choose the 13.1-inch FE+ when you’d rather put a lecture, document, or recipe beside your notes. Both offer IP68 water and dust resistance, so they’re great kitchen companions.

Galaxy Tab S10 Lite is for students, children, and emerging creators. It is a practical, encouraging gift for handwritten learning, organization, drawing, and experimentation.

The Galaxy Tab A11+ is the straightforward entertainment choice. At $199, it’s the cheapest of the Galaxy Tab options, but it doesn’t support the S Pen, so choose an S-series model if handwriting matters.

Choose the Galaxy Tab S12+ for a premium all-rounder, the S12 Ultra for a spacious creative workspace, or the S11 for flagship features in a travel-friendly size.

For school, home projects, and everyday notes, the FE series delivers the features many people actually need. For family streaming and browsing, the A11+ keeps things simple and affordable.

The best Galaxy Tab isn’t automatically the biggest or newest. It’s the one that makes the things you already love doing easier — and gives you a few new possibilities along the way.

swift-transformers is a Swift library that aims to reduce the friction for developers that want to work with local models on Apple Silicon platforms, including iPhones. It includes the missing pieces that are not provided by Core ML or MLX alone, but that are required to work with local inference. Namely, it provides the following components:

Most of the time people use the Tokenizers or Hub modules, and frequently both. Some notable projects that rely on swift-transformers include:

Version 1.0 signals stability in the package. Developers are building apps on swift-transformers, and this first major release recognizes those use cases and brings the version number in line with that reality. It also provides the foundation on which to iterate with the community to build the next set of features. These are some of our preferred updates:

Version 1.0 comes with breaking API changes. However, we don’t expect major problems if you are a user of Tokenizers or Hub. If you use the Core ML components of the library, please get in touch so we can support you during transition. We’ll prepare a migration guide and add it to the documentation.

We are also extremely excited about agentic use in general and MCP in particular. We think that exposure of system resources to local workflows would be 🚀

#10387. TSMC’s $22.6 billion Texas plan wouldn’t make 2nm-or-better chips until 2031

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Reviews, benchmarks, and updates on current GPUs.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

The filing lists an in-fab mask shop and $14 billion of tools and equipment, most budgeted for 2030.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

TSMC has made an application for a new fab and campus near College Station, Brazos County, Texas. The proposed fab would be just one county over from Terafab, would likely share supply chains, and would be positioned to make 2nm-class chips by 2031, with the $22.6 billion plan detailing how the Taiwanese chipmaker is planning to expand its U.S. operations. An application under Texas’s Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation (JETI) program for a school property-tax limit shows TSMC is weighing a new fab site. The fab wouldn’t make 2nm or more advanced chips until 2031, six years after 2nm volume production began in Taiwan. It would come with a school-tax break valued at around $354 million.

This would be the company’s “second campus” for advanced chipmaking in the U.S. and the first outside Arizona. The Comptroller has recommended the tax application for approval, which the school district and the governor still have to grant. The application comes from TSMC Arizona Corporation, which is TSMC’s subsidiary located in Phoenix. Construction is projected to start in 2027, but the plan remains under evaluation, and nothing in the filing commits TSMC to buy the land or to build on it.

TSMC is looking to build out more in the U.S. because most of its large customers are based there and the government has been “very helpful” in pursuing additional fab capacity, Chairman and CEO C.C. Wei said in October. Texas is one option for expanding beyond Arizona, though the filing doesn’t say what drew TSMC there. TSMC judges each site on its tax environment, workforce availability, utility capacity and cost, and site and infrastructure readiness, as well as its “long-term scalability and expansion potential.” TSMC says Arizona offers “established operational efficiencies and lower capital risk,” and that the tax incentive would aid this further.

TSMC has “nearly 20 fabs worldwide in progress,” Wei said on the October earnings call, including 13 leading-edge and advanced packaging fabs in Taiwan and “another five to six fabs overseas.” Annual capacity for its 2nm (N2) family is expected to more than double in 2027. TSMC also expects more of its fabs to be ramping up in the U.S.

Texas wouldn’t begin commercial operations until 2031, and the economic model filed with the plan doesn’t have it at full operations until 2032. By contrast, the second fab in Arizona is expected to begin volume production in Q3 2027, but at 3nm. In Taiwan, N2 has been in high-volume production since Q4 2025. TSMC expects A14, its next full node after N2, to enter risk production in 2027 and volume in 2028. By 2031, A14 is set to have been in volume production for about three years, so a Texas fab that starts on 2nm would be at least a generation behind TSMC’s leading edge. Taiwan has also debated limits on how advanced TSMC’s overseas fabs can be.

A16 (a 2nm-family node) volume production

2nm “and/or more advanced,” commercial operations

The new site would have one or more fabs but, as it stands, Brazos County’s announcement describes one. For scale, we’ve estimated that a single 2nm-class module with about 20,000 wafer starts a month costs $25 billion to $35 billion, so this plan’s $22.6 billion budget falls below the low end of that range.

The price tag is split in multiple ways, with $8.60 billion for buildings and other real property, while 62% of the total, or $14.02 billion, is for tooling, machinery and equipment, a category that on the filing’s list also covers power, HVAC, cleanroom, water and gas systems. The building's spending would come first, in 2027, 2028, and 2029 alone. Tool spending would begin in that last year and peak at $9.05 billion in 2030, with about 65% of the tool budget landing in that year, before ending at $963.9 million in 2032 — the form’s Schedule A stops at 2031 and $21.66 billion total.

The tool spending schedule lines up with a change in how TSMC prints its chips. Lithography, the step in the chipmaking process that uses light to project circuit patterns onto the wafer, requires advanced machines. The most advanced do it with extreme ultraviolet (EUV) light. High-NA EUV tools have a higher numerical aperture, gathering more light to print finer features in one pass. Wei said TSMC intends to use High-NA in 2030, which matches the 2030 peak in Texas tool spending, but that is a company-wide plan, and nothing in the Texas plan gives a delivery schedule or names High-NA tools specifically.

What the plan does spell out is its list of eligible property: fab and central utility plant buildings, cleanroom systems, ultra-pure water and wastewater treatment with water-reclaim systems, bulk and specialty gas as well as automated material handling, and gas-insulated switchgear.

Also named is mask or reticle shop equipment as well as lithography, etch, deposition, implant, chemical mechanical planarization (CMP), diffusion, and clean/wet tools, by type, although the list names no tool vendors, EUV counts, or wafer capacity. The mask shop is highlighted as “co-located within the fab and integral to the manufacturing process.” Masks are patterned plates used by a lithography tool to project their patterns onto each wafer, one per chip layer, and every new design needs its own set. Making them on site suggests the fab is meant to stand on its own. Wei also said TSMC is working with ASML on a 12-inch photomask by 2031, which is the year the Texas site would open.

The plan’s location is in Brazos County, Texas, sited across 86 parcels and almost 3,232 acres of land, which is about five square miles. This compares to TSMC’s Phoenix campus at about 1,078 acres on the county tax roll, with about 902 more purchased in January; this leaves the Texas site at about 1.6 times that total. TSMC would build and manage the site, which sets it apart from Terafab, a fab a TSMC customer is planning one county over: Wei has confirmed talks about using its capacity but said any such fab would have to be run by TSMC.

Residents in development areas for fabs and data centers tend to raise two concerns, and both are related to utility usage. The first is power: a local report says Bryan Texas Utilities provides that for the proposed area, but it’s unclear who would serve the fab. For scale, a utility filing in Arizona reportedly puts TSMC’s built-out Phoenix campus at about 1.9 gigawatts, a figure for the whole campus, not a single fab.

The second is water: Wellborn Special Utility District reportedly provides service, while the developer is said to intend to buy its water from a third party instead. As a comparison, a state document on an unnamed company’s $45 billion, two-fab project in Sherman, as reported by the Dallas Business Journal, lists 8 to 10 million gallons a day to start with a peak at 20 to 25 million after buildout, but this isn’t a 1:1. That project is targeting production in Q4 2029.

Economic impacts are a significant part of the deal: the plan projects 2,099 direct jobs by 2030, while the agreement would require only 35, the legal minimum. Pay, on the other hand, comes with a projected average salary nearly double the wage level that would need clearing.

Texas appears willing to work with TSMC on this, with a recommendation for approval signed by Deputy Comptroller Noah Betz this week. The gross tax benefit would build over 14 years, starting four years before the formal incentive period, and would cut the district’s maintenance and operations (M&O) levy on the project nearly in half. Even so, the full $354.1 million is only 1.6% of the $22.6 billion investment. In return, TSMC would have to post a performance bond equal to 10% of the benefit.

The Comptroller believes the incentive is a compelling factor — TSMC would not invest in Texas without it — but the office says it has not audited or verified the company’s projections. TSMC, for its part, calls the limit “determinative.”

Minimum average wage for the project’s jobs

9,841 a year on average; 18,134 at the 2029 peak

Tax benefit during construction, 2028–2031

Tax benefit in the incentive period, 2032–2041

School M&O tax over 20 years, without the agreement

School M&O tax over 20 years, with the agreement

A potentially far larger incentive is federal: a tax credit worth 35 cents back to every qualifying dollar spent, as long as construction technically begins before the end of the year. “Qualified” means the cost of the fab’s depreciable physical property that is integral to running the fab, meaning the buildings and the tools, in the year each goes into service, and “construction” means actual physical work of a significant nature or paying or incurring at least 5% of the qualifying property’s cost, with work continuing afterward. Construction here is projected to start in 2027, after that cutoff, though off-site work under a binding written contract or early spending this year could still count, and an extension has been proposed in the Senate.

The land doesn’t count in this equation, and neither does office space. This is also a credit off the tax bill, dollar for dollar, not a deduction. The rate was 25% under the 2022 CHIPS Act and rose to 35% for property placed in service after 2025. If the full $22.6 billion qualified, that would be about $7.9 billion back, but not every dollar qualifies.

If Texas doesn’t work out, TSMC is also considering “a new land parcel in Arizona,” which would be closer to the existing North Phoenix site. TSMC says that may make many things easier, such as handling a workforce and the logistics, with the ability to use existing suppliers and relationships on known infrastructure. This is an incentive for the state of Texas to give the tax break.

The tax agreement needs approval from both the College Station ISD board and the governor. The district also owns one of the parcels on TSMC’s list for the site: almost 91 acres, with a 24,496-square-foot building from 2024. The board has set a public hearing for Dec. 10, with public comment, and could approve the project’s reinvestment zone that day.

The district has 30 days from the day it receives the application, which puts its deadline in late December. As for Brazos County, town halls could reportedly begin as early as the first week of December, though the county has promised only one, “in the near future.”

Assuming things move forward, the real measure begins with the first phase on land. Even if production arrives a generation late, it would be a positive development for U.S.-based chipmaking.

#10386. Claude rolling out updated Android app with Material 3 Expressive redesign

Anthropic is rolling out a new Claude app for Android that picks up a Material 3 Expressive redesign.

Confirmed on Twitter/X by Anthropic Product Manager Robert Bye, Claude is now rolling out a Material 3 Expressive redesign for its Android app that, while not a full embrace of Google’s design language, does make a clear attempt to better fit in on Android.

The updated design picks up a bottom-bar UI as opposed to relying fully on the old hamburger menu – it still exists, but it’s mainly for chat history now. You can see M3 elements throughout the app, including in the model switcher and the background of chats. It’s clearly themed to match Anthropic’s aesthetic, and there’s no obvious implementation of Material You colors, but it all fits within the general Material 3 guidelines – much more so than the original app.

The one flaw we spotted was the predictive back implementation, which gets a neat animation to move the search bar but is supposed to show a preview of the previous screen, but that’s just nit-picking, really.

The new Claude app for Android is rolling out now.
